title: A Privacy Company Just Saved the Clearest Flock Surveillance Map I’ve Seen
snippet: The creator of Proton Mail now hosts a powerful, professional Flock camera mapping tool on its site.
fullText:
A powerful, free Flock surveillance-tracking platform is now hosted by Proton, the creator of Proton Mail and Proton VPN. The move provides extra technical and legal protection for the interactive mapping tool, which Flock has repeatedly attempted to shut down through legal threats.

The deal, announced on Wednesday, gives the public access to a free database of Flock Safety’s automated license plate readers and AI surveillance cameras across the US.

Security researcher Joshua Michael first published the interactive map in September before facing a swift trademark complaint from Flock. Despite Flock’s demands for its removal, the map remains publicly accessible.

			

More from CNET

Flock’s surveillance networks capture license plates, vehicle details, human physical characteristics, and audio signals such as gunshots or shouting. While law enforcement agencies use this data to track and search suspects, privacy advocates warn that the technology enables widespread, unchecked tracking.

Proton also says the map shows far more Flock cameras are active than Flock currently says it has. Flock said this summer that it operates more than 120,000 cameras nationwide, but the tool says there are more than 214,000 Flock devices in service, with more than 80,000 in the planning stages. 

A representative from Flock Safety didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The map is one of the most usable Flock tools I’ve seen. Proton’s Flock tool has better visual clarity, faster search responses and a more intuitive interface than other sites I’ve tried and is available without a subscription to other Proton services.

I searched my own city, which canceled its Flock contact over a year ago. The map accurately reported that no active Flock cameras are currently present, but correctly located decommissioned Flock cams. Since the data is based on Flock’s own reporting, I place more trust in it than in crowdsourced tools like the Deflock app, which are subject to errors or misrepresentation.

Proton’s tool is striking to look at and simple to use.Proton

“My research on FlockSurveillance.org documents cybersecurity failures with national-security consequences,” map creator Joshua Michael told CNET. “My research argued that Flock Safety could not detect exports of their data and that because they hold data on nearly every American and their pattern of life, they are a national security threat to our country and people.”

Michael said Flock has “promised to take every measure possible to take my research offline,” he said, offering that as one reason why Proton moved to preserve the map in its Swiss servers. Switzerland enforces some of the world’s strongest privacy laws. Proton’s site notes that under Swiss data protection regulations, the company isn’t required to comply with requests that are not supported by a Swiss court order. Flock is a US-based company.

Camera locations are constantly changing, meaning a surveillance map could rapidly become dated.

“If new and reliable data becomes available, then we will update the map,” a Proton spokesperson told me. “We’re committed to keeping the public informed of all forms of surveillance where reliable data can be sourced.” 

Another surveillance mapping option

While Proton’s map provides a specialized, point-in-time look at Flock Safety’s network, the Atlas of Surveillance offers a broader, historical catalog of the sweeping technologies US law enforcement agencies have quietly adopted over the years. 

Powered by a network of volunteers who analyze public data and official government records, the Atlas database tracks everything from automated license plate readers to cell-site simulators and body-worn cameras. The project continuously updates its findings.

title: Recursive launches Flint, a laptop coding model it says was largely built by AI
snippet: Startup Recursive has released Flint, a free, laptop-sized coding model built largely by its own AI research system, as an early test of AI that improves itself.
fullText:
Recursive, an AI startup founded last year, is starting to live up to its name. The company, which is trying to build AI that can improve itself, released its first model, Flint, on Wednesday. Flint is a free coding model that can run on a laptop and was built largely with the help of AI.

Recursive’s automated research system, which it calls the Eureka Machine, helped with nearly every step of Flint’s development, the company says. That let a small team build the model from scratch in under four months.

Flint is an early public test of recursive self-improvement: the idea that AI can build better AI, which in turn builds even better AI. It’s also one of the most debated ideas in the industry. Some researchers fear that AI improving itself could slip out of human control. For now, Recursive’s version is more limited: an AI research assistant overseen by people that produced a model small enough for a laptop.

The company emerged from stealth in May with $650 million in funding at a $4.65 billion valuation, from backers including GV, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Recursive is led by CEO Richard Socher, Salesforce’s former chief scientist.

Because Flint runs on a user’s own computer rather than a company’s cloud servers, developers can use it offline, keep their code private, and avoid the usage fees that AI cloud services charge based on how much text the model processes. The model is free to download on Hugging Face, the popular site for sharing AI models, under the Apache 2.0 license, an open source license that allows free use and modification. 

Flint is a mixture-of-experts model, meaning it uses only a small slice of itself for any given task: just 2.5 billion of its 40 billion settings, known as parameters, at a time. That makes it light enough for an ordinary laptop and far smaller than Meta’s Muse Spark Open, an open model built for Macs that was released last week. Muse Spark Open uses 816 billion parameters and needs at least a terabyte of memory. 

Flint is also fast. In Recursive’s tests, it generated about 131 tokens (chunks of text) per second on a MacBook Pro with Apple’s M4 Pro chip — roughly twice the 58 to 69 tokens per second that similar models managed on the same machine, including Google’s Gemma 4 and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. On Nvidia’s RTX Spark, Flint topped 150 tokens per second.

On SWE-Bench Verified, a benchmark that measures how well AI can fix real-world software bugs, Flint outperformed other models under 50 billion parameters. On Recursive’s own average across six tests, only one model, Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 27B, scored higher than Flint.

The company acknowledged that Flint would need more guidance than the big paid coding assistants and suggested breaking large tasks into smaller steps. Still, early reviews were positive. Wired’s Will Knight used Flint on a Mac with 48GB of memory to build several small programs, including a to-do list app and a tool that scours the web for research. He found that smaller coding models often ran into errors or were slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed his coding requests every time. 

The Eureka Machine comes up with ideas, runs experiments, and uses the results to decide what to try next. According to the company’s launch video, it contributed to nearly every part of building Flint, from pretraining to post-training and inference. 

Recursive said that Eureka’s contributions include a sparser model shape, low-bit training that shrank Flint by 71% with almost no loss in quality and custom kernels, which are specialized programs that speed up the underlying computations.

Recursive didn’t say how much time the Eureka Machine saved its researchers, but it’s not alone in leaning on AI to do research. OpenAI said last month that by mid-August, its AI agents were logging 3.1 workdays for every one worked by a human researcher.

If Recursive’s bet pays off, each new model should be able to take on longer stretches of work without human help. The company previously told TechCrunch that its $410 million compute deal with Amazon Web Services in June was “less about headcount and more about agent count.”

The longer-term goal, Socher told Wired, is for the Eureka Machine to achieve full recursive self-improvement, with humans overseeing the process and able to stop it if something goes wrong. Recursive says each new model should make the Eureka Machine a better researcher, helping it build the next one faster.

title: While Amazon blocks AI agents, Walmart rolls out the welcome mat
snippet: As Amazon blocks AI agents from shopping on its site, Walmart is taking the opposite approach, introducing new technology that lets AI agents make purchases on customers' behalf, with controls over spending and transaction approvals.
fullText:
Walmart is embracing agentic commerce with the launch of its own Agent Gateway to manage transactions and other new features aimed at customers using AI agents, the retailer announced on Wednesday. The move comes shortly after Walmart’s top competitor, Amazon, began blocking AI agents from making purchases on behalf of online shoppers.

The company’s embrace of AI technology differentiates it from other online businesses, including not only Amazon but also various travel and booking sites, which have responded to the growing consumer adoption of AI agents by locking them out of their websites completely. Walmart, on the other hand, had already announced a partnership with a leading agent in the space, Meta’s Muse, and offers integrations with popular AI apps like ChatGPT, Gemini, and others.

Now it’s expanding on those efforts with more technology to prepare for a world where AI agents become mainstream, said Walmart president and CEO John Furner, speaking at the Masters of Scale Summit in San Francisco on Wednesday. The technology will support agentic shopping from both Walmart and the company’s discount warehouse, Sam’s Club.

It starts with Walmart’s Agent Gateway, the company’s new MCP server, which is designed to help approved agents connect to Walmart over the model context protocol (MCP). The protocol, originally created by Anthropic, allows AI agents to connect to external data sources, tools, and other workflows. In this case, it lets an AI agent search across Walmart’s online inventory and make purchases on behalf of the agent’s user. 

What’s more, the retailer says that its Agent Gateway will be able to help customers shop for their usual brands or items without having to share their personal information or purchase history directly with the agent. 

The company has also developed new technology to differentiate an agent’s purchases from those initiated directly by the customer and to give shoppers more control over what their agents can and cannot do.

With Agent Profiles, rolling out next month, customers will be able to authorize each AI agent they use with a dedicated profile in their account, allowing them to see the agent’s purchases separately from their own. Plus, customers will be in control of how purchases get approved by either requiring approval for each transaction or by authorizing transactions within a certain spending limit they set. 

The retailer says these controls are similar to adding someone as an authorized user on your credit card, where their transactions are identified and you can cap their spending.

The Agent Profiles will be created the first time you use a given agent to shop through the Walmart Agent Gateway, the company notes. To get started, you’ll authorize and link the Agent Profile to your Walmart account, then set your controls or spending limits. You can also delete an Agent Profile at any time. Agent support is available for anyone with a Walmart account; a Walmart+ membership is not necessary. 

Alongside these technologies, Walmart is introducing special “terms” for AI agents, which specify how they must operate and what rights they have to transact on its site. Of note, Walmart says that its returns process applies, including when an agent doesn’t act as intended. That’s a customer-friendly condition that could sway consumers who were worried about being an early tester of agentic commerce, as they won’t fear ending up with products they don’t want because of a misbehaving agent. 

Walmart also says that agents can’t take actions beyond what the shopper intends, can’t access the customers’ payment information, and can only access the information they need for the given task. Agents that don’t comply with the terms will be blocked from accessing Walmart’s site.

title: INMO GO3 smart glasses pack a display and Gemini integration with clever camera privacy
snippet: There are two problems with smart glasses today. Most don’t deliver that futuristic display we all want to have, and the camera has become a serious point of friction. INMO GO3 solve both problems while also supporting Google’s Gemini and more. more…
fullText:
There are two problems with smart glasses today. Most don’t deliver that futuristic display we all want to have, and the camera has become a serious point of friction. INMO GO3 solve both problems while also supporting Google’s Gemini and more.

The promise of INMO GO3 is to deliver an AI-forward pair of smart glasses that help you stay connected and get things done, but without using your phone quite as much. It delivers on that through software, of course, but also the fact that it puts an actual display in front of your eyes. So, unlike most existing smart glasses, you’re able to interact with everything without interrupting a conversation or glancing at your phone. The MicroLED displays – one for each eye – are bright (up to 1,500 nits) and have a 30-degree field-of-view.

One of the core features is translation, with GO3 supporting real-time translation across 98 languages, and even supporting 13 languages fully offline. The glasses detect speech from the person in front of you and put a translation of that right in your eyeline, letting you get over the language barrier without putting your phone in the middle. Similarly, GO3 can take notes during meetings, and coming soon, it will also be able to present summaries directly through the glasses.

The display can also be used as a teleprompter, or to interact with an AI assistant. INMO’s AI assistant is powered by Google’s Gemini and OpenAI’s ChatGPT and can do things such as answer questions, recognize images taken by the camera, and take notes, among other functions. The display can also be used for turn-by-turn navigation to help you get around without using your phone.

	

Despite all the additional functionality here, INMO GO3 remain lightweight. The glasses weigh in at 58g, just a tiny bit heavier than Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses – the ones without a display. The 8mm temples also ensure these don’t stand out in a bad way – they just look like normal glasses!

One of the coolest features here is the battery. Smart glasses by their very nature are limited in terms of how long the battery can go, so INMO designed the battery to be interchangeable. When the first battery drains, simply swap out the power pack with a fresh one that’s on the charger and keep wearing the glasses. The included charging case can still top off the battery, but a replaceable cell gets you up and going faster.

As mentioned, there is a camera on board here, but one of the really thoughtful additions INMO offers is a privacy cover. This physical shade covers the camera lens, providing some visible confirmation that the camera is not in use.

INMO GO3 also gets some boosts from accessories such as a speaker that can be used alongside AI translation to respond to the other person in their language, but using an AI clone of your voice. There’s also a controller ring you can wear to interact with GO3’s software without touching the actual glasses. Finally, you can also add on a sunglasses cover to improve GO3’s usability outside, and there are prescription lens inserts too.

INMO GO3 is on sale now for just $509.

title: Google restricts every free AI Pro trial from Pixel & more compared to paid subscribers
snippet: Google hands out extended free trials to its AI Pro subscription frequently with new smartphone purchases and more, but trial users end up getting less access compared to paid subscribers in what is a bit of a misleading situation. more…
fullText:
Google hands out extended free trials to its AI Pro subscription frequently with new smartphone purchases and more, but trial users end up getting less access compared to paid subscribers in what is a bit of a misleading situation.

Free trials are a pretty standard practice across the industry when it comes to subscriptions, and the general understanding is that you’re getting full access to the same subscription you are later set to pay for unless there’s an upfront stipulation about restrictions.

And that’s where things are getting a bit messy with Google’s AI Pro subscription.

Google One AI Pro is a $19.99/month subscription that delivers access to expanded Gemini usage limits, 5TB of storage across Google products, and bundles in other subscriptions such as Google Home Premium, Health Premium, and YouTube Premium Lite. Earlier this year, we called AI Pro “one of the best deals in tech today.”

	

But the rollout of Gemini 4 Argon to Google’s Antigravity development tool put a spotlight on a restriction on AI Pro’s free trials. Put simply, they’re limited compared to paid subscribers, and it’s not something Google made abundantly clear.

There are two specific downsides with a Google One AI Pro trial compared to an actively paid subscription. As mentioned, Antigravity on AI Pro trials leaves out Gemini 4 Argon. Google has a page that specifically puts a trial account in a completely different bucket compared to a paid AI Pro plan, and it treats the trial as a free user with expanded usage limits rather than a full user as @evowizz was one of the first to point out.

The other restriction is YouTube Premium Lite, which is not available for Google One AI Pro trial users until they start paying.

In Google’s defense, this is technically spelled out on support documents. The YouTube Premium Lite restriction, for example, is clearly spelled out as Google says that the “benefit is unavailable until trials of Google AI Pro conclude and you convert to a paid subscription.” But, as far as we can see, this is not disclosed as clearly at the time of sign-up or alongside advertising of the AI Pro trials.

Another loss here is the lack of Google One’s 10% cashback (store credit) perk in the Google Store, which is lacking in free trials. That one is certainly easier to see the reasoning behind, though.

The Google Store touts the Pixel 11’s AI Pro trial as delivering “expanded usage limits in Gemini, access to Gemini in Google apps, and 5 TB of cloud storage,” as well as Health Premium. Nowhere does Google promise the YouTube perks, but the wording around Gemini also lacks any hint at the restriction found in Antigravity. Pages including offer details also lack any mention of this.

As mentioned, Google hands out free, extended trials to AI Pro all over the place. Just a few active examples include:

6 months free with the purchase of a Pixel 11

12 months free with the purchase of a Googlebook

6 months free for select Verizon customers

12 months free with Chromebook Plus or 3 months with any other Chromebook

6 months free with the purchase of a Galaxy Z Fold 8

And that’s just a few examples – you can absolutely find more.

	

Google explicitly lists all of these trials at their full monthly value (i.e. $119 value for Pixel’s 6-month trial) despite the restricted access that trial users see.

While Google has not addressed the somewhat misleading nature of the AI Pro trial restrictions, one Googler responded to the other headache that exists here – you can’t just press a button to start paying for AI Pro if you’re on a trial. You either have to wait for the trial to end, or reach out to Google for help converting your account. 

What do you think of the situation?

title: Nirva raises $33M for a pendant that only listens to you
snippet: Nirva will ship its $249 ambient AI pendant by the end of the year.
fullText:
Ambient AI is having a moment. Amazon launched a new wrist-worn device with Bee; a former Plaud exec launched ambient apps through a startup called Ambi, which aims to also build its own hardware; and Apple launched Voice Intelligence features during its iPhone launch in September. Now, a company called Nirva is betting on a jewelry-like pendant and its ability to listen only to the wearer.

The startup today announced a new $25 million pre-Series A round, adding to the $8 million it raised earlier in the year from investors like Lightspeed and South Park Commons, bringing its total raise to $33 million. 

Nirva was founded in 2025 by two former Meta Reality Labs employees, Wei Lyu and Jason Chen, along with Hanying Hu, who founded a fashion and jewelry brand.

The company’s first device is a pendant, which can also be worn as a bracelet. The device weighs only around eight grams, making it easy to wear all day. Its battery lasts up to three days on a single charge.

Longer term, Nirva aims to release more devices. 

Image Credits:Nirva

In a call with TechCrunch, Nirva CEO Lyu said that the company wanted to build a wearable that blends in with fashion, but also provides value to users.

“This is a piece of jewelry that only focuses on listening to your own speech. We are not like a voice recorder or like a meeting note taker. One key difference between us, Taya, Vocci, or Sandbar Ring is that we’re always passively listening to your own speech. So it’s always on. It keeps modeling the user and modeling your mind,” Lyu said.

For ambient devices, privacy is a big question, as people might not like to be recorded all the time. Plus, devices like the Ray-Ban Meta have instilled fear in those who are around the person wearing the smart glasses that they are being recorded too.

Nirva gets around this problem by asking users to record snippets of their voice during onboarding and building its model based on that. During use, the device filters out conversations or data captured from the other people around the device. That means it’s only recording the wearer. 

In addition, Nirva by default doesn’t keep any audio data or transcripts after processing the conversations.

Nirva is positioning itself as a personal insights company rather than a productivity startup. However, its app shows you reminders or action items and ways to act on them. Lyu said that through its app, the startup wants to help users show up for others in a better way in their lives. 

“I think there’s no universal way to help everyone to solve their problems. We are building a tool to help people to improve their self-understanding, self-compassion, and self-awareness,” Lyu said.

Image Credits: NirvaImage Credits:Nirva

The companion app parses users’ speech and creates insights that it infers are related to the user’s personality, including patterns, the people who tend to be around them, the places they’ve been to, and other daily notes. Lyu emphasized that the app shows users insights around their emotions, communication style, and ways they can improve.

Wyu gave an example of an incident when she forgot to thank her mother for something, and the app later nudged her with a reminder about this. 

The company also said that, before it discards the audio, it’s able to track the tone, pitch, volume, and speed, which are useful for deriving emotion-related understandings that are then surfaced in the app. 

Nirva will start taking orders for its devices in November, with an aim to ship them to early users by the end of the year. The $249 device will be available in silver, brushed silver, black, and gold.

The startup has competition in the AI wearables area. There are companies like former Apple employees’ Taya, which is also building intelligent jewelry. Plus, startups like Friend and Bee are trying to be companion gadgets as well.

The aptly named 1Password for Agents doesn’t give bots free reign to access all of your connected accounts — you’ll still need to grant approval for sign-in requests — but should make it less cumbersome to use Agents for tasks that require them to log into various services.

”Agents are starting to do real work on our behalf. The old model where you hand over a credential and hope for the best doesn’t work,” 1Password CEO Aashish Tripathi said in a press statement. “An agent should be able to do the job it’s been asked to do without getting permanent access to everything behind the account, and 1Password provides the trust layer that makes this possible across personal agent experiences.”

With this new system, an AI agent uses a unique digital key to verify its identity to 1Password when it reaches a sign-in form. The app then sends you a notification about which account credentials it needs, and why. If you choose to approve the request, 1Password will fill in the required login information instead of handing it to the agent. Approvals are granted on your own device to ensure you’re behind the permissions, making this a similar process to two-factor authentication. After the agent is signed in, it’ll continue with its task, without ever having actually seen your password.

This 1Password access system is designed to work with a variety of popular AI agents, including Meta Muse, ChatGPT Work and Dots, Claude Duet, Grok Bot, and Town. 1Password says more partners are working to bring support to 1Password for Agents, including Browserbase, Browser Use, Dana, Instinct, Kernel, Perplexity, Ramp, Tomo, and Wajo, with “additional integrations to come.”

title: AI agents are ready to shop. Some retailers are wary.
snippet: Using an AI agent to shop for you is a strange experience. Tech companies have marketed them as personal assistants - the democratizing of labor that ordinarily would only be available to the rich and powerful. In practice, at least for buying things, it's more like sending an anxious and apologetic teenager out to the store: They require an inordinate amount of instructions and specifications, run into technical problems regularly, and come back with solutions that are not exactly what you asked for. They did, technically speaking, complete a task, just not the specific one you asked them to, and often not in the way you would have approach … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Using an AI agent to shop for you is a strange experience. Tech companies have marketed them as personal assistants — the democratizing of labor that ordinarily would only be available to the rich and powerful. In practice, at least for buying things, it’s more like sending an anxious and apologetic teenager out to the store: They require an inordinate amount of instructions and specifications, run into technical problems regularly, and come back with solutions that are not exactly what you asked for. They did, technically speaking, complete a task, just not the specific one you asked them to, and often not in the way you would have approached it.

Meta, Google, OpenAI, and others have all introduced some version of agentic shopping tools that promise to make buying things even easier than it already is. Demos show AI agents that can seamlessly book flights and hotels, browse billions of products to find the right one, and secure tickets to sporting events on a human’s behalf. But as AI companies — and their users — are finding out, buying things requires that the other party is willing to sell them in the first place.

The most prominent example of a retailer or service provider refusing to let an AI agent in has been Amazon. The retail giant sued Perplexity, with Amazon saying the AI company had ignored its requests to stop its agent from shopping on the site. More recently, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon. E-commerce sites aren’t the only platforms walling off agents: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank wouldn’t allow outside agents to access accounts, saying it was “too risky” for clients and the company, and some users report they’ve been unable to use agents to book trips from providers like Delta and Amtrak. AI agents can also get caught in the web of general bot blocking systems, meaning that even if a site doesn’t have a blanket ban, existing firewalls can make agents inconsistent — and by extension, less useful for the types of tasks tech companies tout as the future.

Even without hard blocks, agents’ access to retailers is spotty. For example, Muse, which I instructed to look for a specific face moisturizer, was caught in Target’s bot check one day but was able to get through the next. It suggested a listing from a grocery chain that doesn’t ship to my address when I searched for the best price on granola bars. When I asked for mattress recommendations under a certain price point, Muse was once again blocked by Target, despite being able to pull from the site just a few minutes prior.

How successful an agent is at accessing a site may depend on how it went about the task and what safeguards are in place, Target spokesperson Loni Monroe told The Verge in an email. (Target has AI shopping partnerships with OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft.) Agents may be able to access one part of the site but not another, as a way to protect customer data and the shopping experience. In addition, Monroe said that Target has safeguards preventing unauthorized agents and bots from accessing customer accounts and initiating transactions on a human’s behalf.

The lack of Amazon options within agents is also impossible to ignore. Sometimes, the agents will say as much: When I asked Muse to find the best per-piece granola bar price, it offered options from Sam’s Club, Walmart, and Costco, but acknowledged a big caveat: Amazon might have had the lowest-priced option, but it was hard-blocked from browsing, so Muse couldn’t confirm. Between waiting for a response, directing Muse to search for more sites, and clarifying that a West Coast-based retailer wouldn’t ship to New York, it likely would have been faster to search myself. It also explains why agentic AI companies would really like to have Amazon on board — and why Amazon is so fiercely protective of how customers shop on its platform. It’s not that Amazon is against robots shopping in place of humans — the company has its own on-platform agentic shopping feature that monitors prices, automatically reorders items, and purchases products based on rules set by human users. Another feature that uses an agent to purchase products from other sites without leaving Amazon angered smaller businesses, who say they didn’t consent to having their storefronts scraped and featured on Amazon.

Amazon spokesperson Maxine Tagay confirmed that the company “requested that Meta remove Amazon” from Muse.

“We think it’s fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate,” Tagay said in an email.

I instructed Muse to bulk-add all 10 of the newest listings from a favorite brand to my cart

It’s one thing for agents to offer comically spotty, disjointed services — but it’s another, potentially more frustrating experience when they actually do work, because of the implications for humans. In order to test a shopping task that I actually would like to automate, I unleashed Muse on The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion retailer. As secondhand shopping has exploded in popularity, shopping on The RealReal has gotten increasingly competitive, so much so that the company sells a $12-per-month subscription allowing shoppers to get early access to new items. On The RealReal, part of the shopping process is zero-sum: Placing an item in your cart reserves it for you for 20 minutes, making it impossible for other people to swipe it. I instructed my Muse agent to bulk-add all 10 of the newest listings from a favorite brand to my cart, effectively blocking other shoppers from purchasing them before I got the chance to review the latest selections. I had no intention of buying any of these items, but I prompted Muse to keep re-adding the items to my shopping bag each time the 20-minute hold had expired. On and on this went, all day (I eventually ended the task).

If I were a less honest, pure-hearted person, I would deploy an agent to run this personalized, technically allowed reserve system endlessly. But as I watched the items continuously pop back into my cart, exasperation flooded my psyche — on behalf of the other shoppers interested in these items, but also for my future self, who may soon be competing with someone else’s agent doing this same thing. Perhaps I already am.

The RealReal sees AI agents as an opportunity, and is investing in its own AI-powered services while protecting the integrity of the platform, chief technology officer Luke Friang told The Verge in an email.

“Our approach is to remain open to third-party AI agents, allowing them to browse, log in and interact with our marketplace, while maintaining safeguards against automated activity that could disrupt the customer experience,” Friang said.

To be sure, normal online shopping can be tedious, too — the endless array of options on the web can make finding the right thing feel like looking for a needle in a haystack. Agentic shopping is the inverse: It’s like looking at the world through a pinhole. If I don’t like the five options Muse has curated for me, I must ask it to find five more, and on and on. I must give the agent specific parameters and rules, and expand and tweak them as needed, little by little. A more rote task like finding the absolute lowest price on a product you already know you want is where an agent could be truly useful. Without Amazon, though, even that feels like the task was carried out with incomplete information.

If you have preferences about literally anything you spend money on — the price, the return policy, the shipping rates, the ethical standards of a company, the fabric composition — an agent is just another entity to express those preferences to. With the time and patience for hand-holding, Muse could help deepen a search for something specific: For example, I uploaded photos to Muse of a vintage dress I’ve been hunting for, along with the specific year it’s from, a list of keywords associated with it, notes about similar items, and secondhand platforms to start searches on. Muse could not find the dress for sale anywhere, but it did alert me to an upcoming auction of items from the same brand.

The joy and thrill of discovery is largely gone

In an email, Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton emphasized the partnerships the company has forged with retailers and the control human users have over the agent’s actions.

“Importantly, users can take over at any time, Muse is designed to always ask permission before buying, and it applies ethical browsing principles when asked to do things that a human could not - like buying all the tickets to an event,” Clayton said. “The response from retailers has been overwhelmingly positive, and we look forward to working with them as we continue to grow Muse and improve the purchasing experience.”

There’s another thing that nags at me no matter how long I tinker with agentic shopping: The joy and thrill of discovery is largely gone. Buying things is an American pastime. We do it in person, online, from strangers on Facebook, and from professional salespeople on livestreams. We buy things we need and we buy things we don’t, things we know we want and the things we’ve never seen until now that have suddenly become very important. It’s not a stretch to say that for many, shopping is a hobby — one that has become solidly entangled with another, more modern hobby of scrolling on a phone. We don’t just lust after material belongings; we imbue them with identity markers and social status. Buying things is intensive — in resources, in labor, in emotion. AI companies see this pastime as something that can be optimized. Many people would probably prefer that it not be.

title: The Mori Is a Mushroom-Shaped AI Lamp Companion, and I’m Smitten
snippet: The $849 Mori is designed to respond to your environment, knowing when to play and when to stay quiet.
fullText:
So many artificial intelligence devices are trying to command our attention, but when I met the Mori AI robot companion earlier this month, it was refreshing to see a device that’s using AI to exercise some playful restraint — even if its $849 retail price makes it a tough sell.

The Mori, announced Thursday by Oka, is part glowy mushroom lamp and part Furby. The company is behind the cutesy AI gadget. And while it also looks a little bit like a larger smart speaker wrapped in fabric, Mori made it quite clear that it was not interested in playing any of my playlists from Apple Music.

Mori listens to music here, and then hides after becoming shy.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Instead, when activated, Mori pops out of its body and uses its cameras and sensors to respond playfully to you — and, like a Furby, it speaks its own babylike language. It’s 10 inches tall (26.4 centimeters) and uses its sensors to help it tilt its head and move its “eyes” to follow your voice. Oka says the Mori processes images and audio on the device to discern context, then discards them. The Mori does store facial recognition data to distinguish familiar faces from unfamiliar ones, but Oka says that data isn’t uploaded either.

			

More from CNET

When I spoke directly to Mori during my demo, it felt a lot like speaking to a friend’s dog: It will look and respond, but also reacts to other things at the same time. The AI that the Mori uses to understand context seemed to come into play when I commented on how adorable it looked (it cooed and got a little shy) and when I asked Oka CEO Hua Wang if the Mori had a Bluetooth mode for playing music (the gadget made a sound of disapproval).

When withdrawn into its body, Mori turns off its cameras, plays meditative music and becomes a colorful lamp.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

The Mori does play music, though its offerings are limited to meditative sounds accompanied by a glowing light show. Press its head, and it retreats into its body to play white noise-like songs while its head lights up in a variety of colors. The Mori also reacts to music: It started bopping around when I played Carly Rae Jepsen’s Don’t Leave Me on the Dance Floor.

The adorable yet understated personality reminds me of the Furby from yesteryear, or the $599 Ultimate Grogu we saw earlier this year, but the Mori’s use of AI allows it to react more contextually to its surroundings. This more docile take on a pet could appeal to someone who wants something more responsive than a talking toy that also blends in with their living room furniture.

To show it’s paying attention, Mori’s head tilts towards your voice and its eyes can follow you around.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

The Mori costs more than those toys: $649 for its founder edition, $799 for the next round of preorders and, eventually, $849 for its standard edition. However, it’s a lot more affordable than a companion robot such as Sony’s $3,200 Aibo robot dog. The Mori comes bundled with two years of its subscription, and afterward will cost either $17 per month or $80 per year.

Oka, the company that makes the Mori, calls this edition the “Artificat 01” and intends for it to develop its personality as it lives with its owner. If an “Artificat 02” comes along down the road, your Mori’s personality should be able to transfer to its new body.

While I do think the Mori is adorable, it’s worth noting that companion robots already come in a lot of different forms, and we’ll likely see even more this January at CES 2027. These include robots that can float in the air and those designed as assistants and social companions for older adults. The Mori appears to take a gentler approach, with a look that could fit right in alongside living room or bedroom furniture.

title: Blackstone’s Jas Khaira says fears over AI-buildout debt are overblown
snippet: Blackstone’s AI head on why the PE giant isn't panicked by market jitters.
fullText:
Private equity giant Blackstone is putting itself at the center of the AI boom, firm veteran Jas Khaira discussed last week on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt. 

It is writing checks via various strategies, ranging from offering massive loans to data centers to investing in frontier AI models and applications.

Earlier this year, the firm launched Blackstone N1 (BXN1), a San Francisco-based central hub for its AI initiatives. The group is led by Khaira, who relocated from New York to be at the epicenter of AI.

Unlike earlier tech cycles such as mobile or SaaS, which allowed companies to reach significant scale with moderate capital, the transition to AI requires staggering amounts of investment. That need for capital is precisely why Blackstone, with its $1.3 trillion in assets under management, could play such a critical role in this tech shift.

Khaira emphasized that Blackstone sets itself apart from traditional venture capitalists through its focus on compute financing and its ability to offer flexible capital structures, ranging from debt to equity. And it has been investing aggressively.

“We’re the largest owner of compute outside of the hyperscalers today, whether it’s investments in neo clouds, investments in data centers, and being able to use that compute strategically to support companies,” Khaira said.

For instance, BXN1 played a key role in several compute-related deals, among them Crux AI, a neocloud launched in partnership with Google to commercialize its custom TPUs, to which Blackstone committed $5 billion as an investor. It also backed four-year-old Etched, a chip startup whose rapid development has caught investor attention. Neoclouds are cloud providers that rent out AI GPU infrastructure.

Blackstone pioneered a financing structure that allowed it to lend massive sums to venture-backed cloud neoclouds by analyzing both committed customer contracts and using GPUs pledged as collateral.

Blackstone’s first such deal came in 2023 with CoreWeave, shortly after that neocloud saw demand explode following the launch of ChatGPT. Despite having only “30 million of revenue and minimal profitability” at that time, according to Khaira, CoreWeave approached Blackstone for a $2.3 billion loan.

CoreWeave was borrowing against the considerable value of its large collection of Nvidia GPUs, with Nvidia also an investor. Blackstone also grew more comfortable with the loan because CoreWeave had contracts with blue-chip customers like Microsoft.

That transaction quickly became the financing model for how Blackstone and other credit institutions provided billions in follow-on debt to CoreWeave and rival neoclouds.

“One of the primary things that we’re looking to is the nature of the customer. And if the customer is an investment-grade customer — let’s say it’s Microsoft or let’s say it’s Meta — the risk gets priced relative to that customer,” Khaira said.

Building on its success with CoreWeave, Blackstone struck other neocloud financing deals, including co-leading alongside Coatue a $10 billion credit facility for Australian GPU provider Firmus earlier this year.

Khaira acknowledged that in recent weeks, the large debt burdens accumulated by these companies and other neocloud operators have begun to raise red flags. Coreweave’s debt alone has since ballooned to about $50 billion, causing Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner to note in a recent CNBC interview, “The collateral that CoreWeave is putting up which is really only GPUs is not good enough anymore. They used that in the past to get cheap debt.”

Khaira said that on the credit side, the market jitters stem from a combination of factors. Interest rates ticked up in September, and hotter-than-expected inflation signals that borrowing costs may keep climbing. The flood of AI infrastructure debt offerings isn’t helping either.

“We’re also seeing higher credit spreads,” Khaira said, explaining that lenders are charging higher premiums on top of already higher base interest rates to finance the AI buildout. “The cost of capital to price in debt for a Meta or a Microsoft has widened out,” he added, pointing out that even tech giants with massive balance sheets and solid earnings are paying more to borrow.

Concerns about the rising cost of debt have spilled into the stock market. Shares of CoreWeave dropped over 20% in recent days, while Firmus scrapped its planned IPO on the Australian Securities Exchange at a target valuation of roughly $30 billion.

“Ultimately, the market wasn’t there at that valuation, and so I think as a result, that deal didn’t get done,” Khaira said about Firmus’ cancelled listing.

“The market is thinking what is the right price for neoclouds, what is the right price for these businesses in this moment when interest rates are moving up,” he said.

Despite those pressures on some infrastructure providers, AI companies simply can’t get enough compute to power their models. Their appetite continues to drive data center buildout.

Khaira downplayed worries of doom-mongers that the massive accumulation of AI infrastructure debt could lead to a widespread credit crisis, or worse, crash the economy altogether. “This doesn’t feel like something where you’ve got 2008 banks that are shaky credits,” he said.

Instead, he pointed out that because the vast majority of data centers are built for hyperscalers, the debt financing them is ultimately backed “by the most creditworthy companies in the world.”

Beyond funding data centers, Blackstone is helping companies adopt AI through a $1.5 billion joint venture called “Ode with Anthropic,” formed alongside Anthropic and Hellman & Friedman this year. Ode supplies forward-deployed engineers to help companies adopt AI and integrate it into their operations, starting with Blackstone’s 280 portfolio companies.

When asked if Blackstone-owned companies are seeing tangible gains from AI, Khaira conceded that “there is definitely ROI, but it is uneven.” He described technology adoption as something that could move in a “sawtooth-type pattern,” which, to skeptics, can look like an oversupply of compute before adoption catches up.

title: The internet is having a very bad cybersecurity day
snippet: From AI-discovered PHP vulnerabilities to flaws in Node.js and popular AI tool LiteLLM, cybersecurity teams have plenty to worry about this week.
fullText:
The internet is having a bad day, from a cybersecurity perspective. Government websites around the world went offline, Reuters reported, after AI discovered critical security vulnerabilities that impacted the programming language PHP. The issues were severe enough that the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) advised organizations using PHP on their systems to either immediately update or take their systems offline until they could.

But the PHP update wasn’t the only headache cybersecurity folks were facing on Wednesday. Node.js, the open source JavaScript runtime environment, also dropped a security surprise of its own when it shared that four high-severity vulnerabilities were just patched in its latest release. One allowed remote code execution, and two others would have permitted a TLS validation bypass, potentially allowing attackers to bypass checks intended to verify a server’s identity.

In addition, LiteLLM, a popular open source proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, was compromised by an attacker who injected malicious code, the company shared in a post on X on Wednesday afternoon. The malicious artifacts were published to PyPI (Python Package Index), Docker Hub, and GHCR (GitHub Container Registry), the post noted.

The malicious code was said to include an information stealer that targeted cloud credentials, passwords, and AI service credentials, in addition to a remote access trojan that could allow hackers to execute commands on compromised systems.

LiteLLM said it has now removed the malicious releases and images and advised anyone who installed them to follow the remediation guidance it provided.

And wait, there’s more! An Indian certificate authority, eMudhra, had its private keys compromised, potentially allowing attackers to issue fraudulent certificates and impersonate legitimate websites. Security pros have called this a massive cleanup job and one that’s “bigger than Heartbleed.” (The latter is a reference to the critical security vulnerability in the OpenSSL cryptographic software library.)

These issues come on the heels of other security breaches and hacks, including the breach of the cloud-native database-as-a-service, TiDB Cloud, which the company announced on Monday. Other hackers have been exploiting four patched Plex Media Server flaws, collectively called Plex2Shell. And last week, cybersecurity company BeyondTrust warned customers to patch a critical zero-day in its Remote Support product, which had been exploited since August.

Though the issues were unrelated to each other, their back-to-back arrival highlights the challenges cybersecurity teams now face. This is particularly important as AI could make it easier for attackers to exploit vulnerabilities once discovered.

title: Meta says Muse has over 10M users, with shopping a top activity
snippet: Meta Muse users are adopting the app for shopping and personal productivity, the company said during its Q3 earnings call. The AI app now has over 10M users.
fullText:
Meta said during its third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday that its AI app Muse has been adopted by more than 10 million users, confirming estimates released earlier this week by market intelligence firm Sensor Tower.

But it is how people are using it and how much they’re spending that has caught CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s attention. Zuckerberg said about 25% of people who set up Muse now use it daily, helping improve retention.

He also shared that over a quarter of Muse’s engaged users who were shopping via the AI agent had an average purchase size of over $200, which was surprising even to industry insiders.

“Plaid told us that they hadn’t seen activity like they’re seeing with their connector on any other service before,” Zuckerberg said, referring to the financial technology company that connects payment apps to customers’ bank accounts. Muse uses Plaid’s connector to enable agentic shopping.

Beyond shopping, Zuckerberg said other popular uses for Muse include personal productivity tasks, such as connecting the AI agent to users’ email or calendars. The exec stressed that this indicates users trusted Muse’s security setup, which includes a feature called “Muse Secure VM” designed to protect their data and privacy. He also mentioned that the forthcoming “Muse Confidential VM” will prevent even Meta from seeing users’ content.

Now that Muse has achieved “product-market fit,” Zuckerberg said Meta’s focus will shift to scaling the AI agent, increasing revenue, and optimizing its compute costs. Remarkably, the tech company is forecasting that Muse will eventually bring in more revenue per user than its “family of apps” users do today — meaning its users on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger. Currently, that figure is around “several hundreds of dollars annually,” Zuckerberg said.

Meta has said it ultimately intends to monetize Muse by keeping it free for most users but keeping a percentage of the commerce taking place on the platform. Power users who want access to the most advanced AI models or more tokens will also have to pay.

Zuckerberg also noted that Meta believes Muse will be profitable after it scales.

“On the compute side, we are building out the capacity to serve more than a billion people over the next few years,” he told bankers and analysts on the Q3 earnings call. “In the near term, Muse is very compute-intensive to run, but we expect to improve its cost efficiency by more than 10x in the next year, which will enable it to be profitable once the revenue lines are at scale.” 

Muse will also play a central role in Meta’s smart glasses strategy. Reality Labs, the division responsible for smart glasses, VR, and the metaverse, is still losing billions. However, the division’s losses are expected to improve from $19.1 billion in 2025 to $15 billion this year.

Beyond scaling and supporting its hardware strategy, Zuckerberg teased the company’s plans for something he called the “Muse network.” He described this as taking Muse from a “single-player game” to one where “your Muses can work with your friends’ and your families’ [Muses].”

“And if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent,” he added.

title: Meta ordered to pay $25B in case related to Cambridge Analytica scandal
snippet: The payout is related to a recent trial involving the social media giant that revolved around its data privacy practices.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

12:42 PM PDT · October 21, 2026

Image Credits:Andrej Sokolow/picture alliance / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

The tale of the Cambridge Analytica data scandal is long — and it keeps costing Meta gargantuan sums of money.

On Wednesday, a judge ordered the social media giant to initiate its biggest payout yet: $25 billion to the state of New Mexico for the tech giant’s role in deceiving resident users over its data privacy practices, The New York Times reports.

The huge sum follows a two-week trial in which a New Mexico jury deliberated over the company’s alleged wrongdoing. The jury found that the company behind Facebook and Instagram had committed 43 million violations of the state’s consumer protection laws, each of which carried a $5,000 penalty, the outlet notes.

Part of the case revolved around the company’s handling of a third-party app linked to the Cambridge Analytica data breach, The Wall Street Journal reports. Other parts involved its data privacy policies and its efforts to mitigate misinformation on its platform.

Cambridge Analytica was an outgrowth of a British defense contractor, SLC Group, that specialized in influence operations and other political work. The company notably worked with the Trump campaign during the 2016 presidential election. It was also involved in a number of controversial initiatives.

“We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years,” New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez told journalists at a press conference, commenting on the case’s resolution.

Meta said that it will appeal the decision.

“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” said C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, in a statement shared with TechCrunch via email. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge,” he added.

title: OpenAI GPT models are coming to Google Antigravity ‘soon,’ Cloud ‘in the coming weeks’
snippet: A deal struck between OpenAI and Google will see OpenAI’s models coming to Google Cloud and even Antigravity. more…
fullText:
A deal struck between OpenAI and Google will see OpenAI’s models coming to Google Cloud and even Antigravity.

Starting “in the coming weeks,” OpenAI’s GPT models will be coming to Google Cloud. OpenAI says that “Google Cloud customers will be able to purchase OpenAI frontier models via the model garden, transacted through the Google Cloud Marketplace.” This enables enterprise customers with “spend commitments” through Google Cloud to use OpenAI’s models if they choose. 

The Google Cloud model garden already supports Anthropic Claude models alongside open models and Google’s own Gemini models. 

Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, says:

	

We are focused on giving customers a broad selection of models, including those from OpenAI, so they can choose the right model for any given job, helping to deliver optimal quality and lower costs.

Also confirmed in today’s announcement is that OpenAI models are coming to Google’s Antigravity tool, as well as Gemini Agent.

Like Cloud’s model garden, Antigravity already supports Anthropic models including Claude Opus & Sonnet 4.6 for free/Plus/trial accounts (until November 2), with Opus & Sonnet 5.5 models available to paid subscribers on Pro and higher tiers. 

OpenAI and Google have yet to confirm exactly which GPT models will be coming to Cloud and Antigravity, but it stands to reason that GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol may be included.

title: Apple is right about the wild west of AI, and the growing backlash
snippet: Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak didn’t hold back when he described the most ambitious figures in the AI race as the “lunatic fringe” of Silicon Valley. The piece suggested that the iPhone maker is hoping to position itself as being on the right side of a growing AI backlash. Given the pace of development, trying to predict the future of AI is a risky business, but I do think Apple is absolutely right about the dangers … more…
fullText:
Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak didn’t hold back when he described the most ambitious figures in the AI race as the “lunatic fringe” of Silicon Valley. The piece suggested that the iPhone maker is hoping to position itself as being on the right side of a growing AI backlash.

Given the pace of development, trying to predict the future of AI is a risky business, but I do think Apple is absolutely right about the dangers …

The piece cites the familiar refrain that Apple’s slow pace when it comes to AI features could see the company being left behind.

Virtually [all other tech giants] have flung themselves into the AI arms race, pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into training ever more intelligent thinking machines. While Apple trains its own models, it is nowhere near the technology’s frontier, leaving the company vulnerable to being left behind if super-smart AI transforms industry and society in the coming years.

Joswiak counters that the company is focused on launching AI features that will perform useful tasks for ordinary people, and that Apple’s privacy focus will become increasingly valuable in the context of an AI backlash against a “lunatic fringe” of unconstrained acceleration of a technology we can barely control today.

Lunacy is certainly a good word to describe a world in which AI companies fear that their work may destroy humanity, but they are even more afraid that one of their competitors will beat them to it.

AI is the first technological development that has ever threatened such a wide variety of jobs, with a huge number of positions likely to be eliminated in fields as diverse as truck driving, marketing, and software development. Academics have even expressed concern that future generations will no longer become mathematicians or scientific researchers over fears that those roles will be made redundant by AI.

For example, math professor Giordano Scarciotti recently said that when AI models are solving in days problems academics have worked on for years, the results could be devastating because it will seem pointless to future generations to even attempt this type of work.

I explore a potentially devastating consequence of AI’s growing capabilities: what happens when the next generation of talented students no longer sees a reason to become mathematicians? The implications could extend far beyond mathematics and affect the future of scientific progress itself.

	

He argues that when today’s students see no future in academic research, this may leave AI models technically solving scientific problems, but with no one left to understand the implications and to apply the findings in meaningful ways. Similar effects are likely to occur in software development, where there are fewer and fewer humans able to understand the code being generated by increasingly advanced AI models.

The nightmare scenario here is that AI takes on ever more tasks as once-expert human beings become sidelined and marginalized because there’s no point in future generations attempting to compete. And if you think that’s baseless paranoia, I highly recommend listening to the podcast series Suspicious Minds: AI and the Apocalypse.

Quite how much power Apple has to fight back against such a dystopian future is questionable, but it could certainly be argued that at least the company is not applying its vast resources to accelerating the effect. Here’s hoping that the AI backlash grows sufficiently rapidly and loudly that politicians are forced to take steps to bring the current wild west of AI under some form of control.

title: Amazon launches two Bee AI recorders to remember everything you say
snippet: Just over a year after acquiring the AI company, Bee, Amazon has officially unveiled two of its first AI wearables, so you never forget what was said. more…
fullText:
Just over a year after acquiring the AI company, Bee, Amazon has officially unveiled two of its first AI wearables, so you never forget what was said.

Amazon announced two models: the Bee Frontier and the Bee Eclipse. Both can be considered wearables, with one taking on a bracelet form factor that works just fine clipped to a shirt. The Eclipse is a magnetic version of the always-listening device for use with Qi2 or MagSafe-equipped phones.

The Frontier is not dissimilar to the first preview Bee introduced before it was purchased by Amazon. At the time, the company had seemingly high hopes for being a genuine cornerstone of people’s lives to make their lives easier.

Amazon says both models are designed with “privacy principles” in mind, noting that a visible LED indicates when the Bee Frontier or Eclipse is listening. That’s what they do, after all. Both are designed to stay active and compile your ideas, thoughts, and even nonsense into reminders or notes, based on what Bee’s AI model decides you might need.

	

All of that can be found in the companion app, whether on mobile or desktop. Users can connect their Google Account to let it access emails and calendar information. That feeds into the selling idea that Bee becomes your personal assistant so you don’t miss out on a thing.

As for hardware, the Bee Frontier wearable is IP67 and rated for seven days of battery. The magnetic Eclipse model is able to power through a longer workload with up to 21 days of battery on a charge.

Of course, Amazon also added Alexa+ and Amazon.com integration into how the Bee wearables operate. The devices will be able to surface products based on your anticipated needs. That’s fun.

The Bee Frontier is available now for $74.99, while the Bee Eclipse will goi on sale “soon” starting at $99.99.

title: Claude Duet app is Anthropic’s bet on agents
snippet: Claude Duet is available through waitlist for Pro and Max plan users
fullText:
The AI world is flooded with personal and productivity-based assistants, with new ones launching every week. Now, Anthropic is entering this battle in the hopes of gaining user attention with a new app called Claude Duet, aimed at rivaling Meta Muse, OpenAI Dots, Hark, Instinct, Grok Bot, and Fo.

Anthropic said the new agent is meant to cater to professionals and small businesses to help them with automating and managing tasks. The company is making a distinction from personal agents such as Instinct, by noting that Duet isn’t good at handling errands or booking tickets, and it can’t show you its browser use as it happens.

Instead, Duet can build a daily briefing for its users, create dashboards, or suggest actions based on the user’s data. Like other agents, Duet can complete tasks in the background through its own virtual machine while you handle other things, then come back to you if it needs your approval. 

The launch arrives as the market shifts beyond AI assistants to agents that can work on users’ behalf. Many of Anthropic’s rivals are focusing on business use cases. While Meta’s Muse is a personal AI assistant, the company also released a version to cater to small businesses with connections to other apps. OpenAI’s Dots has a business slant as well, with its integration with professional tools.

Anthropic says Duet proactively delivers its recommendations as it monitors ongoing tasks. Built on the Claude Opus 5.5 model, Duet can connect to over 6,000 connectors and plugins in the Claude Marketplace. It can also make online purchases on users’ behalf via Stripe’s ⁠Link digital wallet or Shopify’s Shop Pay. 

The company said sensitive steps like payments would require user approval. However, Duet won’t trade securities or move money between accounts.

Anthropic also released a new classifier to check each message to prevent sensitive information from leaking out. It said that, by default, the agent would turn down requests asking for credit card numbers and government identification.

Claude Duet is available as an app on iOS and Android, and on the web through Claude.ai for Pro and Max customers in research preview. Users have to join a waitlist to try it.

title: Meta wants to pay for its broad AI buildout with a newly created class of stock
snippet: The social media giant is planning a new stock strategy to help power its broad investments in AI models and services.
fullText:
Meta is making a big push into AI, and it’s creating a new kind of stock that could help pay for it.

On Wednesday, as the company reported its third-quarter earnings, Semafor reported the company might issue non-voting stock, meaning shares that don’t give their owners a vote on company decisions, to help fund its push into artificial intelligence.

During Meta’s earnings call, the company confirmed that reporting. Meta’s chief financial officer, Susan Li, said the company plans to “create a new class of non-voting capital stock, which will be distributed to all existing shareholders through a stock dividend.”

Li later added that the company “created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded non-voting stock usable for capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, and other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing Class A and B shareholders.”

The shares will allow the company to maintain its current “founder-led structure,” she added. They will also expand its “funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business, driven by AI.”

Meta’s earnings were strong this past quarter, beating Wall Street expectations. The company made $64 billion in revenue, a jump of 26% from a year earlier. Its costs and expenses also rose too, however, by 68% year over year.

Reality Labs, the division responsible for Meta’s AR glasses, VR headsets, and VR software, continues to lose money, though less than it used to. The company said in its earnings report that it expects the division’s losses to shrink from its 2025 levels to between $18 billion and $19 billion.

Meta has made a big push into AI over the past year. The company has released several AI models, including Muse Spark and Muse Glimmer earlier this year. In recent weeks, it added Muse Wonder and Muse Spark Open, an open-weight model whose underlying parameters are publicly available for outsiders to use and build on. Meta also launched a coding agent for software developers called Muse Code. At its Meta Connect event this year, the company announced a new line of cute and cuddly avatars for AI assistant, Meta Muse, in a push to make its AI services more relatable (and also meme-able).

As far as can be discerned, those AI products are doing well. “In just a month and a half, more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada have set up Muse personal agents,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s earnings call. “Growth continues to be strong, and we have been number one in the App Store almost every day.”

“Now that Muse has clear product-market fit, we are entering a new phase and a more operational phase that is focused on scaling it,” Zuckerberg added, claiming later that the company expects to grow the product’s appeal to eventually “serve billions of people.”

The company also noted that certain storm clouds linger on the horizon in the form of ongoing regulatory and legal issues. “We continue to monitor active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” said Li. “For example, we continue to see scrutiny on youth-related issues in several markets, and have a number of youth-related trials scheduled in the coming months in the United States.”

title: Year-old AI lab Flapping Airplanes raises $1B at a $6B valuation
snippet: Just 9 months after raising a $180 million seed round, Flapping Airplanes has landed a $1 billion Series A for its mission to build AI models "without ingesting half the internet."
fullText:
Year-old startup Flapping Airplanes has wowed Silicon Valley with an impressive founding team and a mission to find ways to train large models with less data. On Wednesday, the company announced it had raised a $1 billion Series A round, co-led by Index and Lux, reportedly at a $6 billion valuation.

The round comes just nine months after the company launched with a $180 million seed round from GV, Sequoia, and Index. That seed round had valued the company at $1.5 billion, so its valuation just quadrupled.

Other participants in the new round included earlier backers Sequoia, GV, and Kleiner Perkins. Valor, Atreides, Kleiner Perkins, A*, and Nvidia are also investors in the company.

Flapping Airplanes was founded by Aidan Smith and brothers Asher and Ben Spector. Smith is a former founder and Thiel fellow who worked at the brain implant company Neuralink during college. Asher Spector was a statistics PhD at Stanford, while Ben Spector was a computer science PhD student at Stanford and founded Prod while at MIT.

Prod is an almost secret-society, five-year-old student-run startup accelerator that has “become one of the most powerful talent incubators in Silicon Valley,” wrote Sequoia partner David Cahn, a Flapping Planes investor, in a post earlier this year explaining why he invested. Together, the founders “are building the ‘young person’s AGI lab,’” as Cahn described it.

The founders describe their work as “the world’s most complete megakernel framework. It can perform entire training runs, serve inference, play video games, and even do all three simultaneously in a single kernel.” (A kernel is a program that runs on a GPU, and a megakernel bundles many tasks into one program.)

The founders claim the framework “can overlap memory-bound inference with compute-bound training,” meaning it can run a task that spends most of its time waiting for data to be fetched alongside one that spends most of its time doing math, so the chip is rarely sitting idle. The premise is that AI has barely scratched the surface of what GPUs can do, and they believe it can create intelligent systems “without ingesting half the internet.”

The goal is systems that cost less to train and run. “A model that’s a million times more data efficient is probably a million times easier to put into the economy,” Asher Spector told TechCrunch shortly after the startup launched.

They now have a fresh $1 billion to hire and attempt to turn that goal into reality.

title: GM is giving OnStar an AI makeover
snippet: It's one of the biggest overhauls ever to the 30-year-old connected car product.
fullText:
General Motors is adding a personal AI assistant to OnStar as part of a broader makeover of the subscription-based connected car service that the U.S. automaker launched 30 years ago. 

The OnStar AI Assistant will debut in the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq EV in the coming months, with more GM vehicles to follow, the company said Wednesday at its GM Forward event in New York, where it made a series of other technology announcements covering software, automated driving, EVs, and its electrical architecture. The company said it will launch a new OnStar mobile app in 2027 that will complement and sync up with its in-car software.

The new OnStar mobile app will replace the current OnStar Guardian app that launched in 2020 as well as vehicle brand apps for Buick, Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC. 

This tech-centric reboot is unlike other attempts to modernize OnStar, and it notably puts agentic AI at the center. The company has updated the safety and roadside assistance service numerous times in its history, especially in the past five years as it tried to stay apace of emerging and tech-forward competitors like Tesla.

In 2021, the company expanded its OnStar Guardian app, which offered crash detection, emergency assistance, and location sharing to anyone with a compatible phone, even if they didn’t own a GM vehicle. A year later, GM started using Google Cloud’s conversational AI Dialogflow to recognize specific spoken requests and expanded in 2023 to give drivers responses to common queries like routing and navigation assistance — all part of GM’s plan to build a $25 billion subscription business by 2030.

GM continued to focus on generative AI but relied on Google to provide the experience. The company said last year that Google Gemini would roll out in vehicles in 2026.

Image Credits:GM

The OnStar AI Assistant is an in-house effort and one aimed at giving the driver and passengers an interactive and custom experience — and become even more embedded in their daily lives. 

“OnStar is now transitioning to be a connected intelligence platform, not just the call center that it’s historically been known as, but a mechanism for interpreting, understanding, and providing predictive, proactive support to its owners,” GM’s VP of global product and chief product officer Sterling Anderson told TechCrunch in an interview ahead of the GM Forward event.

For instance, cameras on the vehicle will be connected to the software to offer live views as well as crash and safety recordings. Users can set up the connected cameras to turn on automatically if the vehicle senses an impending event — such as an aggressive horn honk — then capture the event and upload it to the OnStar app. Users will be able to use voice to control certain functions on the vehicle, including climate, and ask questions about any specific vehicle feature.

The launch coincides with efforts throughout the auto industry to stay apace of Chinese automakers with technology that is central to the vehicle — and no longer a slapped-on gimmick or feature. But that has required GM to change its approach to software development, adopt AI tools, and even design a new electrical and centralized compute vehicle architecture.

The announcement also comes after GM has been criticized and even fined for sharing data with third parties. Earlier this year, the Federal Trade Commission finalized an order that bans General Motors and its OnStar telematics service from sharing certain consumer data with consumer reporting agencies. The finalized order also requires the automaker to be more transparent with its consumers and obtain their explicit consent on certain data collection.

GM said Wednesday that customers will have the ability to decide what data is shared and that the recordings have time limits and are encrypted. GM said it and OnStar cannot access Connected Camera recordings.

A GM spokesperson later stated that third-party sharing is “feature-specific and consent-based, with information shared only as needed to provide requested functionality.” Customers can manage permissions and withdraw consent; however, those who choose not to share certain data may have limited access to related features, while other OnStar services would continue, according to GM.

title: Meta says it has fixed an issue that let its Ray-Ban smart glasses record on their own
snippet: As privacy complaints continue to dominate the conversation around Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, the company is now fixing an issue that was letting the glasses record on their own without the user prompting the recording. more…
fullText:
As privacy complaints continue to dominate the conversation around Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, the company is now fixing an issue that was letting the glasses record on their own without the user prompting the recording.

A number of Ray-Ban Meta users on Reddit note that, recently, their glasses have been invoking Meta AI and, in turn, voice recording, without prompts. The “Hey Meta” wake word was not used and, for some, not even enabled. One user says this happened across three separate pairs of glasses. 

The glasses still alert users to the recordings by lighting up the LED on the inner frame of the glasses, but it’s obviously a bit concerning to randomly have the glasses start recording on their own, even if it is audio only. 

Speaking to Android Authority, Meta confirmed that the issue has been “resolved.”

	

This issue has been resolved. People can manage, review and delete voice logs of their interactions with Meta AI via settings at any time.

The cause isn’t mentioned, but it comes at a time where Meta’s smart glasses are under continual scrutiny for privacy. Meta, in trying to correct its course, has made adjustments to its glasses including rolling out a mandatory update that disables the camera on its glasses if someone tampers with the LED privacy light.
