title: Galaxy S26 Ultra is one of the ‘best inventions of 2026’ thanks to its Privacy Display
snippet: A new 2026 roundup has the Galaxy S26 Ultra included in a list of best inventions for the year, all thanks to what it doesn’t display. more…
fullText:
A new 2026 roundup has the Galaxy S26 Ultra included in a list of best inventions for the year, all thanks to what it doesn’t display.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra split in a slightly different direction. Instead of a display panel treatment with an anti-gflare coating, Samsung decided to pack an entirely different feature into the panel itself.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display allows users to block certain aspects of the screen from nearby onlookers, effectively circumventing the privacy screen protector so many users opt for.

According to Time‘s “best inventions of 2026” collection, the Galaxy S26 Ultra gets its plaudits for not the phone’s performance necessarily, but the Privacy Display. The listing quotes Samsung’s SVP of Mobile Product Management, who points to its flexible nature.

	

It’s undoubtedly a cool piece of display tech. The Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display not only blocks side-angle viewing, but it can do so in isolated portions of the screen to block PIN codes or notifications that drop from the top shade in Android.

It has some drawbacks, though, as we’ve pointed out before. It can be a little inconsistent in certain lighting conditions, and sometimes screen elements can look off. But it’s cool, and a nice addition to a phone that sits at a price range we now consider more affordable than what we’re probably getting here soon.

Time‘s piece goes on to list a couple of other familiar devices, like a lengthy segment on the iPhone Duo, propping it up rather highly. Another product we’re happy to see is the Clicks Power Keyboard.

AS for whether the Galaxy S27 Pro or Ultra will get a Privacy Display, rumors suggest it could happen. Time will tell as Samsung plans to launch the devices early next year.

title: Apple strikes deal with AI startup that lets musicians rework recorded music
snippet: The EU’s List of Acquisitions website was updated today with details of a deal struck in June between Apple and Samplab, a Swiss startup that described itself as offering “music production for the age of AI.” Here are the details. more…
fullText:
The EU’s List of Acquisitions website was updated today with details of a deal struck in June between Apple and Samplab, a Swiss startup that described itself as offering “music production for the age of AI.” Here are the details.

Apple’s string of AI deals continues

Last week, the List of Acquisitions section of the EU’s DMA website was updated with details on Apple’s move to acqui-hire Huxe, a startup founded by former NotebookLM engineers that specialized in generating personalized audio briefings and podcast-style content using AI.

Today, the list was updated yet again, revealing another deal involving Apple and an AI audio company.

Apple Inc. (“Apple”), through a subsidiary, will acquire certain assets of Samplab GmbH (“Samplab”) and offer employment to and hire certain Samplab employees. Samplab develops audio editing tools. Apple (together with its group companies) designs, manufactures and markets smartphones, personal computers, tablets, wearables and accessories, and sells a variety of related services.

Following the deal, Samplab’s website now redirects to Apple’s, while its social media accounts and YouTube channel appear to have been scrubbed of their previous posts and videos.

Previously, Samplab’s website described its “ultimate audio editor for musicians” as a tool that allowed creators to “edit audio files as if you were working with MIDI.” It also touted its ability to:

Detect and edit chords

They stay in key when you change them.

You can even export them as a midi file.

Make any samples sound good together

Samplab matches their tempo and key.

Easily adapt chords, melodies and drums.

Granular stem separation

Separate stems in any audio and

freely modify individual notes.

While Apple has not commented on the acquisition, it isn’t hard to imagine Samplab’s technology eventually making its way into Logic Pro or GarageBand, or even enhancing the audio editing capabilities of Final Cut Pro.

title: What’s going on with the web? The PHP issue and sites going offline
snippet: A significant number of websites have gone offline, and that’s not due to a service outage, but rather a deliberate decision by the site’s owners. The reason is because extremely dangerous security vulnerabilities have been found in a protocol used by most websites – PHP. This issue is unrelated to the separate vulnerability discovered in web certificates … more…
fullText:
A significant number of websites have gone offline, and that’s not due to a service outage, but rather a deliberate decision by the site’s owners.

The reason is because extremely dangerous security vulnerabilities have been found in a protocol used by most websites – PHP. This issue is unrelated to the separate vulnerability discovered in web certificates …

What is PHP?

PHP is one of the weirder acronyms around. While it originally stood for Personal Home Page, it’s now more usually defined as the recursive “PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.” 

PHP is an open-source, general-purpose scripting language, very well suited to web development and able to be embedded into HTML. It’s used by around 70% of all websites.

What happened?

AI models and a cybersecurity researcher simultaneously discovered a major security flaw in PHP in mid-August. A combination of two vulnerabilities allowed an exploit which could give an attacker direct access to the underlying file system or database behind a website. That could expose a vast amount of personal data.

To allow time for the problem to be patched by the PHP Foundation, disclosure of the vulnerabilities was embargoed until this week (though it leaked two days ahead of the embargo). However, not every website has been able to apply the patch as yet, and Amazon Web Services said that the vulnerabilities are being “broadly exploited” across the internet.

The problem is so serious that the NSA has advised that unpatched sites be taken offline until the problem is fixed.

Effective Immediately, all organizations using PHP for their systems are advised to be prepared for an update addressing two critical vulnerabilities. PHP is widely used for web applications. These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or…

— NSA Cyber (@NSACyber) October 21, 2026

For that reason, a great many commercial and government websites have been taken offline until PHP can be updated on their servers.

I’m happy to be able to confirm that 9to5Mac and its sister sites are already protected.

title: Tons of People Are Apparently Asking Meta’s Muse AI Agent to Shop for Them
snippet: A quarter of Meta Muse’s 10 million users are shopping online via the AI agent with an average spend of $200 per purchase, according to Mark Zuckerberg.
fullText:
We’re about to be immersed in the busiest shopping season of the year, and if Mark Zuckerberg has his way, people will completely hand over the responsibility of buying stuff to their own personal AI agent. In fact, according to the Meta CEO, that is already happening.

During the company’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday, Zuckerberg said that over a quarter of Meta Muse‘s engaged users — now totaling more than 10 million — were using the AI agent for shopping, with an “average purchase size of over $200.”

“Plaid told us that they hadn’t seen activity like they’re seeing with their connector on any other service before,” Zuckerberg said, referring to financial services company Plaid, which facilitates payments between stores and buyers. He added that, due to higher-than-expected volumes, Meta had to work with payment app Stripe to raise credit limits to meet the shopping demand by Muse users.

			

More from CNET

Now that the AI agent has achieved what Zuckerberg referred to as a “product-market fit,” the name of the game for Muse in the long term is that we may be living in a reality where you have your own personal AI agent communicating with a business’s AI agent to complete transactions without you ever needing to speak with someone directly.

“Billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together,” Zuckerberg said, painting a picture of what a large-scale Muse network could look like. 

One of the goals is to get Muse to scale up its revenue, which he believes will eventually surpass the earnings of Meta’s combined existing family of apps: Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Threads and Messenger.

‘The Muse network’

Then there’s the coming integration of Muse into Meta’s smart glasses, which will launch next month. Soon, you’ll be able to access Muse on the go, without having to pull out your smartphone to use it.

“Having your personal superintelligence with you throughout the day will be the most important part of the experience,” Zuckerberg said.

How will all this work together? That remains to be seen, but during the call, Zuckerberg referenced something called “the Muse network,” which he said is Meta’s plan to, if I understand things right, gamify the whole personal AI agent experience.

A Meta spokesperson didn’t immediately respond to CNET’s request for comment.

“It’s not just a kind of single-player game where you have your Muse, but making it so that your Muses can work with your friends’ and your families’ [Muses],” Zuckerberg said, before bringing the conversation back to shopping, “And if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent.”

Meta announced third-quarter revenue of $64.6 billion, a 26% jump from the $51.2 billion announced this time last year. Costs were significantly higher, however, up by 68% to $51.6 billion due in large part to the company’s “agreement with 52 attorneys general to resolve litigation related to teen mental health and social media, which provides for payments of up to approximately $18.59 billion.” Net income was up by 264% year-over-year to $9.9 billion for the quarter.

title: Honor’s new gaming phone & tablet have 10,000+ mAh batteries, fans, up to 240Hz OLED display
snippet: The Honor Win2 series and the Honor Tablet are pushing the boundaries of mobile tech, with impressive specs, built-in fans, and the same excellent eye care features the company is known for. more…
fullText:
The Honor Win2 series and the Honor Tablet are pushing the boundaries of mobile tech, with impressive specs, built-in fans, and the same excellent eye care features the company is known for.

If you thought refresh rates couldn’t get any higher, it’s time to think again. Honor just announced four new devices, all of which push OLED refresh rates in impressive ways. The most impressive on the docket is probably the Honor Win Tablet, which packs an unbelievable 240Hz OLED display onto an actively cooled 8.4-inch tablet.

Honor looks to be pushing extreme processing speed with an included 15,000rpm fan build into the camera island on the back, which should keep the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 nice and cool. The display sports 6,000-nit peak brightness, 4,400Hz or 5,920Hz PWM dimming (refresh rate-dependent), a 10,000mAh battery with 66W charging, 12GB or 16GB RAM, 256GB or 512GB storage, and Honor’s Android 17-based Magic OS 11. The Win Tablet starts at CNY 4,499 (~$670).

The Honor Win2 is this year’s flagship gaming phone from the company, sporting two active cooling fans. One ramps up to 20,000rpm, while the side fan cranks that up to 31,000rpm, ensuring this thing should never, ever overheat despite the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 alleged overheating issues.

	

The Win2 sports a new top-of-the-line OLED panel with 10,000-nit peak brightness, a 185Hz refresh rate, 5,920Hz PWM dimming, 16GB RAM, 1TB of storage, a 200MP 1/1.4-inch main camera with OIS, 10,100mAh battery (not a typo!), 100W wired and 80W wireless charging, IP68/69/69K ratings, and Honor’s Android 17-based Magic OS 11. Holy cow what a flagship, and it starts at CNY 5,499 (~$990).

And if that’s not enough for you, there’s also the Honor Win2 RT, which dials the processor back just a tad to a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, keeps the active cooling fan, uses a physically smaller 200MP camera sensor, and even somehow increases the battery capacity to 12,070mAh. This one starts at CNY 4,199 (~$630).

Lastly, the Honor Win Turbo is the company’s mid-range offering for the line, packing a Snapdragon 8s Gen 4, drops the main camera to 50MP, and ditches the active cooling fan, but still retains the absurdly amazing 12,070mAh battery of the Win2 RT. The Win Turbo starts at CNY 3,299 (~$500).

Like the previous Honor Win series, this one appears to be largely relegated to China only. Honor confirmed to us that there won’t be a global release, but that doesn’t count specific regional releases out of the question.

title: Xiaomi 18 Pro gears up for global debut with rumored battery cuts and €1,449 starting price
snippet: Ouch. That’s the reaction many will probably have around pricing for the Xiaomi 18 Pro series when it lands globally, with prices starting at €1,449 according to a new leak. more…
fullText:
Ouch. That’s the reaction many will probably have around pricing for the Xiaomi 18 Pro series when it lands globally, with prices starting at €1,449 according to a new leak.

YTechB reports that the Xiaomi 18 Pro series is headed to Europe with major price hikes in tow. Where last year’s Xiaomi 17 had a starting price of €999 with the Ultra at €1,499, the Xiaomi 18 Pro is starting the lineup at €1,449 this year. That’s a huge price jump seeing as it’s just €50 short of last year’s Ultra device.

Pricing is rumored to land as follows:

Xiaomi 18 Pro (256GB): €1,449

Xiaomi 18 Pro Max (512GB): €1,849

The report goes on to cite the EU’s EPREL labels to confirm that global variants of the Xiaomi 18 Pro series will be cut down from the Chinese models. Xiaomi 18 Pro has a 7,000 mAh battery in China, but will only have a 6,000 mAh battery in Europe. Similarly, the Pro Max has an 8,500 mAh battery in China, but will be cut to 7,050 mAh in Europe. The base Pro is limited to 90W charging in the EU for reasons unclear.

	

The Xiaomi 18 Pro series is among the first to adopt Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip and launched in China last month. The timeline for a global release remains unclear at this point, but the MWC tech conference in Barcelona each Spring is often when Xiaomi kicks off availability. For 2026, Xiaomi 17 launched on February 28, with MWC 2027 start to start on March 1.

title: Gemini 4 Argon is now rolling out to Google’s Antigravity for AI Pro subscribers
snippet: Google is now rolling out support for Gemini 4 Argon to Antigravity, its AI coding tool. more…
fullText:
Google is now rolling out support for Gemini 4 Argon to Antigravity, its AI coding tool.

Gemini 4 Argon is Google’s latest flagship AI model, announced at the end of September and having widely rolled out to users earlier this week. Now, it’s also available within Antigravity.

Antigravity is an agentic development platform, as Google describes it, which leverages AI and agents to assist in coding and building apps. Google announced that Argon would be available in Antigravity earlier this week, and it’s now actively rolling out to AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers – we’re seeing it live on our end, too.

Google restricts every free AI Pro trial from Pixel & more compared to paid subscribers

In a post on Twitter/X, Google adds that there’s “a separate weekly-only Argon quota” on top of the existing quota for Gemini 3.8 Flash, meaning you’ll be able to use the model that best suits your needs. Google says that Argon is “designed to tackle your hardest problems.”

	

Google also provided a host of examples of how Argon in Antigravity has been used internally, including:

YouTube comment optimization: Argon in Antigravity helped the team cut the CPU footprint of YouTube’s comments frontend in half. By tracing production profile data, Argon identified that redundant emoji rendering alone accounted for nearly 45% of server overhead, leading to 12 targeted optimizations. The updates reduced server comment-load latency by 30 ms and dropped client end-to-end latency by 20 ms.

Debugging Wing drone physics simulator: Argon in Antigravity reviewed Wing’s proprietary internal drone physics simulator, reasoning through the underlying physics and math rather than just the structure of the code. It highlighted areas for improved physics simulations and proposed 18 targeted modelling improvements across aerodynamics, propulsion, and structural dynamics to resolve long-standing legacy issues.

Burning down the backlog: Argon in Antigravity took an aging queue of 134 open bug reports spanning multiple services, and ran agents to work out which were still real, cross-referencing commit histories, checking whether candidate fixes actually reached production, and inspecting live telemetry for whether the error still occurs. In under 3 hours it closed 97 stale or duplicate bugs with documented commit proof (a 72.4% queue reduction) and sorted the remaining 37 by owner with no unassigned tickets left.

Migrating legacy code: For decades, vital scientific research has been locked inside fragile legacy codebases like Fortran. Using a custom skill within Antigravity, a team deployed Argon to map and execute a complete rewrite into modern Rust. Argon autonomously delivered the modernized codebase, achieving a 1.8x performance boost and memory safety while giving scientists a robust foundation for future work.

Performing security audits: Argon in Antigravity was used to audit a batch of access-control changes. Argon traced how permissions actually flowed at runtime rather than just reading the code diff, and found four critical security bugs. Two earlier frontier models had audited the identical code and both concluded there were zero security holes.

Triaging production support tickets: Argon in Antigravity batch-processes dozens of tickets from an on-call rotation. It sorts them by issue type, tracing root causes through the code and logs, proposing fixes and drafting the replies for human approval. This has freed up 2-3 hours per shift, enabling the team to focus on resolving issues faster.

Marketing website localization: The Antigravity DevRel team used Argon in Antigravity to localize hundreds of pages of developer documentation into 17 languages in a matter of hours. This improved the accessibility and UX of the website by shrinking a multi-week process down to hours and shifting human effort exclusively to high-quality review.

Accelerating data center pipeline modernization: Demonstrating how AI-augmented execution helps teams do more with less, a Data Science Technical Program Manager leveraged Argon in Antigravity to fast-track development of a 3,200-line Google Data Center fleet analytics pipeline (Python, SQL, and dashboards) into production in days. Pairing with Argon to rapidly resolve complex multi-system edge cases, eliminate hardcoded legacy assets, and optimize timeseries queries against timeouts drove end-to-end efficiency — delivering a clean, production-grade, and extensible architecture for fleet-scale analytics.

Vetting sales prospects: Argon in Antigravity built an automated qualification workflow for an account executive in Ads sales that checks prospective company website traffic, confirms the site has clear conversion funnels, and cross-references the sales database to see whether the account is a qualified prospect. This reduced research time by 90%, saving the account executive upwards of 10 hours of manual work each week so they can spend time on direct client outreach instead.

Financial planning and analysis: With custom finance plugins, a finance lead used Argon in Antigravity for end-to-end financial reconciliations, budget tracking, contract extraction, and daily executive briefings across 80 separate workflows. Over seven business days, 15.5 hours of human direction produced about 335 human-equivalent hours of validated financial output, saving more than eight weeks of manual work.

title: I Went From AI Prompt to 3D-Printed Armor in 18 Hours
snippet: What started off as a dare became a fully fledged app in less than a day
fullText:
Tuesday morning, I received a notification from Google saying I could try out the new Gemini 4 Argon model. Normally, I just ignore it — I don’t really care which model it is, as long as it can help me with my day-to-day — but this time Google teased me with something close to my heart.

Gemini said it could “Create an app to model lampshades that I can 3D print.” My response, as CNET’s resident 3D printing expert, was, “I bet you can’t.”

Turns out, yes, it can.

			

More from CNET

I went from these first few screenshots to a fully 3D-printed object in under 18 hours, and I’m impressed by how easy it was.

Having a conversation with Gemini 4.0 is a lot like chatting with a designer or developer.Screenshot by James Bricknell/CNET

I’ll say upfront that I don’t really like generative AI. I think it uses people’s art and creative work without fair compensation, and I want to pay artists for their work. I changed the project from making lampshades to making cosplay armor and deliberately limited it to things I can already make myself. I know how to model greaves, pauldrons and vambraces, so this takes away nothing.

In my mind, this is analogous to a blacksmith who gets an apprentice to make the blanks for steel armor. The fine detail and character of the work is done by one person, but the grunt work is done by another. I can’t make very good chestplates or helmets, so I removed them from the app to focus on what I can make.

The planning stages

Talking to Gemini 4 feels the same as talking to any of the Gemini models. It understands what I’m saying and, more importantly, my intent. The first app Gemini created looked terrible on mobile. There were too many windows and not enough visuals of the model we were making. Explaining that the app was too messy and that we needed to clear it up got the response I wanted, rather than a bunch more questions.

The difference with Gemini 4 Argon is its ability to accomplish complex tasks at speed. Things like making complex web apps seem easy, and the time it took to give me new iterations was far less than with the Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite model I’m used to using.

I have Gemini Plus because I have a Google One plan, and I hit the token limit several times as I developed the app, but waiting an hour for a reset wasn’t that big a deal. If you have the Pro version, you’ll likely be OK.

The first few versions had too many options.Screenshot by James Bricknell/CNET

The first few versions of KeriForge (the name I settled on for my armor web app) were surprisingly usable right away. All the sliders for adjusting the model size worked. While they weren’t all intuitive, they had enough features to get me started. I kept going back, though. I removed some features, such as the helmet generator, and added new ones, including the strap hole marker and circumference calculator.

Gemini understood that these changes needed to reflect the physical nature of the end result. Instead of trying to cut holes in the digital model for the straps, it created marks on the model, so I could cut them out in the real world. 3D models need to be manifold — all their faces need to face the right way and connect to be “watertight” — otherwise, they can fail on the print bed. Making random holes in the model would most definitely cause it to fail.

Slowly getting the app dialed in.

At one point, I asked Gemini to let me “Download this onto my iPad Pro to make it easier to use.” Gemini understood that I didn’t want to make an iPad app, but that I wanted the web app to be available offline on my iPad. It made the app available as HTML and, once I got it up on Google Sites, told me how to download it using Safari.

It also has its own preview that lets me see the app running directly from the Gemini app on the iPad, so making changes was easy and instantaneous. It took around 10 iterations to reach KeriForge 8.2 and a state that I felt was good enough to produce a physical print.

The finishing touches?

Nomad Sculpt is powerful, and I ‘ve barely scratched the surface.

Creating the app was a lot of fun, and I learned a lot about how Gemini works and ways to prompt it to get a better finished article, but my original skepticism wasn’t that Gemini couldn’t make the app, but that it couldn’t produce a fully 3D-printable design that I could make physically.

I spent some time measuring my arm and adjusting the blank vambrace to make sure it would fit if it did print, then I hit the export button. Because I used my iPad, I got to export it directly to Nomad Sculpt, a 3D sculpting tool that let me add some random squiggles and an approximation of my name on the side of the model.

From there, I exported the file once again, this time to a browser app called Layerling. This app lets me edit the STL file — STL is the format for plain 3D models without any color — to cut the holes the straps need to go through. It’s a much more comprehensive program than the one I just made, so I know it can handle cutting the model while keeping it 3D-printable. I’ve only used Layerling a few times, but the more I do, the more impressive it becomes.

Making the holes in the model was simple, and since I had already asked Gemini to ensure there were guide markers, finding the right location was painless. Once I had cut those holes, it was onto the final stage: printing.

But will it actually print?

The defects were caused by the material, not the model Gemini produced.

Once I had the final STL ready for printing, it was a simple matter to export it over to Bambu Slicer and start the actual print. I chose to print it in TPU 75A, a flexible material I was already testing. TPU is a soft, rubbery material, so it can conform to my arm better than the more rigid plastics like PLA and ABS.

This was the moment when my bet with Gemini would come to fruition. After 7 hours of printing and about 11 hours of iterating and fiddling with Gemini, we would see whether the model actually worked or ended up as spaghetti all over my printer.

Printing it upright may not have been the right call.

The screenshot clearly shows that it did, indeed, work. You can see that, despite some errors that weren’t caused by the model, it produced a fully manifold and usable 3D print. The dimensions were perfect, fitting my forearm length and wrist circumference exactly.

The errors you can see on the model stem from the TPU being too soft and the model being too tall. As the printer increased the model’s height, the tension relaxed, causing the model to wobble under the print head. In the future, I would need to support it better in the slicer or print it lying down to achieve the print quality I expect.

An impressive AI tool

The final form of KeriForge works almost as I intend it.

I’m not an AI power user. I like to use Gemini to organize my emails, help me sort out spreadsheets, and that’s about it. I assumed that creating a web app capable of producing a fully physical product, such as a 3D model, would be arduous; that I would have to constantly refine my prompts to get it to understand my needs and wants. That wasn’t the case, though. Gemini Argon seemed to understand the context of what I wanted far better than I gave it credit for.

The term “prompt engineering” has always made me shy away from using these products. I don’t want to spend time trying to get an AI to understand what I need when a person could do it much more quickly. I can see now that by using that term, gatekeepers can put AI behind a knowledge wall: to present it as a mysterious, complex thing. It simply isn’t the case with the latest models.

I still don’t like generative AI, but I can’t help but be impressed by something that can take me from an idea to a physical product in less than a day. I went into this challenge betting Gemini 4 couldn’t do what it said it could, and was humbled in the process. I’m not going to start using AI for everything I do, but I’ve already thought of some fun ways it can help me with upcoming projects. Something that inspires my creativity can’t be all bad, can it?

title: DeepSeek reportedly raises $15B days after US restrictions
snippet: DeepSeek has reportedly raised $15 billion in one of China's largest funding rounds, just days after the US ordered federal agencies to remove its technology over national security concerns.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

6:11 AM PDT · October 22, 2026

Image Credits:GREG BAKER/AFP / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Just two days after the U.S. ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek’s AI technology from their systems over security concerns, the Chinese AI lab has raised about $15 billion, about 100 billion yuan, one of the biggest funding rounds in the country, Bloomberg reported.

Potential investors include Chinese battery maker CATL and Tencent, the company behind WeChat, among others, according to the report.

The reported funding follows DeepSeek’s investment round in June, when it raised more than $7 billion at a valuation of $50 billion. The company was also reportedly seeking an additional $1.5 billion at a valuation of around $71 billion in July, with plans for a potential IPO in China as early as next year.

The Hangzhou-based AI startup is ramping up spending on AI infrastructure and open models for domestic and international markets, even as it faces restrictions in the U.S., the report said. Its expansion could further intensify competition among domestic rivals.

The massive funding round is the latest sign of investors pouring billions into AI companies around the world, including those in China, to compete in the global AI race.  Chinese company Kimi developer Moonshot AI secured $2 billion at a $20 billion valuation in May. Manus AI raised more than $500 million earlier this month. Meanwhile, Chinese companies Zhipu AI (Z.ai) and MiniMax, which both went public in Hong Kong in January, have market capitalizations of roughly $29 billion and $7.2 billion, respectively, as of today.

DeepSeek was founded in 2023 by Liang Wenfeng, who previously co-founded Chinese quantitative hedge fund High-Flyer, which helped finance DeepSeek’s early development. The AI startup gained global attention in early 2025 with its free-to-use, open-weight RI reasoning model, challenging the dominance of US AI companies.  Liang still retains an estimated 81.6% stake in its Chinese operating entity following its earlier funding round, according to corporate ownership data analyzed by WireScreen.

DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a TechCrunch request for comment.

title: Google support pages start defaulting to AI chatbots – it might be for the best
snippet: Google is starting to move its support pages from detailed articles to AI summaries with a chatbot, with an added set of steps to access the full details of the any given page. more…
fullText:
Google is starting to move its support pages from detailed articles to AI summaries with a chatbot, with an added set of steps to access the full details of the any given page.

The Google Help portal is full of detailed articles that provide step-by-step processes for using a feature, documentation on where features are available or restrictions on them, as well as troubleshooting steps if something goes awry. It’s a massively useful resource, but one that Google is now changing.

Starting with support pages under Google Account Help, the company is shifting these support articles to an AI summary rather than a dedicated article. “Ask Google Help” will display a condensed version of the support article with direct troubleshooting steps, with the user then able to type in queries to have Gemini help figure out the next step forward.

A “View Sources” button at the bottom of the AI response allows users to still access the original article, but direct links to any of these articles now defaults to the AI experience.

	

An example can be seen below on the “Secure a hacked or compromised Google account” page that Google’s own support account directed users to within the past few days. It can also be seen on the “Fix common issues with 2-Step Verification” page and, as far as we can tell, any support pages on the Google Account Help forum.

Google, as of right now, appears to only be testing this on select support topics. The Google Pixel Help section, for instance, still defaults to articles, whereas the Google Chrome topic has also moved to the new experience.

Beyond support pages alone, this new design also impacts the central hub, with links to topics no longer showing by default in exchange for an AI chatbot that helps you find the relevant page.

Ironically enough, the Gemini topic is one of the ones missing this Gemini-powered experience.

9to5Google’s Take

While my initial reaction to this was skeptical, I think this is a rather good use of AI.

Google’s support page collection tends to be a bit of a labyrinth of links and vague search terms. Finding the specific page needed to address the problem you are running into can be very difficult. Meanwhile, Gemini’s inherent ability to understand natural language queries and find associated sources is very powerful in this regard.

I’m still a bit iffy on whether or not dedicated support articles should be converted into an AI summary (which Google still warns could be inaccurate), but using Gemini as a search and troubleshooting tool in this specific regard really highlights a strength of the technology.

What do you think?

title: Tech Issues Are on the Ballot This Midterm Election Season: What to Know
snippet: AI, data centers and Flock cameras are key tech policy issues shaping the campaigns, candidates and voters.
fullText:
The midterm elections are scheduled for Nov. 3, with early voting already off the ground in some states. In campaigns across the country, politicians are talking about the biggest controversies in tech, from privacy and cybersecurity to child online safety. These hot-button issues are exposing major gaps in US legislation and foundational vulnerabilities that now fuel intense debate over emerging technologies like AI.

Big Tech executives are also ramping up political contributions ahead of the elections, exerting major financial influence over electoral races. Elon Musk is one of the biggest donors, funneling around $366 million into conservative causes and right-wing candidates, according to The Guardian. The venture capitalist firm Andreessen Horowitz has spent $91.3 million this year on Republican-aligned groups. OpenAI President Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, made a $25 million personal donation to a pro-AI PAC called Leading the Future. (The Brockmans were also among the largest individual donors to a MAGA super PAC in 2024.)

Here’s what you need to know about three of the biggest tech policy debates that may show up on your ballot or affect your vote this November. Make sure to review your state’s board of elections website or other sources like Vote.org to check your registration, find your polling place and see a sample ballot. You can also read CNET’s tips for spotting political deepfakes and scams.

			

More from CNET

Data center construction

Data centers have found a rare point of agreement across the political spectrum:  70% of US adults — spanning Republicans, Democrats and independents — are opposed to local data center construction, according to a July Gallup poll. 

Residents have good reason to be wary of these massive server farms. To keep generative AI programs running, data centers eat up enormous amounts of electricity and water. Some neighborhoods have seen rising electricity costs passed onto them or had their water contaminated during construction. 

Pro-data center advocates claim these facilities create jobs and long-term investment, but critics warn that there aren’t many long-term positions available once construction is complete. 

Facing significant public backlash, states have already begun legislating. In July, New York enacted a temporary pause on hyperscale data center construction, and many other state legislatures are considering similar bills. Back in April, a similar measure was proposed in Maine, but outgoing Democratic Gov. Janet Mills vetoed the bill. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree has said Mills was wrong to veto the “incredibly urgent” moratorium.

President Donald Trump has been a staunch supporter of data centers, claiming that data center opposition is “Chinese PR” and that communities that don’t allow data centers will end up “backwards and poor.” There’s no proof either claim is true.

Despite Trump’s political and financial allegiance to Big Tech’s data center projects, politicians in both red and blue states are feeling pressure from their respective constituencies. A leaked GOP strategy memo called data centers “a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle,” one that can dramatically sway public opinion and alter results. 

Nowhere is this issue more relevant than in Virginia, home to more data centers than any other state, where both Senate candidates have spoken about needing to rein them in. During a Q&A with local news, incumbent Democrat Mark Warner said that data centers shouldn’t be allowed to pass on their electric costs to residents, and Republican Bert Mizusawa said that he would support communities being able to block data centers from moving in. 

It’s a leading issue in Texas, too. Republican Gov. Greg Abbott announced a “pause” on data center construction, but recent reports show it failed to slow down development. Meanwhile, The Texas Tribune revealed that Abbott took $5 million in donations from data center owners. His Democratic challenger, Gina Hinojosa, has called for a genuine freeze on new data center facilities.

Flock surveillance cameras

AI-enabled cameras and automated license plate readers made by companies like Flock have sparked intense debate over surveillance and privacy, reaching a fever pitch in local and state governments this year. 

Flock Safety says its tech helps law enforcement do its job and reduce crime. Over 6,000 communities across the US have Flock cameras, according to a July estimate from the company. 

Flock cameras are popping up across the country.Bloomberg/Contributor/Getty

Lawyers and digital rights advocates like the Electronic Frontier Foundation have highlighted how Flock violates the Fourth Amendment and how its capabilities are easily abused. Law enforcement officers have allegedly used Flock cameras to stalk ex-girlfriends, track people seeking abortions, aid ICE activity and carry out warrantless searches. In one memorable instance that quickly went viral online, a costumed Darth Vader praised Flock at a San Diego city council meeting, saying: “The emperor is a fan of Flock.”

Opposition to Flock is another national issue that crosses party lines, based on shared concerns around government overreach and civil liberties. In Texas, Democratic Senate hopeful James Talarico said, “Flock cameras have no place in Texas,” and Abbott paused the state’s funding for Flock. More than 200 cities have canceled or chosen not to renew their Flock contracts, the BBC reported in September. Some districts also have ballot measures about the tech, like one in York, Maine, that lets voters decide whether to ban automated license plate readers.

AI regulation

Unsurprisingly, artificial intelligence has taken center stage among this election season’s tech concerns. And for good reason: The controversial tech is far more pervasive now than it was in 2024, and fears about AI have grown in tandem with its capabilities.

Nearly half of US adults under 30 say AI will have a negative impact on society, and across age groups, more than 60% say AI is advancing too quickly, the Pew Research Center found in July. There are widespread public concerns over job loss, the spread of misinformation, the proliferation of deepfakes and economic volatility. 

UNC-Chapel Hill students and local residents protested Big Tech outside the G20 forum.Katelyn Chedraoui/Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

One of the biggest AI policy debates is over the role of the federal government in regulating the tech, with many of the major labs arguing that they are capable of “self policing.” The Trump administration has been vocal about avoiding AI regulatory policies and touting frameworks that give more power to AI companies than regulators, including during the G20 this fall.

While AI itself won’t be directly on the ballot like local initiatives around data centers and Flock cameras, it’s become a critical flashpoint for voters. The tension was vividly illustrated during the summer elections, most notably in New York’s congressional primary.

Democratic State Assemblymember Alex Bores, who authored some of the country’s strictest state-level AI safety laws, found his congressional bid transformed into a multimillion-dollar proxy war. He garnered national attention with his call to regulate Big Tech more forcefully, which then resulted in more than $8 million poured into attack ads and his opponent’s campaign. Bores ultimately lost, but the race signaled a major tech battlefield, where advocacy of AI guardrails goes against the deep pockets and lobbying influence of Silicon Valley.

title: PHP Armageddon: OpenAI, Google’s Wiz find ancient holes, panicking the internet
snippet: This is the kind of security issue that was found and prevented by AI, but is also a high risk because of AI.
fullText:
The U.S. National Security Agency’s sent out an alarming warning on Wednesday that two critical holes had been found in PHP, with patches already issued by the PHP Foundation.

PHP is a server-side programming language so widely used for web applications that it powers roughly 70% of the websites on the internet; by some accounts, that’s more than 33 million sites. It is also used by popular content management systems like WordPress.

The NSA warned that these holes are so severe that if a website can’t be patched immediately, it should be pulled off the web until it can be. The holes allow attackers to infiltrate the server’s file system or a database that may be used by the web app.

Interestingly, these holes have been tucked away in all versions of PHP since version 5, which was released in 2004. Websites not running relatively current versions of PHP will have some updating work to do, as PHP 8.1 and older versions are no longer supported. The recommendation is to update the web server to the current version of PHP, which is 8.5.12.

So how did two such ubiquitous, decades-old flaws that affect nearly every website on the internet suddenly come to light? AI, naturally, particularly via OpenAI and Google’s Wiz.

Security testing company Calif was engaged in OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” initiative to find flaws in open source software. Using GPT‑5.6 Sol, it found one of the flaws, OpenAI disclosed in a blog post. Separately, the Wiz team also used AI, namely its Wiz Atlas security AI agent, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol to find multiple vulnerabilities in PHP.

Both OpenAI and Wiz followed responsible security research practices and worked with PHP on patches before publicly disclosing the flaws. Then they all worked together to flesh out what they found, and test the patches, drawing in a host of others to help. 

Wiz thanked Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare, Fastly, Imperva, Microsoft, and Vercel. (While WordPress sites use PHP, WordPress has issued a statement saying that the flaw isn’t WordPress specific, and sites running its CMS must patch their servers and work with their web-hosting companies to ensure their sites are protected.)

OpenAI says that these flaws were found by researchers before hackers discovered them. So there were no reports of exploits in the wild. This is also in part because, before AI, these flaws were too hard for hackers to exploit. “With AI this is no longer a barrier. LLMs can help adapt an exploit to different PHP versions, configurations and memory layouts,” Wiz warned in its blog about the flaws.

In other words, this is the kind of security issue that was found and prevented because of AI, but is also a high risk only because of AI.

Now that the issue has been disclosed, hackers are fully in the know. The race is on for the internet to patch tens millions of websites before hackers can attack the unpatched ones. Hence the NSA’s guidance that if you can’t patch your PHP website right away, you’re better off pulling it offline until you can.

title: Just because Tesla’s Optimus is in production doesn’t mean it’s actually ready
snippet: On Tesla's earnings call Wednesday, CEO Elon Musk announced that the company had begun early production of its humanoid robot on its high-volume line in Fremont, California. Then he laid out what still needs work: the robot's hands, its safety, reliability, and durability, and the artificial intelligence needed to make it a productive tool. "There's still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks," Musk said. "At some point, there will be more humanoid robots on Earth than there are humans." ELON MUSK These are substantial caveats for a product slated for volume production. … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
On Tesla’s earnings call Wednesday, CEO Elon Musk announced that the company had begun early production of its humanoid robot on its high-volume line in Fremont, California. Then he laid out what still needs work: the robot’s hands, its safety, reliability, and durability, and the artificial intelligence needed to make it a productive tool.

“There’s still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks,” Musk said.

“At some point, there will be more humanoid robots on Earth than there are humans.”

— ELON MUSK

These are substantial caveats for a product slated for volume production. Musk expects the pieces to come together around the end of 2027, when Tesla could begin delivering Optimus to outside companies, but didn’t say which or what exactly the robots would do for them. In the meantime, Tesla needs to build a fleet of robots that can practice tasks and generate training data, then feed what they learn back into the system. It also needs to integrate a new chip that Musk says will give the robots far more computing power.

Tesla called the machines coming off the Fremont line its first “production-quality bots” and said its manufacturing process was suitable for a commercial product. But the company did not disclose how many robots it has produced, what tasks they can currently perform autonomously, or how often they can complete the tasks without human intervention. The announcement marks a step toward manufacturing Optimus at scale, not evidence that Tesla has a robot ready to do even the initial jobs Musk envisions — dangerous, repetitive industrial work performed around the clock — let alone become the general-purpose household machine he ultimately imagines.

“You can produce them, but the software is lacking,” Ken Goldberg, a robotics professor at the University of California, Berkeley, told The Verge. “If you have a lot of hardware without the software, I think that’s a big problem.”

Musk himself spent much of his discussion of Optimus explaining why investors shouldn’t expect finished robots to immediately pour out of the factory. Production will follow an S-curve, he said, with a slow, bumpy beginning. “There’s like 10,000 things that have to go right for production of the robot,” Musk said, “and it will move as fast as the slowest.”

Most of the equipment for a line intended to produce a million robots annually is already in Fremont, according to Musk. But reaching a rate of 20,000 robots a week will take “at least a year, maybe a little longer,” he said.

“There’s still parts of the design that are changing,” Musk said. “You’ve got to basically build up an entire gigantic global supply chain and have domestically a very, very big factory, and everything has got to work.”

“If you have a lot of hardware without the software, I think that’s a big problem.”

— KEN GOLDBERG

Those production challenges are only one part of the unfinished work.

A robot that can repeatedly perform a carefully defined task has a different job from a general-purpose humanoid expected to adapt to varied objects and surroundings. Musk described industrial applications as the first market for Optimus, with at-home purchases coming as the robot develops a much wider range of capabilities.

Optimus is “going to do like 1,000 times more things than a car would do,” Musk said.

Some of Goldberg’s more pessimistic colleagues think a truly useful humanoid robot is still 25 years away, he said. Goldberg believes the field will solve its hardest problems — including reliability, speed, and dexterity — sooner than that. But even he doesn’t expect them to be solved on Musk’s timeline.

Robots have become adept at walking, running, and jumping, Goldberg said, but dexterity remains much harder. Manipulating flexible materials, such as wires and fabric, or assembling products is incredibly difficult; doing it quickly and reliably enough for real work is harder still.

“I’ve been working on these problems for 40 years,” Goldberg said. “I don’t think they’re going to be solved in the next year or two.”

Musk acknowledged that Tesla is ramping production before resolving Optimus’ main hardware problem: its hands. “We’re building robots that do not have perfected hands,” he said.

Unlike human hands, robot hands can’t heal themselves. Yet they must withstand repeated use while remaining soft enough to handle delicate objects without damaging their sensors. “What an incredible thing the human hand is at the end of the day,” Musk said.

Durability is a challenge for the rest of the robot, too. “It can’t, like, wear out after a month,” Musk said.

Closing the software gap will require training data Tesla doesn’t yet have. Unlike its cars, Optimus has no vast installed base from which the company can gather information. Musk said Tesla therefore needs to build roughly 10,000 to 20,000 robots to practice tasks at what he called “Optimus Academy.”

“With Optimus, we have to bootstrap it by making the robots and having them do self-play, which is really how a human learns to navigate the world,” Musk said. He compared the process to a toddler gradually mastering increasingly complex skills. “Eventually, they learn to wipe their own ass, which is a big milestone,” Musk said. “And then they learn to read and do all sorts of things.”

Goldberg described learning through self-play as a hypothesis whose success in software doesn’t establish that it will work as well in physical hardware. “When you get into hardware, it’s not so clear,” he said.

Tesla is also waiting on hardware that has yet to be integrated. Musk said he hopes to put the company’s AI5 chip into Optimus around April 2027, providing roughly 10 times the computing power of AI4. He expects the new chip, improved software, and mechanical refinements to come together before customer deliveries.

If all that works, Musk expects Optimus will eventually have a hand in its own production. “The Optimus robots will build the future Optimus robots,” he said, describing a self-reinforcing production loop that would grow “extremely fast.”

“At some point, there will be more humanoid robots on Earth than there are humans,” Musk predicted.

Before then, Musk promised a video within a month or two showing Optimus performing tasks that aren’t preprogrammed. He criticized humanoid demonstrations that look impressive but wouldn’t translate into useful real-world performance. “If you actually try to use that humanoid robot in the real world, you would have a lot of trouble,” he said. “It wouldn’t work, basically.”

Goldberg calls the problem “video emptor.” A video might show the one successful attempt out of a thousand, he said, hide a person controlling the robot offscreen, or depend on a precisely arranged setting. In robotics labs, task success rates have stalled at around 70 to 80 percent, Goldberg said. “That’s not acceptable for real industry.”

Musk remains convinced Optimus will become “the biggest product on Earth.” While Tesla’s announcement brings it closer to manufacturing Optimus in large numbers, building a robot customers can depend on – and actually use – remains a separate milestone.

title: Tesla starts Optimus robot production in California as profit falls 43%
snippet: Tesla's revenue was flat and its expenses skyrocketed as it pressed the accelerator on its Optimus robots, AI, and autonomous driving.
fullText:
Tesla has started production of its Optimus humanoid robot at its factory in Fremont, California, in a manufacturing space once dedicated to making electric vehicles, the company announced Wednesday.

“The bots coming off this line are the first production-quality bots that we have manufactured,” Tesla wrote in its third-quarter letter to shareholders. “While we will continue to iterate on the hardware and manufacturing process, we have proven that the current manufacturing process for Optimus is suitable for a commercial product.”

Tesla CEO Elon Musk said on a conference call that he considers this “early production” and that the ramp will be slow and “somewhat bumpy because it is such a radically new product.” He nonetheless claimed Tesla will be able to make 20,000 of them per week by the end of 2027.

“There’s still some things we need to tweak about the design, because you need to deliver a robot that is safe and reliable and has long duration, so it can’t, like, wear out after a month,” he said. “And there’s still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks.”

That forward-looking development wasn’t enough to lift the company’s otherwise middling third-quarter earnings, results that typify a company in the midst of a major bet. Tesla’s revenue was flat and its expenses skyrocketed as it pressed the accelerator on its Optimus robots, AI, and autonomous driving. The end result was a 43% drop in profits.

The company’s revenue was largely driven by EV sales, which were flat year-over-year at $20 billion. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter, about 6,000 more than the previous quarter, but fewer than in the same period last year. 

Tesla’s total third-quarter revenue was $28.04 billion, a skosh below the $28.09 billion it generated in the third quarter of 2025. Tesla’s third-quarter revenue was also about $200 million lower than the previous quarter’s haul of $28.23 billion.

Tesla saw a 16% year-over-year decline in revenue from its solar and energy storage business to $2.8 billion, which it blamed on tariff-related customer refunds. There was some positive revenue growth in its services business, a category that includes customer subscriptions to its Full Self-Driving advanced driver-assistance software. Tesla’s services business grew 33% year-over-year, bringing in $4.6 billion and accounting for a record $734 million in gross profit for the quarter.

None of this was enough to outpace Tesla’s spending on artificial intelligence projects and its Optimus robot, which took a big bite out of profits.

The company reported $787 million in net income, a 43% drop from the same period in 2025, when it earned $1.37 billion. Lower regulatory credit sales also put pressure on its profitability. 

Tesla executives on the earnings call, including Musk, CFO Vaibhav Taneja, and Ashok Elluswamy, vice president of AI software at Tesla, all took bullish positions on the company’s FSD product, even as the timeline to give consumers the “unsupervised” version was delayed yet again. Today, Tesla owners can subscribe to a supervised version of the software that requires the driver to pay attention and be ready to take over at any time. The unsupervised version would be the equivalent of Level 4 autonomous driving capabilities similar to those used in robotaxis. 

“We suspect somewhere around Q2 next year is when we can turn on some of the first customer vehicles to be part of the robotaxi fleet,” Elluswamy said, referring to when privately owned Tesla vehicles equipped with FSD (Supervised) would receive a software update enabling unsupervised driving. 

Musk said during the company’s earnings call in April that the unsupervised version would “probably” be released in the fourth quarter of this year.

title: AI and Data Centers Will Impact Midterm Voting, According to Experts
snippet: Americans are mostly negative on AI and oppose new data centers near them, another poll shows.
fullText:
As far as public opinion goes, artificial intelligence is not a bed of roses. With the Nov. 3 elections looming nationwide, an issue that was barely a blip a year ago has become a full-blown backlash and a likely spoiler in the midterm elections.

A new poll from ABC News, the Washington Post and Ipsos found that a majority of Americans (57%) believe AI is bad for society, with many more pointing to its dangers than the potential benefits the tech could bring. An even larger number of those polled (66%) are opposed to the construction of new data centers in the US, and more (72%) would be opposed if it were in their community. 

Opposition to AI crosses party lines. The technology has faced a surge in public disapproval this year, putting political candidates on blast and potentially affecting outcomes in key races, political and polling experts told CNET.

			

More from CNET

Ambivalence about AI also feeds into negativity toward data centers, which have, in a short time, become a rare bipartisan issue everyone’s talking about, according to Christopher Lee, partner and senior political strategist for Foresight Strategic Advisors.

Lee, who has closely followed election trends in southwestern states such as Nevada and Arizona, said the issue of data centers — massive AI server and compute farms that consume vast electricity and water resources — is going to “hammer” some candidates, especially those who weren’t transparent with constituents in the past about the cost to communities. If a politician voted for the construction of a data center earlier this year, their “political career is going to run into a stone wall,” he said.

Reading the room 

The ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos survey asked a wide range of questions about how Americans will vote in the midterms and what they think of the political parties. Alongside the economy, immigration and the war against Iran, the AI rollout is a critical issue. 

As noted by CNET reporter Katelyn Chedraoui, AI regulation and data center construction have been the subject of controversy, protests and increased legal action in communities.

The poll confirmed as much: 67% of respondents felt the government isn’t doing enough to regulate AI, with risks including widespread job losses, psychological dependency, economic inequality and even human extinction. Fears and negativity toward AI also extend to the election process itself, with AI election interference among Americans’ top 10 fears for 2026. 

A national PR campaign funded by tech leaders and supported by the Trump administration, meant to tout the alleged benefits of data centers, such as job creation and technological advancements, doesn’t seem to be having the intended effect. Some politicians, especially those running for congressional seats, seem to be better at reading the room. 

According to Lindsey Cormack, an associate professor of political science at Stevens Institute of Technology and co-host of the podcast Government That Doesn’t Suck, many candidates are paying close attention to how they communicate about AI developments, with a particular focus on the problems they present rather than the benefits they provide. 

“It’s difficult to persuade people with promises of economic development when they’re worried about their electricity bills or water supply,” she said.

Cormack, creator of the congressional newsletter archive DCinbox, has tracked a sharp rise in lawmakers linking data centers to consumer energy costs. In an email to CNET, she noted that between January and September 2025, just 5% of Republican newsletters discussing data centers mentioned electricity bills or ratepayers (4 of 76). Over the same period in 2026, that figure surged to 54% (97 of 180). Democrats showed a similar focus, with 40% of their data center newsletters (71 of 176) raising the issue in 2026.

The midterms won’t be the end of the battle. AI and data centers are “going to be an issue in 2028 and 2030 and way beyond that,” Lee said.

He lives in the Texas Hill Country.

title: Lawsuits Allege Delivery Robots Recorded Biometric Data Without Permission
snippet: As delivery robots roll through cities like Chicago, they’re fueling fears about unregulated surveillance in public spaces.
fullText:
Food delivery robots might not just be carrying burritos. They could be taking a measurement of your face. 

Two proposed class action lawsuits in Chicago accuse Coco Robotics and Serve Robotics of collecting biometric information without consent and using it to train their artificial intelligence systems. The Cook County residents allege that the companies violated Illinois’ Biometric Information Privacy Act, which requires companies to provide written notice of the types and purposes of data collection, obtain prior written consent, and maintain set retention and deletion schedules.

Plaintiff Mitchell Breidinger said that even though he hadn’t chosen robot delivery for his DoorDash groceries, a Coco robot showed up at his home in September 2025. Breidinger said that while he was entering a pickup code, the robot’s cameras captured his face, head and hands and that lidar — a type of 3D imaging technology — measured the geometry of those body parts. Breidinger also alleged that a Coco remote operator watched the delivery on video and that the company didn’t notify him in writing of its intent to collect his biometric data or how long it would retain it.

			

More from CNET

The other plaintiff, Barry Schain, said he received three Serve Robotics deliveries with his Uber Eats orders even though he hadn’t selected robot delivery.

The lawsuits seek statutory damages of $1,000 per negligent violation or $5,000 per intentional or reckless violation, plus other unspecified relief. Both companies have denied the claims, saying they don’t record the biometric data of customers or people who walk by the robots on the street.

A Serve Robotics spokesperson said in a statement to CNET that its robots “use cameras and sensors to navigate the sidewalks of Chicago safely. Serve does not use that data to identify individuals, and our systems are not designed to identify individuals or create biometric profiles.”

Coco Robotics didn’t respond to a request for comment, but a company spokesperson told the Associated Press that the company collects only navigational data “to make sidewalks safer for all users” and that it does “not share data from the beginning or end of delivery trips under our data sharing partnerships.”

The robot privacy pitfall

Robotic deliveries have expanded significantly since Starship Technologies’ inaugural package delivery nearly a decade ago. Starship said it surpassed 10 million deliveries globally by midyear.

Coco Robotics now operates about 1,000 robots for deliveries in Chicago, Los Angeles, Washington, DC and Miami. Serve Robotics has more than 2,000 in Los Angeles, Atlanta, Dallas-Fort Worth, Miami, Chicago and Alexandria, Virginia. Both companies primarily deliver food for DoorDash, Uber Eats and Grubhub.

According to most projections, global robotic delivery will expand rapidly over the next several years. One forecast estimates that the US market will grow from $252 million in 2025 to $3.1 billion by 2035. And it won’t just be food and groceries. Deliverables could include medicine, industrial parts and a wide variety of retail goods, and there could also be a rise in delivery by drone and boat.

As fear and anger mount over technology increasingly encroaching on people’s everyday lives, delivery robots — which use AI, cameras and lidar to navigate sidewalks — are advancing rapidly. Just as the backlash against other AI surveillance tools and Flock Safety cameras has cropped up all across the US, there’s a growing pushback against potential privacy violations from delivery robots, which have been punched, kicked, tipped over and defaced, according to a recent story by The New York Times. 

Privacy experts and digital rights activists also raise concerns that autonomous courier technology will eliminate delivery jobs and be used by the government or corporations to track people’s activities.

title: Sensor Tower: Meta’s Muse app tops 10 million US downloads in 40 days
snippet: According to a new report from Sensor Tower, not only did Meta’s Muse become the 12th app ever to reach 10 million US downloads in 40 days, but it is also outpacing its peers in user retention. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
According to a new report from Sensor Tower, not only did Meta’s Muse become the 12th app ever to reach 10 million US downloads in 40 days, but it is also outpacing its peers in user retention. Here are the details.

A few weeks ago, Sensor Tower reported that Meta’s Muse app had surpassed 5 million downloads in the US, thanks to a mix of popularity and Meta’s massive ad push.

At the time, the app had spent 12 consecutive days at the top of the US App Store. Muse has since slipped to second place, but Sensor Tower now reports that it has become just the 12th app to reach 10 million US downloads within 40 days of launch, since the firm began tracking apps in October 2015.

For comparison, Sensor Tower says ChatGPT, Grok, and Claude reached just 3.7 million, 500,000, and 200,000 US downloads, respectively, during their first 40 days.

Per Sensor Tower data, ChatGPT scaled to ~15mn global downloads in its first 40 days post app-launch, as its global reach expedited its growth. ChatGPT’s top regions by downloads during the studied period included the US, Japan, Brazil, and Germany, which accounted for 25%, 9%, 6%, and 5% of the global downloads, respectively.

The report also noted that ChatGPT’s US downloads have declined 25% over the past 30 days compared to the previous 30-day period. ChatGPT is currently the fourth most downloaded free app on the US App Store, while Claude ranks seventh and Grok 34th.

As for the other apps that reached the 10 million milestone within 40 days, Sensor Tower didn’t name them all, but noted that nine were mobile games. The most recent app to achieve the feat was Meta’s own Threads, back in July 2023.

	

Today’s report comes amid fresh privacy concerns surrounding Muse, after security researchers discovered that shared conversations could expose sensitive personal and business information. Meta has since suspended the sharing feature while it investigates the issue.

Despite the privacy concerns, Sensor Tower’s data suggests that Muse is doing a better job of retaining users than its AI competitors, which is not surprising, since this is one of Meta’s strongest suits:

US Muse users are returning to the app, which is averaging a 30% retention rate after 7 days, and a 23% retention rate after 14 days. Meta is currently outpacing AI competitors in its retention at the 7 and 14 day mark, as ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok averaged a 19% and 16% retention rate, respectively.

Finally, Sensor Tower notes that Meta continues spending heavily to promote its AI assistant. According to the report, the app accounted for 39% of Meta’s advertising spend in the US so far this month, up from 23% in September. Muse also reportedly climbed from 73rd to 21st place among US brands ranked by advertising impressions.

title: My Favorite Budget Camera Brand Is Finally Getting 4K Plus and a Mile-Long Range
snippet: Blink’s newest line of cameras includes features the brand has never tried before, but prices remain affordable starting at $50.
fullText:
Amazon’s Blink is one of my go-to security brands for long battery life and affordability. It also sports one of the easiest security camera apps to learn and has one of the lowest subscriptions if you want to add cloud or AI features. But those benefits come with restrictions, and Blink has focused on only a few camera lines with relatively few choices. Today, that changed.

Blink has announced five new security cameras that significantly expand its current offerings. Not only are they all available for preorder right now, but they include features Blink hasn’t dabbled in before. Prices may be a bit higher than usual for this new tech, but they’re still affordable compared to alternatives, and I can’t wait to test them all out. Here are the features I’m most interested in trying.

4K resolution at last

Blink’s new Mini cams have tricks, like a boosted 4K resolution.Blink

Blink only recently updated its cameras to 2K resolution, but now it’s time for another leap. The Blink Mini 4K Plus ($80) is made for both indoor and outdoor use, packing in more detail than any other Blink camera. It has a 115-degree field of video and two-way audio, too. Most major security companies have at least a couple of 4K models available for those seeking better visuals, and now Blink joins them with a cam more compact than most high-resolution offerings.

			

More from CNET

The Mini 4K Plus is still larger than the other Blink Minis I’ve tested and a bit more expensive, as well. That’s one change these fine cameras have in common — prices that push most of them out of the budget range, although these are still generally affordable compared to many similar alternatives.

Extra long-range models for Wi-Fi worries

Blink’s new model offers a huge range for off-site and large property monitoring.Blink

Another significant evolution comes with Blink’s two new XR Plus cameras, made to be used with a Blink Sync Module XR Plus hub to reach extra-long distances beyond your usual Wi-Fi range. The first is the Fronter XR Plus ($200), with a shape similar to Blink Outdoor cams but with an antenna and optional trunk strap for mounting on a tree. It can reach a range of up to 7,000 feet in the right conditions.

Accompanying the Fronter XR Plus is a new Blink Outdoor 2K XR Plus ($150). It’s a more compact version with a lesser 2,700-foot range, but it is still able to connect to watch areas standard Wi-Fi can’t reach, like the end of long driveways or detached sheds and garages.

Chris Liguori, general manager at Blink, told CNET, “With XR, we’re extending that same approach beyond the reach of ordinary home Wi-Fi. The Frontier XR Plus brings a new option to the trail camera category, combining extended-range connectivity with the features and experience customers expect from Blink.”

It’s interesting Blink is calling the Frontier model a “trail camera” since this usually makes people think of viewing wildlife or mountain trails in remote areas. But the brand makes it clear this cam is focused on more property-oriented tasks. If your property entrance is half a mile away at the end of a road, the Frontier could keep an eye on it. It could also watch distant activity on farms or monitor a remote job site, as long as the XR Plus hub is placed correctly.

A compact and completely wireless spotlight camera

A battery spotlight camera requires careful testing, but Blink’s model intrigues me.Blink

While Blink has dabbled in floodlight cameras before, it’s now releasing its first spotlight cameras, the Blink Spotlight Cam 2K Plus ($110), with a unique design unlike any spotlight model I’ve seen. This cam is entirely wireless, so you can mount it nearly anywhere without worrying about junction boxes or outdoor outlets.

Blink didn’t give any info on the total lumens of this spotlight model, but the brand did say the spotlight is controlled via the motion detector. If it’s like the floodlight versions, you’ll be able to control the brightness, motion sensitivity and other settings to change how the lights work.

However, I really want to test this model to see what the battery life is like, since LED lights can drain batteries quickly. Frequent activations of Ring’s new Spotlight Cam, for example, quickly brought battery life down, which is why I was glad that model came with room for two battery packs. Blink doesn’t appear to have any design changes made to mitigate battery loss.

Pan/tilt features on a particularly versatile camera

Blink’s final new camera has broad coverage.Blink

Finally, Blink is releasing a pan/tilt camera, the Blink Mini Pan-Tilt 2K Plus ($50), the most budget-friendly of this new crop with an indoor/outdoor design and 350-degree panning plus 115-degree tilting for more coverage. Like many pan/tilt cams these days, it autotracks when it picks up significant movement, like following a figure across the yard.

I like this coverage solution much better than the awkward, unnecessary experiment with the dual-cam Blink Arc. Note that outdoor use requires an outdoor adapter, which isn’t included in the sales price.

If you’re interested in any of these new camera preorders, you should know Blink’s cloud storage plans start at $4 per month, or you can spend a few dollars more if you want AI features, like video descriptions. Blink does sell certain types of Cync Modules you can connect to flash drives or microSD cards for local storage, although I’m not sure this approach is compatible with the XR Plus models. Finally, as an Amazon company, Blink has excellent compatibility with Alexa but typically doesn’t offer support for Siri or Google Home.

I’ll let you know what I think of these new cameras and details like these when I get a chance to test them out.
