title: Claude did not invent scorpion antivenom
snippet: An investment research firm wanted to prove AI could revolutionize drug development. So they teamed up with Anthropic to see whether an unreleased version of Claude could make scorpion antivenom. It couldn't. It came up with some promising starting points, but nothing close to an actual drug, experts tell The Verge. Citrini Research, the firm behind the experiment, admitted that "none of us could claim to know anything about AI as it related to biology." That didn't stop it from trying to make a drug from scratch - or publishing a blog post titled "We Wanted to Use Claude to Create a New Drug. Here's What Happened." The account came comple … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
An investment research firm wanted to prove AI could revolutionize drug development. So they teamed up with Anthropic to see whether an unreleased version of Claude could make scorpion antivenom. It couldn’t. It came up with some promising starting points, but nothing close to an actual drug, experts tell The Verge.

Citrini Research, the firm behind the experiment, admitted that “none of us could claim to know anything about AI as it related to biology.” That didn’t stop it from trying to make a drug from scratch — or publishing a blog post titled “We Wanted to Use Claude to Create a New Drug. Here’s What Happened.” The account came complete with rhetorical questions like “Why don’t we try to use AI to create a new drug?”, a blow-by-blow account of its amateurish scientific adventures, and a quote from Charles Darwin.

If the name Citrini sounds familiar, that’s because the firm was behind a widely circulated piece of fiction imagining an AI-induced economic catastrophe that gained traction on social media and rattled real-world markets. It also claims to have visited the Strait of Hormuz in April to get a firsthand perspective on what was happening in the volatile region.

For its latest venture, Citrini enlisted the help of Anthropic, which, mere weeks out from its hotly anticipated IPO, has a few reasons to talk up AI’s potential in drug development and the life sciences — two areas it’s actively pursuing.

The collaboration came about after Citrini ran into Claude’s biosecurity guardrails while trying to get the model to research drug candidates. The post’s author said they “spam called anyone in my contact list who worked at an AI lab,” eventually finding a willing partner in Anthropic. The AI lab agreed to drop the restrictions and give the team access to a more advanced, unreleased model on the condition that they work from its offices. “Luckily,” Anthropic also agreed to foot the hefty compute and token bill, which came just shy of $50,000.

After weighing a few options, the team settled on scorpion antivenom, a costly treatment that can be difficult to produce, often involving injecting venom into horses. The goal was to use Claude to design proteins that could bind to the toxins in scorpion venom. Armed with a 35-page prompt, they set the AI to work, unleashing some 300 subagents to discover suitable proteins.

In its own more sober account of the experiment, Anthropic said Claude generated nearly 320,000 candidates, whittling them down to 180 designs after discarding those that resembled known toxins or existing proteins. The entire process took 64 hours. Anthropic said the team worked “with Claude” to add another 31 designs, bringing the total to 211.

Citrini then sent the designs to two outside laboratories — Swiss biotech company Adaptyv Bio and US-based Twist Biosciences — to test whether the proteins could actually bind to their intended targets, a key step for developing an effective antivenom. That cost another $150,000, give or take. It’s unclear why Anthropic could not have conducted these tests in-house at its biology wet lab in California. Seventeen of the proteins passed muster, collectively binding to four of the five scorpion toxins the team had hoped to target. Not one of the proteins bound to more than a single toxin, Citrini said.

Even if they had, Citrini would still be a very long way from a working antivenom. Binding to a toxin does not mean a protein can actually neutralize it, let alone function as a safe and effective treatment. Citrini acknowledges this itself, noting that “no experiment has yet tested whether they actually stopped the toxin working.”

In other words, the experiment had not succeeded. Citrini set out to make a new drug, but experts tell The Verge it had only accomplished the relatively “easy” part of the process. “It is easy-ish to discover a good binder against snake and scorpion toxins,” said Andreas Hougaard Laustsen-Kiel, a professor of antibody technologies at the Technical University of Denmark. “The hard part is to translate it into a medicine.”

Melisa Benard Valle, an assistant professor, and Anne Ljungars, a senior researcher, both at the Technical University of Denmark, agreed. “The results are technically promising, but some of the excitement is premature,” they wrote in a joint email, describing the findings as “far from a medicine and hyped.” Much remains unknown about the proteins Claude designed, they said, including their safety, stability, how they behave in the body, and whether they can be developed into viable treatments. “Translating these binders into an actual medicine is likely still a long and challenging process.”

The most novel aspect of Citrini’s experiment, they said, was the “autonomous discovery process rather than the biological results.” AI has huge potential to accelerate discovery, they added, but warned “turning promising molecules into effective medicines remains a much greater challenge.”

Nor is the underlying approach particularly new. Andreas Bender, a professor of machine learning in medicine at Khalifa University in Abu Dhabi, told The Verge existing methods like high-throughput screening “are often able to find a multitude of hits at manageable cost,” even without any AI. Designing proteins that bind to targets is “kind of” a solved problem, said Bender, who is also a visiting professor at the University of Cambridge. The much harder challenge is turning those results into treatments that actually work in living systems. “It’s exactly this translation that lacks.”

While it failed to make a drug, Citrini declared the experiment a success of sorts. The firm argued it offers a glimpse into the investment opportunities emerging in the upcoming era of AI-enabled drug discovery. As for why it didn’t bother to take the research further? Citrini accused critics of “nitpick[ing]” and added, “Not to beat a dead horse, but we are an investment research firm - not a biotech startup.” Citrini and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment.

But it still made a bullish case for companies that might benefit. Naturally, the specifics were reserved for paying subscribers, though Bloomberg reports the firm highlighted companies involved in the testing side of drug development, including Charles River Laboratories, which supplies primates for animal research. In a video discussing the experiment, Citrini described the AI portion as “free,” conveniently overlooking the tab picked up by Anthropic.

title: iOS 27 adds scam-prevention feature to iPhone, here’s how to enable it
snippet: iOS 27 introduces a new security feature called ‘Impersonation Risk Detection’ that helps protect you against scams, but it’s off by default. Here’s what the feature does, and how to enable it. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 introduces a new security feature called ‘Impersonation Risk Detection’ that helps protect you against scams, but it’s off by default. Here’s what the feature does, and how to enable it.

Impersonation Risk Detection in iOS 27 can detect suspicious activity in real time to prevent scams

Every day around the world, people get tricked into sharing sensitive information like bank details or other financial info with bad actors.

This commonly happens via text messages, emails, or phone calls to iPhone or Android devices. And while iOS has built-in tools like call and message screening, those tools can’t prevent a scam if you choose to take action on it.

But iOS 27 introduces a new level of scam-prevention with a security feature called ‘Impersonation Risk Detection.’

Here’s what it does, per Apple’s website:

Impersonation Risk Detection helps protect against active social engineering scams. In these scams, an attacker might pose as a bank, government agency, or someone you trust to pressure or guide you into making a payment or changing your account details. Traditional security measures like two-factor authentication can’t always detect this kind of scam. That’s because you’re taking the action, even though you’ve been tricked or pressured.

Impersonation Risk Detection analyzes information about your device and Apple Account to help detect signs of an active scam. Based on this analysis, it returns a risk level to the app. The app receives only the risk level, not the underlying information used to generate it. The app decides what to do next. For example, it might ask you to verify your identity, add a delay, or show a warning.

You can turn Impersonation Risk Detection on in iOS 27 by going to Settings ⇾ Privacy & Security ⇾ Impersonation Risk Detection then toggling on ‘Share with App Developers.’

Impersonation Risk Detection is only available in supported apps, and Apple hasn’t published a list of those apps at the moment. But once enabled, it provides the app with a “risk level” while omitting the underlying information driving it. Risk levels include:

Unknown: No evidence of suspicious activity was detected

Medium: Some signs of suspicious activity were detected

High: Significant signs of suspicious activity were detected

Once the app has this risk level, it decides what action to take. For example, it may prompt you to offer additional authentication, or show a warning message related to scams.

For more details on how the feature works using ‘Trust Insights,’ see our coverage here.

title: Google says Chrome’s Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection mode makes users 10x safer
snippet: Chrome today announced the latest features for Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection. Google says this mode makes users ten times safer from phishing, social engineering, notification abuse, and other scams compared to Standard Protection. more…
fullText:
Chrome today announced the latest features for Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection. Google says this mode makes users ten times safer from phishing, social engineering, notification abuse, and other scams compared to Standard Protection.

Chrome is adding suspicious site warnings in the address bar “when a page exhibits deceptive patterns commonly associated with known malicious sites.” There are two tiers:

Suspicious sites (lower confidence verdict, possible risk of user harm)

Dangerous sites (high confidence verdict, high risk of user harm)

Suspicious sites (above) will trigger a shield icon in the Omnibox, with a dialog box letting you “Mark as safe” or go “Back to safety.” 

Dangerous site alerts (below) will continue to appear as a “full-page red interstitial warning.”

	

Meanwhile, Chrome is continuing to boost scam detection by leveraging Gemini models in the cloud after using on-device approaches. This protects Enhanced Protection users from a broader range of threats, including fake antivirus and browser update scams.

This model evaluates page content to analyze key indicators, such as the brand represented, the intent of the page, and a scam likeliness score, giving us rich threat data needed to identify deceptive sites.

Safe Browsing uses the Gemini analysis “in combination with domain reputation and other security signals.” Google will process page content ephemerally, “meaning it is never logged, retained, or used to train models.”

The final Enhanced Protection update defends against ClickFix social engineering that “tricks users into manually copying and executing malicious commands on their own computers in order to ‘fix’ a fake issue.” In reality, this is used to “carry out malicious actions such as downloading and setting up malware.”

Because these utilities are native to the system and trusted by security software, bad actors use them to blend in and hide their activity, and by shifting the download process out of the browser and into the terminal, attackers completely sidestep existing Chrome and Safe Browsing download protections.

When a potential ClickFix script is copied, Chrome will remove personally identifiable information from the clipboard and send it to Safe Browsing for further analysis. The browser shows a warning if a “dangerous verdict is returned.”

This system is designed to be high precision, in order to protect users in real time while minimizing disruption to legitimate developer activity.

Enhanced Protection was introduced in 2020, and Google said it was enabled by 1 billion users in 2025. It can be enabled in Chrome Settings > Privacy and security > Security.

title: Perplexity’s Computer can now run entirely on your Mac, even offline
snippet: Perplexity is adding a new local-first mode to its Mac app that lets Computer work entirely on the device. This includes running tasks without an internet connection. more…
fullText:
Perplexity is adding a new local-first mode to its Mac app that lets Computer work entirely on the device. This includes running tasks without an internet connection.

Perplexity brings fully local AI tasks to Mac with new Computer mode option

The launch follows Hybrid Compute, which arrived in September. That feature splits tasks between cloud models for research and reasoning and a local model for working with private files.

Local-first takes things further by running both the AI model and the agent directing the task on the Mac.

Perplexity says planning, reasoning, and file processing can all happen on device, with files only reaching the cloud when the user approves.

With permission, Computer can work with local files and supported Mac apps, including Notes, Messages, Mail, and Numbers.

Perplexity Computer can now run fully local on your Mac.

Work with your native Mac apps and local files, and run tasks without sending sensitive data to the cloud. The model and the agent both run on your Mac.

Available now in the Perplexity Mac app. pic.twitter.com/tnvCgCXD7v

— Perplexity (@perplexity_ai) October 20, 2026

One example Perplexity gives is reviewing recent messages and emails, identifying deadlines, and creating an action list in Notes.

Users can still authorize cloud access when a task needs current information, browser use, or connected apps. Hybrid Compute also remains available in the same Mac app.

The new local mode is available to Perplexity Pro, Max, and Enterprise subscribers. 

It launches with Qwen 3.6 and PPLX Pro as local model options, which users can download and set up through the app.

You need an Apple silicon Mac with at least 36GB of unified memory for the best experience. You can learn more about the latest Perplexity Computer upgrade here.

title: Constrained iPhone Duo availability is annoying, but a mixed blessing for Apple
snippet: Estimated iPhone Duo delivery dates started slipping dramatically, literally within a minute of pre-orders opening on Friday. Even some of those who got in within the first few minutes got estimated shipping dates into January of next year. That undeniably poses problems for Apple, but some have gone as far as calling it “a major mistake” to launch with such limited stock. Personally, I’d say it’s annoying for customers but more of a mixed blessing for Apple … more…
fullText:
Estimated iPhone Duo delivery dates started slipping dramatically, literally within a minute of pre-orders opening on Friday. Even some of those who got in within the first few minutes got estimated shipping dates into January of next year.

That undeniably poses problems for Apple, but some have gone as far as calling it “a major mistake” to launch with such limited stock. Personally, I’d say it’s annoying for customers but more of a mixed blessing for Apple … 

Apple always builds up inventory before launching new products, but with new product categories like the first foldable iPhone it can be hard for the company to predict demand. 

In many ways, the company is in a no-win position with this balancing act of supply and demand. If demand greatly exceeds supply, Apple risks irritating some of its most loyal customers – those who are willing to go all in on a first-generation product. But if supply exceeds demand, and a new product remains available for immediate delivery, commenters will inevitably point to that as evidence for it being a flop.

The balance of supply and demand

In truth, none of us knows the true position here. The imbalance may be due to the iPhone Duo being wildly more popular than Apple anticipated (as the company implies), or it may be that demand is modest but manufacturing complexities mean that supply is even more limited. My own view is that it’s likely a mixture of the two: relatively high demand and rather constrained supply.

Relatively high demand because, while foldables in general are still a rather niche product, it’s very clear that Apple put in a lot of thought and work into making this one the best on the market. The company has seemingly addressed the two main issues that beset Android foldables to date: a visible crease and poor durability. The company then created software features to take full advantage of the form factor of the device, and topped it off with an absolutely superb launch video. I think some of those who had previously ruled it out on the basis of price changed their minds once they saw it; It’s been a long time since we’ve seen such excitement levels around a new Apple product.

Rather constrained supply because it’s clear that the complexity of the device, and most especially the hinge, means that it’s very difficult to manufacture, and it’s likely that yield rates are relatively low.

A mixed blessing

One of the biggest problems of the world we live in today is polarization of views. Large swathes of the population seem to have lost sight of the fact that two different things can be true at the same time.

	

Yes, pre-ordering a product in October within minutes and then having to wait until January to receive it is both annoying and frustrating. If I were in that position, I would absolutely be pissed at Apple.

But also yes: this immediate slipping of delivery dates adds to the narrative of a wildly popular new product, serving to further boost the hype around it. 

If Apple could have perfectly predicted demand, then it would likely have wanted a position where delivery times slipped sufficiently for the launch to be viewed as a success, but not so much that customers get annoyed. This situation isn’t ideal, for sure, but in my view it’s more of a mixed blessing than a strategic error.

Finally, if you are the position of having been given a lengthy wait for your order, the reality may not be quite as bad as it appears. Apple tends to present customers with the worst case dates initially, often bringing them forward subsequently. Additionally, retail staff tell me that there will often be unexpected walk-in stock available at some stores, again due to imperfect forecasting of online versus offline sales, as well as varying demand at different stores. That’s always worth trying from the day after the new devices go on sale.

fullText:
If you are in the market for a new device, you cannot go wrong with the Galaxy S26 Ultra with a deal bringing the device below $950 on Amazon right now.

Galaxy S26 Ultra at Amazon

This is a heck of a lot of phone for your money, especially when you consider that the Pixel 11 Pro XL starts around the same price and has a lot of drawbacks that aren’t here on Samsung’s best phone. The prices of brand-new tech are still ballooning due to RAM price hikes, but if you’re a patient buyer, it’ll pay off. There are even rumors that the S27 might ship with 8GB RAM in the near future, so stocking up is an easy way to beat the crunch.

$450 off the usual retail price of the S26 Ultra makes it a great deal for one of the most reliable handsets on the market. You could do much worse and get a lot less for your money elsewhere.

snippet: Apple has released the first iOS 27.2 release candidate for iPhone. The update brings Apple’s next iPhone software release one step closer to its public launch. more…
fullText:
Apple has released the first iOS 27.2 release candidate for iPhone. The update brings Apple’s next iPhone software release one step closer to its public launch.

iOS 27.2 reaches release candidate stage

After several beta versions, Apple is putting the final touches on iOS 27.2. If testing doesn’t uncover anything that requires another build, the release candidate could be the version that reaches everyone.

	

The beta cycle has introduced Group FaceTime Dual Capture, more Siri AI languages, Apple TV app profiles, and changes to how Apple Podcasts organizes episodes.

Apple Music also has a new app icon and updated color scheme. The black-and-white icon replaces the familiar red design, while blue now highlights the active tab inside the app.

One feature that Apple pulled from testing is the overhauled Health app. It appeared in earlier iOS 27.2 betas before Apple restored the previous Health app in beta 4. The upgrade is still planned for release later this year.

We’ll update our coverage with any notable changes discovered in the release candidate. Spot anything new in iOS 27.2 RC? Let us know in the comments below!

title: Apple’s new App Store rules crack down on AI nudification and ‘bait-and-switch’ apps
snippet: Apple updated its App Review Guidelines today with a series of changes meant to strengthen protections against harmful content and deceptive app review practices. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple updated its App Review Guidelines today with a series of changes meant to strengthen protections against harmful content and deceptive app review practices. Here are the details.

A bit of context

Over the past year alone, there has been no shortage of reports and controversies involving apps that skirt Apple’s App Review Guidelines and expose users, including minors, to harmful or inappropriate content.

In January, the Tech Transparency Project (TTP) identified dozens of AI-powered “nudify” apps on the App Store.

The group published a follow-up investigation in April, revealing that Apple’s App Store search suggestions and advertisements were also directing users to such apps. In July, San Francisco officials ordered Apple to remove eight apps capable of generating nonconsensual intimate imagery.

Also in July, a 9to5Mac investigation uncovered dozens of apps disguising gambling platforms as simple games and utilities to evade App Store review, many of which were available to children.

These apps behaved as advertised when accessed from outside Brazil, but revealed hidden betting platforms when opened from Brazilian IP addresses.

And then there was the Grok controversy, which saw Elon Musk’s AI chatbot used to generate nonconsensual sexualized images of women and minors, prompting lawmakers and advocacy groups to call on Apple to remove X and Grok from the App Store. Apple later confirmed that it had privately warned xAI that Grok could be removed unless the company addressed the issue.

Today, Apple updated its App Review Guidelines in an attempt to address problems such as these.

Apple’s updated App Review Guidelines

Under Section 1.2, which covers user-generated content, the guidelines now read (changes in bold):

Apps that enable users to create, generate, upload, share, or otherwise contribute content present particular challenges, including intellectual property infringement, nonconsensual intimate imagery, and anonymous bullying.

Apple’s new terms add that “Developers who fail to implement appropriate safeguards or fail to remediate identified violations after notice may be considered in violation of the Developer Code of Conduct.”

In another particularly important change, Apple strengthened its rules against so-called ‘bait-and-switch’ apps, which “misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as “nudification” — after approval,” as the company puts it.

The newly created section 2.5.19 reads:

Don’t include any hidden, dormant, or undocumented features in your app; your app’s functionality should be clear to end users and App Review. Attempting to hide undocumented features in your app binary, such as through code obfuscation or other methods, is grounds for removal of your app from the App Store and termination of your developer account.

While the prohibition on hidden functionality was already present in Section 2.3.1, Apple has now made the rule more explicit, specifically calling out code obfuscation and emphasizing that violations can lead to an app’s removal and the termination of the developer’s account.

Finally, under Section 5 (Legal), Apple also strengthened its language around apps that facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children, explicitly stating that they “will be removed from the App Store and blocked from alternative distribution.”

title: Googlebooks just aren’t ready
snippet: The Acer Googlebook 14 (left), Lenovo Googlebook 15 (center), and HP Googlebook 14 (right). | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge EEvery Googlebook laptop we've tested so far has great hardware. The problem is the software. While Googlebook OS has exciting ideas for how a laptop and phone can work together, right now it's mostly a frustrating experience filled with annoying bugs and lackluster app support. It often feels like using an Android tablet with a keyboard and trackpad grafted on, rather than a cohesive laptop OS. It's too bad, because those keyboards and trackpads - and pretty much all the laptops' hardware components - are great. Frankly, they should be. The cheapest is $900, a price where you start to expect quality processors, metal builds, higher-quality … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
EEvery Googlebook laptop we’ve tested so far has great hardware. The problem is the software. While Googlebook OS has exciting ideas for how a laptop and phone can work together, right now it’s mostly a frustrating experience filled with annoying bugs and lackluster app support. It often feels like using an Android tablet with a keyboard and trackpad grafted on, rather than a cohesive laptop OS. It’s too bad, because those keyboards and trackpads — and pretty much all the laptops’ hardware components — are great.

Frankly, they should be. The cheapest is $900, a price where you start to expect quality processors, metal builds, higher-quality displays, good speakers, and great keyboards and trackpads (even haptic ones in some cases). The Googlebooks have those covered, and they also have very good battery life and at least 16GB of RAM.

Google wanted Googlebooks to feel premium, and HP, Acer, Lenovo, Dell, and Asus all delivered. It’s Google’s software that needs to catch up. In their current state, we don’t recommend you buy any of them. But it’s worth reviewing the hardware to determine which shows the most promise if the software one day improves — or if crafty modders manage to install other operating systems. Since the software is the same on all Googlebooks (save for some preinstalled manufacturer apps), and we’ve already covered that software at length, we’re strictly talking about Googlebook hardware here. The scores, however, cover hardware and software as they stand today. Brace yourself — the scores are bad.

If you’re a dedicated Google user or Pixel fan and you really want to be an early adopter / paying beta tester — or if you’re just here for some schadenfreude — here are our collective thoughts on each and every Googlebook.

4

Verge Score

$899

The Good

The most affordable of the Googlebooks (for now)

Nice screen and build

The Bad

Googlebook OS feels like a beta

No portrait orientation in tablet mode

The Acer Googlebook 14 is the only 2-in-1 convertible of the bunch, and it’s one of the nicest-feeling and -looking Acers I’ve ever used at this price. It’s light, with a sturdy metal chassis and a great 2880 x 1800 / 120Hz OLED touchscreen with stylus support. I find 2-in-1s pretty handy, even if they look clunkier than tablets like a Microsoft Surface Pro or an iPad with a keyboard case, but Googlebook OS doesn’t yet support portrait orientation, which limits the Acer’s stylus potential. Like all Googlebooks, the Acer has an Auto-Rotate toggle in settings, but it only flips the orientation 180 degrees — a strange oversight.

The speakers don’t have a lot of bass, and they can get muffled in tablet mode depending on how you hold the laptop, but they’re decent and sound balanced overall. The webcam is a slight weak point, as colors and contrast are a touch drab. But nothing here is bad. This isn’t like some of the Acer Aspires or Swifts I’ve tested in the past where you had to deal with a terrible screen and shoddy build quality for the sake of a good chip. It’s just an all-around nice package. That extends to the battery life, which lasted me eight to nine hours of light-to-mixed usage.

1/7I love a good tent mode. Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

If this was running Windows or a proper Linux distro with the same hardware and price, it’d be a rare bright spot in our ongoing RAMageddon hellscape. But thanks to Googlebook OS, it’s not. And an Acer rep told us its $900 launch price is only available for a limited time. That might sound like an incentive to buy one before a price increase, but please allow me to tap the “Don’t buy it now for what it might do later” sign. Actually, picture me tapping it as you read this whole article.

— Antonio G. Di Benedetto, Laptop Reviewer

5

Verge Score

$999

The Good

Small and light

On the cheaper side of Googlebooks

Great keyboard and trackpad

The Bad

Googlebook OS feels like a beta

Anti-glare display has some issues

Only the two USB-C ports

Here’s my theory: If Googlebooks are going to work anytime soon, they’re going to work as secondary computers. Maybe they don’t need to replace your primary work machine if they can instead be light, fast, simple, and fun to use. (Yes, I agree that $900 or more is a lot to pay for this kind of device, but hey, iPads pull it off!) I already see glimmers of possibility here, even through the bugs of Googlebook OS. “A Chromebook, but also it runs all my apps” is not a bad pitch for an off-day computer.

That’s why, of all the available Googlebooks, the Dell XPS Googlebook makes the most sense to me. At 2.2 pounds, with a 13.4-inch screen, and starting at $999, it’s one of the smallest and lightest Googlebooks available. (And unlike the cheaper Acer Googlebook 14, it doesn’t offer a bunch of flippy tablet modes that don’t really work.) Like the other models we’ve tested, it’s a lovely piece of high-end hardware; I love the keyboard and trackpad, I appreciate that I can open the thing with one hand, and the Qualcomm chip inside does its job fine for all my practical purposes. The battery got me through a full day of travel and then some.

1/4The XPS has the most unique color of all the Googlebooks. Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

My only real complaint is with the anti-glare coating on the display, which does help tamp down reflections but also creates that slight rainbow-shimmer effect that makes the screen appear a little less sharp and clear. The coating also dims the screen a bit — I’ve used the XPS Googlebook mostly at max brightness, just to get it up to normal. I am generally extremely in favor of these matte displays, but I’d trade the XPS Googlebook’s for a glossy one in a heartbeat.

As we keep saying, there’s simply no way around the fact that Googlebook OS isn’t ready. Google is fixing and improving it quickly (adding the ability to run any website as an app was a big win), but I can’t get past the apps that don’t work properly with a keyboard, don’t work on this size screen at all, or simply don’t exist on Googlebook OS (bring back Linux apps, now!). If you’re in the market for an overpriced second computer and you want easy access to Google Messages and your Drive files, a Googlebook might be exactly what you need. Someday. Maybe by then Dell will have fixed the screen.

— David Pierce, Editor at Large

4

Verge Score

$1200

The Good

Sturdy, metal chassis

Up to 1TB storage

The Bad

Googlebook OS feels like a beta

One of the heaviest Googlebooks

Limited ports

HP’s Googlebook 14 is more proof that of all the problems facing these early Googlebook models, the hardware isn’t one of them.

Starting from $1,199.99, this Googlebook is about the same size and weight as a MacBook Air 13, despite fitting in a larger 14-inch display. It’s a great panel, too: a 2880 x 1800 resolution, 120Hz, OLED touchscreen with a slim bezel, good viewing angles, and punchy brightness. The Snapdragon X Elite chip has proved reliable so far (and for what it’s worth, my Asus model with an Intel chip has been solid too, despite early concerns), with 16GB of RAM and the option to bump memory up to 32GB and storage as high as 1TB, but I haven’t pushed it through anything more demanding than image editing in the infuriating mobile versions of Lightroom and Photoshop.

The body is mostly metal, so the whole thing feels tough and solid. The keyboard’s comfortable and the haptic trackpad expansive, and the privacy shutter on the webcam is always a welcome touch. There are only two USB-C ports and a headphone jack, so grab one of the other Googlebooks if you know you need HDMI or USB-A.

1/7HP made its Googlebook look sharp with that nicer lid logo. Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

I’m a fan of the Googlebook-specific hardware touches too, which you’ll find across the lineup. I’m already building the habit of using the Caps Lock key for its Quick Insert function instead, with easy access to features like the clipboard, emoji, and Rambler dictation — though the latter gets its own dedicated function key too. It’s joined by keys for the classic Android navigation buttons and a shortcut for some flexible screenshot and screen recording options. The Glowbar is a little less impressive; it’s a cute design but doesn’t actually do very much, and since it’s on the lid you’ll rarely see it in action anyway.

From the hardware side this feels like a $1,200 laptop through and through — it’s the software where we still have questions.

— Dominic Preston, News Editor

4

Verge Score

$1299

The Good

Lots of ports

Great keyboard and a matte OLED display

The Bad

Googlebook OS feels like a beta

Most expensive Googlebook (currently)

Asus’ entry in the first slate of Googlebooks was able to keep up with me better than I expected, with solid hardware that helped soften the blow of software frustrations.

At $1,299, the Asus Googlebook 14 is the priciest of the first five Googlebooks. The base configuration has an Intel Core Ultra 5 325 CPU, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage (you can also get the 512GB model for the same price at Best Buy). I rarely felt like I was pushing those specs to their limit — the Asus got pretty toasty when I was running games on it, but that’s true of just about any laptop. It breezed through things like managing a dozen or more Chrome tabs and hopping between a few different apps at once. Asus says the 70Wh battery lasts up to 18 hours, and while I didn’t get quite that long, I didn’t have trouble getting through a typical day without charging.

1/5The Asus Googlebook’s Glowbar. Photo: Dominic Preston / The Verge

One major plus is the Asus’ wealth of ports: two USB-C, two USB-A, a headphone jack, and even HDMI. That’s more than most of the other Googlebooks have, or my MacBook for that matter. I was able to hook up the Asus to my monitor, keyboard, mouse, and a wired controller without needing a USB-C hub or a docking station.

I mainly used the Asus without my external monitor, though, largely because it has a fantastic keyboard — it’s satisfyingly clicky with good key travel and tactile feedback. The 14-inch OLED (2880 x 1800) display doesn’t disappoint, either. It has a 120Hz refresh rate and a nice matte finish. The few games that ran well on the Asus, like the Android version of Dredge, looked great.

The Asus Googlebook 14 has some real highs, but the current Googlebook OS experience makes it a tough sell at $1,299. For the same price, you could get the 13-inch M5 MacBook Air with similar specs or, for $100 more, you could also get Asus’ new Windows ExpertBook A7.

— Stevie Bonifield, News Writer

4

Verge Score

$1099

The Good

Sizable OLED in a lightweight laptop

Sleek color and finish

The Bad

Googlebook OS feels like a beta

Keys are a little wobbly, making for an only okay typing feel

AI Mouse is basically just an RGB mouse

The $1,099 Lenovo Googlebook 15 is the largest of the launch lineup, and it’s low-key my favorite. I love a bigger screen, especially in a lightweight laptop. At around 2.8 pounds / 1.27kg, the Lenovo Googlebook is nearly half a pound lighter than Apple’s 15-inch MacBook Air. It’s not as thin or nice as a MacBook Air, but it makes up for that with more ports (HDMI 2.1, two USB-C, and one USB-A). It also has a bright 2880 x 1800 / 120Hz OLED display and a large haptic trackpad that feels and sounds like a tight drum when you click it. Despite that sizable OLED, the battery easily lasted me an eight-hour workday of navigating Chrome tabs with a handful of extra apps like Apple Music and Signal running. And its light gray color and satiny finish is just charming.

Of the three Googlebooks I’ve tested (I tried the HP as well), this has been the one I used the most because of that larger screen and satisfying trackpad. The speakers are good too, with a touch of stereo separation due to the laptop’s size, and they get surprisingly loud. On the other hand, the keyboard is only fine. It’s got a nice clacky feel, but the keycaps are slightly wobbly, and overall it lacks the tight, satisfying tactility of other Lenovo laptop keyboards (like ThinkPads). And while I love this laptop’s off-white color, the bright white keyboard backlight sometimes makes the legends harder to see unless you’re actually in a dark space (this is one place RGB backlighting would actually help).

1/8The Lenovo’s light gray color looks white in brighter lighting. It’s a sharp look. Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Also included with the Lenovo Googlebook 15 (at least, if you buy it directly from Lenovo or Google) is an AI Mouse. Uhh. It’s a Bluetooth mouse. It’s got a light-up button for launching Gemini. That’s about all that makes it an “AI Mouse.” Having a Glowbar that actually faces you seems like a nice idea, but just like the ones built into the lid of every Googlebook, the one on the mouse doesn’t do much. You can pick different lighting colors and patterns in the preinstalled Lenovo Vantage app, and the Glowbar does a brief colorful flourish when you summon Gemini — but that’s about it. It’s just a fine ergonomic mouse that matches this fine laptop hardware.

And that’s the story with every Googlebook so far: The hardware is fine, and even great. But until the software is worthy of the hardware, that’s just not good enough.

— Antonio G. Di Benedetto, Laptop Reviewer

title: Spotify’s ‘QR code verification’ cracks down on sharing and could ban you for a year
snippet: Spotify is rolling out a new method of cracking down on Family plan sharing, with “QR code verification” that’s not particularly hard to work around, but has major consequences if you miss the window. more…
fullText:
Spotify is rolling out a new method of cracking down on Family plan sharing, with “QR code verification” that’s not particularly hard to work around, but has major consequences if you miss the window.

Cracking down on password and/or account sharing has become very common in the world of streaming subscriptions, and Spotify is now trying a new method of limiting the use of its Family plan through a new method – QR code verification.

Spotify details this on a support page, explaining that Family plan members may need to “verify they live with the plan manager by scanning a QR code.” The code appears on the device of the plan manager and is scannable following a pop-up that appears on the device of members of the plan.

Spotify explains the process:

	

The plan manager opens the QR code on their phone. Find it by tapping your profile picture, then Your Premium, then Manage.

The plan member scans the QR code with their phone camera.

Both the manager and member need to be in the same place to complete the scan.

Users on Reddit spotted this rolling out, adding that the QR code changes “every few seconds.” That makes it harder for a screenshot of the page to be used to complete the process. Some quickly found that using multiple devices and video calls, though, they could work around the process. 

Image via Reddit

Spotify says that users have a 7-day window between when the QR code prompt first appears to complete the verification process. Spotify’s Family plan terms require users to live in the same household. 

	

If you miss the 7-day window for scanning the QR code, the consequences are major. Spotify says that users that miss the window “can’t join a different Family or Duo plan for 12 months,” but can still sign up for their own Individual plan. Otherwise, they’re automatically pushed down to the free plan as soon as the window closes.

Plan members have 7 days to complete the QR code scan after getting the notification.

If a member misses the window or can’t complete verification:

They can’t join a different Family or Duo plan for 12 months

They can choose a different plan at www.spotify.com/premium

The same 12-month sharing ban is imposed on address checks that Spotify has used in the past, but the QR code method is significantly harder to get around.

Let us know in the comments below if you’re seeing this.

title: Nobody should buy the $299 Apple TV 4K, but it could have been worse
snippet: My colleague Zac Hall described HomeView as one of the best ways to spend $299 on an Apple device and the Apple TV 4K as the worst. Almost nobody thinks anyone should buy the latter at that price, but things could have been even worse … more…
fullText:
My colleague Zac Hall described HomeView as one of the best ways to spend $299 on an Apple device and the Apple TV 4K as the worst. Almost nobody thinks anyone should buy the latter at that price, but things could have been even worse … 

	

The 4th-gen Apple TV 4K has been launched at an eye-opening price of $299 (and only a little less on Amazon). You do get some new features for your money, including built-in microphones, an upgraded remote, and support for surround sound with the HomePod mini 2. But the tech world consensus appears to be that almost nobody should buy this model, especially given you’ll get Siri AI support with a 2nd- or 3rd-gen box. You can buy entire large-screen TVs for less.

Tech journalist Glenn Fleishman put together a chart showing that the price increase is well above inflation when upgrading from almost any of the previous models. That’s true from the 2nd-gen Apple TV, which went on sale at $99, through to the 3rd-gen Apple TV 4K at a launch price of $129.

But the same comprehensive chart also shows that things could have been very much worse. The very first Apple TV box went on sale at $299 way back in 2007. Adjusted for inflation, that’s the equivalent of $491 today …

title: Apple says American suppliers make almost 100 parts for iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo
snippet: Apple says that American companies are supplying “critical materials and components” for both the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo. In all, it says that nearly 100 components across the two phones are produced by American companies in more than a dozen states. The company has named two of its US supply chain partners, stating that one of them will be making tech used in the variable aperture camera in the iPhone 18 Pro … more…
fullText:
Apple says that American companies are supplying “critical materials and components” for both the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo. In all, it says that nearly 100 components across the two phones are produced by American companies in more than a dozen states.

The company has named two of its US supply chain partners, stating that one of them will be making tech used in the variable aperture camera in the iPhone 18 Pro … 

	

Apple today announced one new partnership and a second expanded one through the American Manufacturing Program (AMP).

Through its American Manufacturing Program (AMP), Apple is partnering with Perryman Company, a Pennsylvania-based titanium producer, to supply titanium for Apple products, including iPhone Duo. Apple is also expanding its partnership with Qnity Electronics, headquartered in Delaware, to produce technology for the new variable aperture in the iPhone 18 Pro camera system — the most advanced Apple has ever made […]

“We’re thrilled to expand our work with companies producing advanced materials and components for our newest iPhone lineup right here in America,” said Sabih Khan, Apple’s chief operating officer. “American ingenuity is vital to all our products, from the titanium crafted for iPhone Duo to breakthrough camera innovations in iPhone 18 Pro. We’re proud to work with Perryman and Qnity Electronics to continue expanding our American Manufacturing Program and support U.S. jobs.”

The company says it’s committing up to $100 million over the next three years to assist Perryman in making the grade 5 titanium used in the enclosure for the iPhone Duo. It says Qnity Electronics will be making a component used in the variable aperture lens of the iPhone 18 Pro.

Qnity, which joined the American Manufacturing Program in March, will produce advanced films essential to the new variable aperture camera system on iPhone 18 Pro. 

Apple highlighted the work performed by five additional US suppliers:

Broadcom is expanding and modernizing its Fort Collins, Colorado, facility under a $1.5 billion capital investment announced in July, producing advanced radio frequency components for a wide range of Apple products. The multiyear agreement will produce more than 15 billion U.S.-made chips.

Corning, an Apple partner since the original iPhone in 2007, produces specialty glass for Apple in Harrodsburg, Kentucky, including Ceramic Shield. By the end of 2026, all of the cover glass for iPhone — including iPhone Duo — and Apple Watch sold worldwide will be produced at this facility.

Coherent continues building on its multiyear agreement with Apple, supplying new vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser technology from its Sherman, Texas, facility. This technology enables Face ID and other key features across iPhone and iPad, including the redesigned, even more useful Dynamic Island on iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.

TSMC’s Arizona fab continues to scale its production of advanced chips used across a range of Apple products, including iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch — producing more than 100 million chips for Apple in 2026. Construction on the north campus is progressing as Apple’s partnership with TSMC in Arizona grows.

Amkor Technology broke ground on its first high-volume packaging and test facility in Peoria, Arizona, in September 2025, and began shell construction earlier this year. Phases 1 and 2 of the project are expected to support a workforce of more than 3,500 local hires. Apple will be one of the facility’s first customers, marking another step toward expanding the scope of U.S. advanced manufacturing.

The iPhone maker says the new partnerships include increased use of recycled materials, and that all of its direct suppliers are required to power their entire Apple manufacturing operations with renewable energy by the end of the decade.

title: Here’s how iPhone Duo’s battery capacity compares to other iPhones
snippet: After pre-orders for iPhone Duo opened, Apple uploaded an EU regulatory document that finally revealed the true battery capacity for iPhone Duo: 4883mAh. Here’s how that compares to other iPhones. more…
fullText:
After pre-orders for iPhone Duo opened, Apple uploaded an EU regulatory document that finally revealed the true battery capacity for iPhone Duo: 4883mAh. Here’s how that compares to other iPhones.

4883mAh definitely falls towards the high-end of the battery spectrum, though it’s by no means the best.

iPhone Duo features two battery cells: one 2962mAh and another 1921mAh cell, totaling 4883mAh. This places it pretty much exactly in between the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, which offer 4288mAh and 5567mAh batteries, respectively.

title: GM is betting compute and AI will help it compete with Chinese automakers
snippet: To compete with Tesla, Rivian, and a host of Chinese automakers, GM’s fourth-gen EV platform will roll out a new central computer and electrical architecture that will debut in 2028 in the Cadillac Escalade IQ.
fullText:
When GM announced its new fourth-generation EV platform on Wednesday, what the automaker didn’t share was almost as notable as what it did. 

The new EV platform, part of a series of technology-focused announcements made during its annual GM Forward event in New York, didn’t talk about suspension geometries, dash-to-axle ratios, and torsional rigidity, all nerdy automotive terms that translate to how people will experience a car. Is it supple or sporty? Does it have a refined stance? When it hits a pothole, does it feel like a bank vault or a paper plate?

Instead, GM’s announcement centered on novel battery chemistries, revamped electric motors, and an entirely new central computing platform and electrical architecture that will connect every system in the car, including acceleration and power, steering, braking, and active safety features as well as software. Lots and lots of software.

“We think vehicles can become a more capable and helpful part of everyday life if we make them spaces that understand context, reduce friction, and give people back moments that would otherwise be consumed by the demands of the road,” Sterling Anderson, executive vice president, global product, and chief product officer at GM, told TechCrunch in a recent interview.

That sure doesn’t sound like a traditional automaker’s pitch. Then again, since the arrival of Tesla, Rivian, and Chinese automakers, the industry hasn’t been the same. Ride and handling still matter, but they’re table stakes. What sets vehicles apart today is largely defined by software. 

Anderson has talked about this future GM before. Last year, the company announced plans to overhaul the electrical and computational guts of its future vehicles in a bid to deliver faster software, more capable automated driving features, and a custom, conversational AI assistant. 

This year, GM is providing more details and dates. This technological overhaul is set to debut in 2028 with the Cadillac Escalade IQ. The company will also roll out an autonomous highway driving feature in 2028 that will allow drivers to have their hands and eyes off the road and without the need to be ready to take over.

The software race includes hardware

Image Credits:GM

European and U.S. automakers have spent years chasing the prospect of software-defined vehicles but have often fallen short. Volkswagen Group had so much trouble with its own in-house effort, including its troubled Cariad unit, that it struck a $5.8 billion joint venture deal with relative newcomer Rivian.

GM has been on its own capitally intensive software adventure. The company has bet heavily on software in recent years. It ditched the popular smartphone projection technology Apple CarPlay for nearly all of its EVs, and instead turned to a Google-based infotainment system, which is actually quite capable even if it doesn’t yet live up to the standards set by Tesla and Rivian. 

It’s poured billions into software and autonomous vehicle technology development too. GM’s capitalized software amortization expense in 2025 was $866 million, which gives a sense of how much it is spending even as it spreads out the cost over years. 

Like many legacy automakers, GM has come to the conclusion that the old approach to electronics, which scattered computer chips throughout the vehicle, was holding it back. 

For fourth-generation EVs, GM will centralize much of those functions on a central compute unit (CCU) that’s 40x more powerful than its existing systems. Eliminating smaller chips on the edges will help trim wiring by 30%, saving weight and simplifying assembly.

GM notes that this new CCU will work on fossil fuel models, too, though it will debut in the Cadillac Escalade IQ, a vehicle that is shaping up to be the automaker’s technological flagship.

The CCU will handle the usual propulsion and chassis controls, as well as perception and active safety. That should help pave the way for more advanced autonomy features, which GM also announced on Wednesday.

Such a move was perhaps inevitable. Pressure on automakers has been building on all sides. 

Domestically, Tesla has been pushing the boundaries of autonomy, in part because it developed a true software-defined vehicle. 

Automakers like GM are also feeling pressure from Chinese manufacturers, which have shortened development cycles to two to three years, down from the usual four to five years.

GM intends to match that cadence. Alongside announcements about battery chemistries and autonomy, GM outlined how enterprise AI tools have sped up vehicle development across every sector as it pushes to slash its traditional four- to five-year development timeline in half.

GM gave a brief glimpse of its revamped development strategy. One example: Engineers went through 300,000 virtual designs of a new lithium-manganese-rich battery pack before they assembled the first physical prototype. That helped the concept move to an approved program in one month.

Such speed will help GM save costs as it races to preserve profitability amid a historic upheaval in the automotive industry. But will it be enough to catapult it back into the leadership position it once enjoyed?

The rise of Chinese automakers won’t make it easy. Their factories are capable of producing far more than Chinese consumers can absorb, and coupled with government subsidies and cheaper labor, these vehicles have flooded markets from Europe to South America with inexpensive vehicles. 

Chinese automakers’ cost advantage is so steep that, without trade barriers, “they will pretty much demolish most other companies in the world,” Elon Musk said in a 2024 earnings call. In response, he has been trying to pivot Tesla from an automotive company to an AI and robotics company.

GM’s move into autonomy signals a similar shift. But to deliver true autonomy, GM realized it didn’t have the platform it needed. With a new architecture, it should have a fighting chance.

title: I’m Baffled by Oppo’s Find X10 Pro Max, but I Love It Anyway
snippet: Oppo launched two excellent phones within six months of each other. I’m confused, but maybe you can figure it out.
fullText:
It feels a bit weird to be writing about Oppo’s new Find X10 Pro Max flagship phone. I only reviewed the company’s last flagship, the Find X9 Ultra, back in June. But as the larger number in the name suggests, the X10 Pro Max is the first of Oppo’s next generation of Android phones, packing a whole suite of new tech, from fancy new camera sensors to the new MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro chip. 

I’ve been testing it for the past week or so, and there’s no question it’s a powerhouse phone that’s well worthy of its flagship title. But I said much the same about the Find X9 Ultra, with both phones boasting incredible Hasselblad-branded camera setups and potent processors. Both also make use of detachable telephoto zoom lenses for shooting long-distance photos. 

It’s not that I have any problem with the X10 Pro Max so far — it’s great in every respect — it’s just that I don’t know why it needs to exist so soon after the X9 Ultra debuted. I’ve already been quite vocal about companies launching new flagships every year and the X10 Pro Max doesn’t seem to have moved the story on all that much since the X9 Ultra. And at a starting price of £1,499 in the UK (roughly $2,010) the Pro Max costs roughly the same as the X9 Ultra, too. It does come with a “complimentary accessory” in the form of either the detachable telephoto lens or an Oppo smartwatch.

			

More from CNET

The glass and metal design looks classy.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Between the Find X9 Pro launched last October and the X10 Pro Max seen today, there are clear upgrades across the board. But between the more recent Find X9 Ultra and the Find X10 Pro Max it’s less clear-cut. Right now, I can’t tell you which has the better camera — both the X10 Pro Max and the six-month-old X9 Ultra have awesome setups, and I’ve taken great photos with both. 

The Ultra phones have traditionally stood apart from the Pro phones by having better screens, processors and camera systems. With the X10 Pro Max matching — or beating — the X9 Ultra’s performance across the board, I’m struggling to understand why you’d pick one over the other. Maybe this distinction will become clearer later.

Or for a more positive spin, I find myself in a situation where both these phones appear so equally superb that I can’t choose between them. 

If you live in the US, this is something of a moot point. Oppo doesn’t officially sell its phones in your country, so you can’t buy either of them. If you’re still keen to know more about this phone, here’s what I like so far. 

Oppo Find X10 Pro Max: Great cameras with new tech

I’ve been impressed with the cameras on Oppo’s recent phones, and the Find X10 Pro Max is no exception. It echoes some of what I saw in the Find X9 Ultra (200-megapixel main and telephoto lenses), but it bumps the ultrawide to 200 megapixels and adds an interesting upgrade to its main camera sensor. 

There are a whole bunch of cameras and sensors on the back.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The main camera uses a Samsung Isocell HPC sensor with something called DeepPix technology. What this essentially does is allow for more light information to be captured, resulting in a dynamic range (the difference between the brightest and darkest parts of an image) of around 17 stops. That’s up there with professional cinema cameras, but it also sounds like similar technology to the LOFIC (lateral overflow integration capacitor) sensor seen in phones like the Leitzphone by Leica and Xiaomi and in the recent DJI Osmo Pocket 4P. 

Because I’m neither an image sensor engineer nor a physicist, I can’t tell you exactly how these technologies differ — or if it really matters, as fundamentally they aim to achieve the same thing: better-looking images with more light information captured. 

Technicalities of the sensor aside, I’ve been pleased with many of the images I’ve taken with the phone so far. Dynamic range is (perhaps unsurprisingly) excellent, with colors that look punchy yet natural in both tone and saturation. 

Taken with the main camera, this shot has great dynamic range, with bold colors that still look realistic.Andrew Lanxon/CNET
And again, I love the vibrant but natural tones of this scene from the main camera. It’s pin-sharp, too.Andrew Lanxon/CNET
I like this shot, but I do think it looks a bit too “HDR” from the image processing.Andrew Lanxon/CNET
This shot is a little drab, but it’s still packed with detail.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

While some images can look a bit overprocessed, with unnaturally lightened shadows, I think the phone gets the balance right better than many Android cameras. Oppo also says it’s taken a lighter-touch approach with artificial image sharpening, instead giving images a more natural appearance when it comes to fine details. I think this has worked for the most part, although I sometimes find it goes too far the other way, with some highlights having a noticeable haziness and lack of definition around them. 

I shot this in the Master mode in order to take manual control of the white balance, as well as make extra edits in Adobe Lightroom.Andrew Lanxon/CNET
I used Master mode here too to choose my own white balance as well as use manual focus to ensure focus was on the owl and not on the bars of the cage.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Like with the Find X9 Ultra, I found that some of my favorite shots were taken using the Master mode where I took manual control of settings, including white balance, and in some cases shot in DNG raw to apply my own edits in Adobe Lightroom. 

The ultrawide has been bumped to 200 megapixels and its shots are crystal clear. I used one of the color filters here to add some drama to the scene.Andrew Lanxon/CNET
Taken at 6X zoom, this shot of a man with his falcon looks great.Andrew Lanxon/CNET
At 3X optical zoom this shot is vibrant, with rich colors. There is a softness to the highlights around the yellow pylons in the middle, however.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

There’s little color shift between the main and ultrawide lenses, and the 3x optical telephoto camera captures crisp details, with almost no noticeable drop in quality when you push the zoom to 6x by using digital cropping.

With the telephoto lens attached I could snag this shot of a seagull needlessly trying to ride a boat. Surely it knows it can fly?Andrew Lanxon/CNET
You can go right up to 40X zoom, though the details become noticeable softer at this point.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

If you want to take the zoom even further, slap on the physical telephoto zoom lens to achieve an optical zoom up to 10x and a digital zoom up to a whopping 40x. I’ve used these lenses on the X9 Ultra and the X9 Pro before and they’re good fun, especially if you’re into wildlife photography and want to capture a bird off in the distance. 

The quality isn’t great when you push it right to 40x, and the phone uses AI to upscale some of the details, but it’s far better than what you’d achieve with the phone by itself. I don’t know exactly how much the X10 Pro Max’s telephoto lens will cost, but keep in mind that the Hasselblad lens for the Find X9 Ultra was a princely $400 accessory. 

I used one of the camera’s color profiles to give a slight filmic look to this scene.Andrew Lanxon/CNET
There are a variety of new filters to choose from, all of which use a grid-based adjustment system, not unlike Apple’s Photographic Styles.Andrew Lanxon/CNET
I love taking panoramic images like this.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The camera comes with extras like the Hasselblad XPAN mode for taking wide, narrow panoramic images, along with a new color filter tool that’s basically identical to the color and tone grid Apple uses in its Photographic Styles. Still, I’m not complaining — it works well and it’s easy to craft a more creative look for your image. I suspect Apple may not be thrilled at the similar interface.

I’m overall impressed with the camera on the Find 10 Pro Max. It’s more than capable of taking stunning images, especially if you’re into your zoomed-in shots. But I can’t say if it’s any better than the Find X9 Ultra, or even if it’s supposed to be. The new sensor technology should mean it’s the better camera, but the Find X9 Ultra has a second telephoto zoom camera, a longer telephoto accessory and it’s covered in Hasselblad branding and colors. 

To understand the minute differences between their camera capabilities, I need time to put the two phones side-by-side. I also want to test it against the Leitzphone to see how the DeepPix sensor compares to the LOFIC one. The Leitzphone’s sensor is also physically larger, and the phone itself offers unique photography tricks like its continuous telephoto zoom, its physical settings wheel and its variety of Leica film profiles, all of which make it the camera phone to beat, in my opinion. 

Oppo Find X10 Pro Max: Solid performance, too many apps

The Find X10 Pro Max is powered by the latest MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro chip, rather than a Qualcomm chip as you’ll find in the Find X9 Ultra. There are some differences in performance between the two processors, with the X10 Pro putting in better processing scores on Geekbench 7, while the Find X9 Ultra’s Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip consistently outperforms on 3DMark’s graphics benchmark test. 

It’s a high performance phone in every sense.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

In everyday use, the X10 Pro Max was capable of handling everything I could throw at it, from demanding games like Genshin Impact to editing images in Adobe Lightroom. I honestly can’t say I find the phone to be any more (or less) powerful than the X9 Ultra, so if you were hoping to choose between the phones on benchmark tests alone, then you’re out of luck. 

What continues to bug me with Oppo’s phones is the needless amount of junk you’ll find preinstalled the first time you turn it on. There are third-party apps such as Temu, TikTok, ChatGPT and LinkedIn, and apps I’ve never heard of, including Bigo Live and iQiyi. Throw in the wealth of Oppo’s own apps, shopping services and theme stores, and the phone feels cluttered before you’ve even had a chance to download anything of your own. 

This is nothing new, though — I leveraged the same criticism at the Find X9 Ultra, and indeed many other Android phones. Yes, you can uninstall any of the garbage you don’t want, but it irks me that these expensive phones feel ad-supported because of the casserole of nonsense clogging your app library. 

Oppo Find X10 Pro Max: Battery life and other features

The Find X10 Pro Max packs a whopping 8,000-mAh silicon-carbon battery, at least in my test version; some EU regions will have a slightly smaller 7,150-mAh battery. After an hour of our YouTube streaming rundown test, the phone had dropped from full to 98% remaining and by the third hour was only down to 89%. 

I don’t love the amount of preinstalled junk on the phone.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

That’s not bad at all, putting the phone in line with top performers like the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra although not quite troubling the epic stamina of the iPhone 18 Pro Max. It also didn’t quite beat the scores achieved by the Find X9 Ultra. Still, it’s a great effort and you should comfortably expect the phone to offer at least a full day of demanding use with enough spare to get you a fair way into day two. 

The phone supports 80-watt wired fast charging which should make it extremely quick to put some juice back in the tank if you’re running short before heading outside. Though you’ll need to get a compatible fast charger. Oppo also reckons the battery is optimized for longevity, promising the battery capacity will only drop to 80% after five years. 

While I obviously haven’t been able to test this, I’m pleased that there’s a focus on longer-lasting hardware to keep your device going for longer. Oppo offers five years of software updates and six years of security updates, which is a step behind the seven years Google and Samsung offer, but I suppose it could be worse. 

Oppo Find X10 Pro Max: Should you buy it?

As I mentioned at the start, I find this phone’s existence confusing. It’s a camera powerhouse, but it comes right off the back of another Oppo camera powerhouse — there’s a huge amount of overlap in what these phones offer and who might be interested in buying them. They’re both superb, no question about that, but it’s like inviting two Michelin Star chefs to cook the same meal for your party — there might be subtle differences that mean some like one over another, but at the end of the day, why have both?

I rarely wish for companies to offer less in their product lineups, but in this instance I feel Oppo might have been wise to hold back some of its camera innovations — especially the new sensor tech. Instead, the Find X10 Pro Max could have been more focused on general lifestyle, productivity and gaming, giving the Find X9 Ultra a bit more breathing room. 

Everything is great about this phone from its vibrant display to its awesome cameras. But I loved the same about the X9 Ultra, too.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Then, after Spring next year, the company could launch the Find X10 Ultra, packed with incredible camera tech that totally changes the game and makes it feel fresh and exciting. Instead, the X10 Pro Max feels so close to its six-month-old sibling that I’m struggling to work out which one is actually better and, more importantly, why both need to exist at the same time. 

Early adopters who shelled out the high price for the Find X9 Ultra specifically for the camera performance may well feel a little cheated that the company has so quickly launched a phone with brand-new, superior image sensor technology. It feels like Oppo is at risk of diluting its impact, cannibalizing sales of its own products and potentially even alienating existing customers.

But company strategy aside, the X10 Pro Max is excellent, offering everything you’d need from a flagship phone right now. It’s got enough power for any of your daily tasks and the camera is well-equipped to capture your world as you see it. How it compares to the competition remains to be seen.

title: PHP Vulnerabilities Could Put Much of the Internet at Risk, Experts Warn
snippet: Up to 70% of all the websites on the internet could be affected.
fullText:
An agency that monitors the PHP programming language issued a severe warning on Tuesday that it had identified two major cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Fixes should have been deployed on Wednesday at 10 a.m. ET, but security experts are urging website administrators to take immediate notice and precautions.

The warnings are unusually severe, rated 9.2 out of 10. On Wednesday afternoon, PHP released some technical details about the two exploits. They allow bad actors to run malicious code on a site’s web servers. The very best thing you can do to keep your website safe is to immediately install the latest version of PHP. Older versions of PHP that have been sunsetted are also getting an emergency update with the patches.

PHP is a free, open-source programming language that much of the web is built on. According to the Wall Street Journal, 70% of the world’s websites could be vulnerable. Security agencies around the globe, including the US’s chief cyber agency, the US National Security Agency and the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, are urging website administrators to install the updates or take their sites offline until they’re able to patch them.

			

More from CNET

Effective Immediately, all organizations using PHP for their systems are advised to be prepared for an update addressing two critical vulnerabilities. PHP is widely used for web applications. These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or…

— NSA Cyber (@NSACyber) October 21, 2026

Cloudflare’s chief technology officer Dane Knecht said Wednesday morning that the company has deployed a fix to its firewall. Cybersecurity company watchTowr says it was able to successfully reproduce one of the exploits. “As expected, watchTowr Intel is already observing in-the-wild exploitation of the latest PHP vulnerabilities,” Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence, said via email on Wednesday morning. “Whilst nobody has been successful to date, we don’t expect that will last long.”

OpenAI said in a blog post on Wednesday that the vulnerabilities in PHP were discovered by Calif, a self-described hacker team, using its AI model, GPT-5.6 Sol. Wiz, an AI cloud cybersecurity company, also independently identified the vulnerabilities, according to the ChatGPT maker. 

Artificial intelligence has been a double-edged sword in cybersecurity, providing both cyber defenders and attackers with powerful tools. And AI companies know this, with OpenAI saying this incident “highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.” Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have begun slow-rolling the release of their AI models to let cybersecurity experts to use them first to shore up their own defenses and identify any issues before a wider release.

But for everyday internet users like you and me, the concern is that while AI is great at spotting these bugs, it can take longer to get them patched. Even OpenAI says it “expect(s) similar findings to increase sharply in the coming months.”

title: iPadOS 27.2 adds convenient new feature from the Mac
snippet: iPadOS 27.2 launches next week, and among its many new features, Apple has also brought over a recent Mac addition: a Siri popup when text is selected. more…
fullText:
iPadOS 27.2 launches next week, and among its many new features, Apple has also brought over a recent Mac addition: a Siri popup when text is selected.

Siri AI is the tentpole addition to iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and companion releases. And as such, Apple offers lots of ways to access the new, supercharged assistant.

On iPad you can invoke Siri via a “Siri” or “Hey Siri” voice prompt, pull down from the top of the screen, use the new Siri option in the edit menu, open the new Siri app, or my personal favorite: use CMD + Space to open Spotlight and ask Siri a question from there.

But iPadOS 27.2 adds yet another option that’s borrowed directly from the Mac.

In macOS 27 Golden Gate, in many situations when you select some text, a small Siri icon appears in the top-left corner of the selection. When you hover over the icon with your cursor, it expands to offer an ‘Ask Siri’ text box.

This wasn’t available in iPadOS 27. But now, if you have a trackpad connected to your iPad, that same behavior is available in iPadOS 27.2.

As seen in the images above, the new Siri icon starts out small and stays out of the way, but it’s very convenient to just hover over it to make the ‘Ask Siri’ box appear.

If you don’t have a trackpad attached, selecting text will still reveal the full edit menu where you can tap to open Siri. But it’s a more smooth and seamless experience with a trackpad.

macOS is full of small productivity-focused features like this that speed up everyday interactions, yet are missing from iPadOS. So it’s exciting to see such a recent Mac feature be brought over to the iPad.

title: Google upgrading Gemini for Android Auto with Personal Intelligence
snippet: Google is beginning to roll out Personal Intelligence for Gemini on Android Auto and Android Automotive (cars with Google built-in). more…
fullText:
Google is beginning to roll out Personal Intelligence for Gemini on Android Auto and Android Automotive (cars with Google built-in).

Like in the Gemini app or AI Mode, Personal Intelligence taps into your Google Workspace (including Gmail and Calendar), Photos, Maps, Search, and YouTube to personalize responses. Your prompts and commands don’t have to include specifics as Personal Intelligence can pull those details from emails, photos, or a “place you saved in Google Maps.”

This allows for complex or natural queries, like “What’s my flight gate? And is my flight on time?” or “Take me to my doctor’s appointment.”

“You don’t have to hunt for the confirmation email, then do a separate search for delays. Gemini gives you both answers in one go.”

“You don’t have to remember the street address or look it up before you drive.”

Additionally, Gemini is aware of your preferences when you say: “Find me an indoor restaurant along my route that matches my usual vibe.” This saves you from having to specify you’re vegetarian with every command.

	

Other examples include:

Retrieve details without pulling over: Trying to return to a place you saw earlier? Say, “Find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.” You don’t need to scroll through your camera roll or pull over to get the name and directions. 

Pick up where you left off: Heading out for the morning? Say, “Take me to the coffee shop we were talking about yesterday”. Gemini will handle the digging and send you on your way.

	

On the privacy front, Personal Intelligence is opt-in, though it will come to Android Auto automatically if you enabled it for the Gemini app on your phone.

If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you.

Meanwhile, on Android Automotive, Personal Intelligence will only share personalized responses “when you’re in the car with your phone connected.” 

Personal Intelligence is rolling out starting today to Android Auto, with Android Automotive availability in the coming months.
