title: ChatGPT gets deeper Google Chrome integration including control over tabs
snippet: OpenAI this week announced deeper integration between ChatGPT and Google Chrome, including the ability to hand control over your tabs to the AI assistant. more…
fullText:
OpenAI this week announced deeper integration between ChatGPT and Google Chrome, including the ability to hand control over your tabs to the AI assistant.

In a thread on Twitter/X, OpenAI details improvements to the ChatGPT extension for Google Chrome. The browser add-on now features deeper integration with Chrome, including the ability for ChatGPT to look at your open tabs and get things done with that context.

That starts with the ability to ask questions within ChatGPT that the AI can answer using the context of your open tabs, or even to control those open tabs to do things.

…ChatGPT can control your Chrome tabs to get things, like sending messages, filling out forms, or downloading files. It can even help you organize and group that pile of tabs you have open.

There’s also a sidebar UI that you can use ChatGPT through, similar to how you can use Chrome’s built-in Gemini integration.

	

Two videos show off the integration in action:

OpenAI lists examples including:

Compare the three couches I have open by dimensions, material, delivery time, and return policy.

Explain this article in plain English. What’s the main argument, and what evidence supports it?

Compare these pricing pages against our requirements. Which plan includes everything we need?

Use the details in this event brief to fill out the registration form, and stop before submitting. 

Put the vendors in these tabs into my comparison sheet, with pricing, key features, and source links.

Look at all the tabs I have open and compare the contractor services. Then draft an email to the one that fits my home renovation.

Fill out the form I have open in @chrome ahead of seeing my new dentist. Also, can you add the appointment to my work and personal calendar.

The ChatGPT extension is now available in the Chrome Web Store.

title: Ohio State Makes a Stink by Digitally Sending Scents
snippet: The scent-sending technology could be used in online shopping, healhcare diagnoses and just for fun.
fullText:
Want to celebrate your faraway friend with a sniff of fresh-baked birthday cake? Wake up a sleepy dorm daughter with the scent of coffee or oranges? It’s still a Jetsons-style dream for regular folks to send scents across the miles, but researchers at the Ohio State University are bringing us closer. They’ve developed a new system capable of detecting and transmitting smells across vast distances.

That system, outlined in a study released Wednesday, includes two different devices. First, an AI-powered e-nose detects and analyzes an odor. Then, it sends that scent data to a receiver called a Scentronic, which recreates the smell for someone else.

The team created a few versions of the Scentronic, including a wristband, a handheld model and a necklace. Each one is equipped with a five-channel scent distributor that uses a piezoelectric atomizer to spray the scents. (Piezoelectric refers to the use of pressure to create an electrical charge.) The entire device is powered by Wi-Fi and a cloud server that stores and transfers the scent data between devices.

			

More from CNET

The team used five scents: cake, beer, red wine, coffee and oranges. The e-nose detected one of those aromas, sent it to the Scentronic, and then the Scentronic reproduced the scent for the 16 people testing the system. Those people accurately identified all five scents.

Chunyu Yang, a doctoral candidate at OSU and lead author of the Scentronic paper, told CNET in an email that these scents were deliberately chosen because they represented familiar but distinctive smells people encounter regularly in the real world. 

Researchers suggest that this technology could be used in a variety of applications, including online shopping, to let people smell products before buying them. The technology could also be useful in healthcare diagnoses. A common symptom of COVID-19 is loss of smell, while migraines, pregnancy and other conditions can cause hyperosmia, a heightened sensitivity to smell.

There’s also an element of sheer entertainment.

“One exciting potential application is remote scent sharing,” said Yang. “For example, imagine enjoying a delicious meal and being able to share its aroma with a friend or family member who lives far away. This could add a whole new dimension to long-distance communication and make remote interactions more immersive.”

Another contender in digital scents

The e-nose uses an AI-assisted sensor and machine learning to learn a scent, and the piezoelectric atomizer shoots the scent to the end user.The Ohio State University

The first time a scent was transmitted over data was in 2014 with a product called the oPhone. That device used scent cartridges called oChips and an iPhone app to release 10-second aromatic bursts, called oNotes. The various cartridges mixed together to create approximately 300,000 distinct smells, allowing people in Paris and New York to send smell-o-grams to one another. 

Similar devices exist in the market, but they can’t analyze a smell. Users can choose only from a selection of predefined smells. 

That’s where the Scentronic stands out. The system can both analyze smells and send them.

“Scentronic uses a gas-sensor array combined with machine learning to recognize odors,” Yang said. “This approach allows us to develop a more compact sensing system that can be integrated with wearable devices.”

Another company, Osmo AI, is also using AI to digitize smells. Osmo AI uses gas chromatography and mass spectrometry to map the scent at the molecular level and then synthesizes the scent in a clear liquid cartridge that can be dispersed to recreate aromas.

Yang says that Osmo’s setup provides “detailed chemical information,” but that its equipment is much larger, whereas the Scentronic is designed for wearable use.

title: Not upgrading to iPhone 18 Pro or Duo? Here’s what’s coming next year
snippet: iPhone Duo preorders just begun, and iPhone 18 Pro has been on the market for about a month. Of course, iPhone Duo is backordered through January right now, so whether or not you’re considering buying these phones – it makes it really easy to think about what’s coming next. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo preorders just begun, and iPhone 18 Pro has been on the market for about a month. Of course, iPhone Duo is backordered through January right now, so whether or not you’re considering buying these phones – it makes it really easy to think about what’s coming next.

2027 is going to be a relatively big iPhone release year for Apple. First, the company will be continuing the iPhone 18 lineup after it introduced a split release schedule last month. Then, in the fall, the company will debut a new round of flagships in celebration of the 20th anniversary of the iPhone. Here’s what to expect.

Spring 2027

iPhone 18

For the first time, Apple will be introducing its base iPhone in the spring. Upgrades for the iPhone 18 aren’t quite clear, though more RAM is one of the key rumors. Thermal upgrades will likely happen as well, as well as the new Apple C2 modem.

It’s possible Apple will update the design to fall more in line with the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro, though we don’t yet know.

This phone will of course equip the A20 chip, and it’ll probably start at the same $899 price point that iPhone 17 currently sits at – after it was increased from $799 last month.

iPhone 18e

This phone will most likely just end up being a chip bump from the A19 to A20 chip, and debut in the Spring alongside the iPhone 18. Earlier this year, reports indicated that Apple would share many components between the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e, though it isn’t quite clear what that could mean for the devices.

iPhone Air 2

Out of all of the spring iPhone releases, this one is the one to look forward to. After receiving a lukewarm reception with the initial iPhone Air model, Apple went back to the drawing board and decided to modify the design to fit an ultrawide camera into the device. This meant the phone couldn’t be released last month.

Personally, I don’t think an ultrawide camera is too important – though many people will see one camera on the back of the phone and immediately assume it’s less premium, so it’ll probably end up being an important upgrade for the sake of sales. Plus, ultrawide photos can be fun at times.

While not confirmed, I wouldn’t be surprised if it integrates a smaller Dynamic Island, similar to iPhone 18 Pro. iPhone Air 2 will likely also jump from Apples C1X modem to the C2.

It should also have a larger battery, reportedly as large as 3500mAh. That’s a roughly 10% improvement from the original iPhone Air.

Fall 2027

iPhone 20 Pro

For the 20th anniversary of the iPhone, Apple is expected to debut a fully redesigned iPhone to celebrate. It’ll reportedly be much more glassy, feature significantly slimmer bezels, and ditch the flat edge design of the iPhone 12 and later. It should also offer a much smaller Dynamic Island, likely with a hole punch selfie camera and under-display Face ID.

Personally, I’m slightly skeptical that this’ll truly be a replacement to the “Pro” phone for thermal reasons, but time will tell. iPhone Duo seemingly has strong thermals while not featuring an aluminum unibody, so my concern might not be relevant. It’ll offer two, larger display sizes: 6.4-inch and 7-inch. This largely comes from the bezel reduction.

	

If you’re holding out for iPhone 18 Pro, this “iPhone 20” is definitely the phone to wait out for.

iPhone Duo 2

Lastly, Apple will release a successor to its just-announced iPhone Duo next fall. There aren’t many substantial rumors for this phone, though one could hope Face ID and better cameras are in the pipeline. Of course, you can expect next-generation Apple Silicon with the A21 Pro chip next year.

title: Google Pixel’s solution to using Face Unlock in the dark seems to be just blinding you
snippet: Google’s Face Unlock feature on Pixel phones works really well, until the lights go out. The company appears to be building out a new upgrade to this with “active illumination” which is… just turning up the screen brightness. more…
fullText:
Google’s Face Unlock feature on Pixel phones works really well, until the lights go out. The company appears to be building out a new upgrade to this with “active illumination” which is… just turning up the screen brightness.

Face Unlock as it exists on Pixel 8 and newer relies on the camera and Google’s software to deliver biometric authentication that’s actually strong enough to let you unlock secure apps such as banking and password manager apps.  

While the fingerprint sensor serves as a fine backup, not having Face Unlock in dark rooms can be a tiny bit frustrating. And Google’s solution appears to be just raising the screen brightness.

The folks over at Android Authority uncovered a new option being built out in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 2 which is simply titled “Brighten screen in low light.” Google’s summary of the feature reads:

	

Automatically boost screen brightness so Face Unlock works in dim lighting.

Sounds fun in a dark room.

An assortment of strings related to the feature further detail what to expect, with Google seemingly set to offer granular settings around if the feature is used when Bedtime mode, Do Not Disturb, or driving is detected, as well as a setting to tailor just how bright the screen can get.

“Reliable” sounds like it might turn up the brightness higher to ensure an accurate reading from Face Unlock, while “Comfortable” seems to trade brightness for, well, not blinding you. 

	

Some of the strings mention:

Brightness level – Reliable, Comfort – Lower settings may reduce reliability

Complete darkness – Can brighten to find your face when it’s too dark. When turned off, only brightens if your face is partially visible

Bedtime mode – Can brighten when Bedtime mode is on

Driving – Can brighten when a car ride is detected

“When this feature is turned on, the following accessibility settings may temporarily behave differently: extra dim, remove animations, or color inversion”

“Can brighten when Do Not Disturb is on”

It still doesn’t sound like a particularly elegant solution, but it’s certainly better to have the option available. As for when Google might roll this feature out, that also remains to be seen. 

Would you opt to have your screen brightness raise for the sake of using Face Unlock on a Pixel? Let us know in the comments.

title: Apple blocks web certificates that could be used by scammers, but Mac vulnerability remains
snippet: Apple has blocked eight web security certificates that could have been used by scammers to impersonate legitimate websites. However, one cryptography engineer has warned that Macs may continue to trust the compromised certificates because macOS does not check for revocation … more…
fullText:
Apple has blocked eight web security certificates that could have been used by scammers to impersonate legitimate websites.

However, one cryptography engineer has warned that Macs may continue to trust the compromised certificates because macOS does not check for revocation … 

The issue concerns what are known as intermediate certificates. These are used to prove ownership of a website, so if you visit apple.com, for example, Safari will check that you are visiting the real site.

However, an error in a script used to generate these certificates led to a number of private keys that could be trivially discovered by testing just 256 possible numbers. The eight compromised certificates have now been revoked, and steps taken to ensure that the vulnerability won’t affect any future certificates issued.

Bleeping Computer reports that Apple, Google and Mozilla have each blocked the compromised certificates in their respective web browsers. However, Mozilla cryptography engineer Dennis Jackson warns that Macs may continue to trust them.

Jackson also warns that macOS’s built-in /usr/bin/curl utility may continue trusting the compromised certificates because its certificate bundle does not check revocation information.

In other words, if your Mac has already accepted one of the certificates, then it will continue to do so. However, there is currently no evidence of them being used in the wild, and it’s something that Apple is likely to be able to fix in an upcoming security update.

title: Sony just canceled a promised Android 17 update for one of its Xperia phones
snippet: Sony isn’t exactly known for speedy Android OS updates, but the company has now completely canceled an Android 17 update for one of its Xperia phones. more…
fullText:
Sony isn’t exactly known for speedy Android OS updates, but the company has now completely canceled an Android 17 update for one of its Xperia phones.

In a notice on its website, Sony says that it will not provide an Android 17 update to the Xperia 10 VI despite initially promising “three Android OS upgrades” for the device. 

Sony announced the Xperia 10 VI in 2024 as an upper-mid-range device. It has a Snapdragon 6 Gen 1 chipset, 8GB of RAM, and 128GB of storage, with Android 14 having been pre-installed at launch. Android 17 was the last promised update even though it wasn’t included in the initial roadmap Sony posted in September. 

The company says that Xperia 10 VI “does not support an Android 17 upgrade experience that we consider adequate” due to a “limitation” related to the phone’s storage. The exact reason isn’t entirely clear, but Sony says security updates will continue on as promised, and that other Xperia devices due to get Android 17 will no be affected.

	

Sony explains:

We announced at launch that the Xperia 10 VI would receive three Android OS upgrades. However, after a detailed technical assessment, we determined that due to limitations related to the device’s storage configuration, the Xperia 10 VI does not support an Android 17 upgrade experience that we consider adequate. Accordingly, we have decided not to make this upgrade available. We recognise that this falls short of our original announcement, and we wish to apologise for this change.

On the other hand, our security update commitment remains unchanged. Sony will continue to provide security updates for four years from the product’s launch date, as previously communicated.

This issue is specific to Xperia 10 VI’s technical specifications and will not impact other Xperia models.

It’s certainly an odd situation, and one that we don’t often see. While it’s not uncommon for Android phones to not be promised as many updates as they should recieve, it’s rare for a promised software update to be canceled outright.

title: Report: Apple gains ground on rivals, but iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo face challenges
snippet: In a new investor note sent out this week, GF Securities’ Jeff Pu and Henry Huang project that Apple will be the only major smartphone manufacturer to grow shipments in 2026, even as the global market is expected to shrink by more than 14%. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a new investor note sent out this week, GF Securities’ Jeff Pu and Henry Huang project that Apple will be the only major smartphone manufacturer to grow shipments in 2026, even as the global market is expected to shrink by more than 14%. Here are the details.

Apple bucks smartphone market downturn

For the past few weeks, several reports from IDC and Counterpoint Research have been mapping out the impact of rising memory costs on smartphone sales.

And while the numbers may vary slightly, it is increasingly clear that Apple has been able to weather the downturn better than its competitors.

This week, Pu and Huang released a new investor note reinforcing that trend, projecting that Apple will gain significant market share in 2026 as most of its major competitors see shipments decline.

According to the report, Apple is on track to close out 2026 as the only major smartphone manufacturer to increase shipments, with a projected 4% year-over-year gain to 257 million units.

That would keep Apple ahead of Samsung, which is expected to ship 241 million smartphones, essentially unchanged from 2025. Apple also topped the rankings in 2024 and 2025.

Apple’s share of global smartphone shipments is also projected to climb to 24% in 2026, compared to 20% in 2025 and 19% in 2024.

Market-wide, the report projects a 14.2% drop in total shipments to 1.08 billion shipped smartphones for 2026, and further pegs 2026-2027 as “one of the most challenging periods for the industry, driven primarily by sharply higher memory prices, which have already pushed OEMs to reduce shipments and raise device prices.”

Back to Apple, the report reiterates that the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max have received a relatively lukewarm reception, which the analysts partly attribute to competition from the iPhone Duo and criticism of their weight. The analysts also cite production constraints affecting both the iPhone Duo and the iPhone 18 Pro lineup:

Due to hinge constraints, we are reducing the iPhone Duo EMS build plan from 7m to 6m units in 2026. We also lower the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max build plan to 72m units given the constraints associated with the adjustable‑aperture camera.

The iPhone Duo went up for pre-order earlier today and is already showing delivery estimates stretching into late January in the US and even further in other countries.

With all of that in mind, the report maintained its “Hold” rating on Apple stock, with a price target of $369. Apple shares closed at $343.46, up 0.43% on the day, making it the only major tech stock to finish in the green amid the ongoing sector-wide sell-off.

title: YouTube says it’s not hiding the dislike button – this is what’s actually happening
snippet: Reports of YouTube moving the dislike button behind a menu have been showing up lately but, according to YouTube itself, this isn’t the change you think it is. more…
fullText:
Reports of YouTube moving the dislike button behind a menu have been showing up lately but, according to YouTube itself, this isn’t the change you think it is.

The dislike button has been a topic of contention in the YouTube community for years now, ever since YouTube removed the count that showed alongside it. So when some users noticed that the dislike button was suddenly no longer visible and hidden behind an overflow menu, there was plenty of confusion around the change.

In a statement to 9to5Google, though, YouTube directly confirms that this is not a test or a change that you’ll see on YouTube videos. Rather, this update to the dislike button’s location appears solely on the video page for a creator’s own video. In other words, you’ll only see this altered location on your own videos.

A YouTube spokesperson explains:

	

We are not testing hiding the dislike button on YouTube for users. We’re introducing a new UI for creators on their own uploaded videos, where dislike is behind the three-dot menu, and as always, they can find their full dislike counts in Studio, alongside other analytics.

And, sure enough, we were able to immediately replicate this behavior when we tested it out on one of our own videos.

title: Apple calls iPhone Duo pre-order demand ‘extraordinary’ as shipping dates slip
snippet: Apple has issued a short statement following strong initial demand for the iPhone Duo, with shipping estimates already slipping into next year. Here’s what the company said. more…
fullText:
Apple has issued a short statement following strong initial demand for the iPhone Duo, with shipping estimates already slipping into next year. Here’s what the company said.

As soon as iPhone Duo pre-orders opened today, shipping estimates began slipping from late October into November, then December, and eventually January. In some countries, including Brazil, estimated deliveries have already been pushed into early February.

While there had been reports warning that initial iPhone Duo supplies could be limited, the speed and extent of the shipping delays still caught many by surprise.

	

Apple, meanwhile, is putting a positive spin on the strong initial response. In a statement shared with CNBC, the company described pre-order demand as “nothing short of extraordinary”, and added:

“We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers’ hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online.”

With shipping dates slipping well into next year, scalpers on eBay and X are already looking to cash in, with asking prices reaching as high as $10,000.

This has led to criticism of Apple’s handling of pre-orders, with some calling on the company to identify and cancel orders placed by scalpers.

What’s your take on how Apple has handled the iPhone Duo pre-orders so far? Let us know in the comments.

title: iPhone Duo walk-in purchases might be challenging at launch, per report
snippet: According to a new report from MacRumors, Apple employees are being told to warn customers that iPhone Duo likely won’t be available for purchase on launch day if you didn’t already place a pre-order. more…
fullText:
According to a new report from MacRumors, Apple employees are being told to warn customers that iPhone Duo likely won’t be available for purchase on launch day if you didn’t already place a pre-order.

Right now, Apple’s website suggests that you can check back for iPhone Duo availability on October 24th. However, this isn’t a guarantee of any stock actually being available, per MacRumors:

Apple Store employees told MacRumors that they have been advised that there will likely be no ‌iPhone Duo‌ stock available for walk-in purchases on launch day. Staff have been instructed to discourage customers without pre-orders from coming in expecting to buy the device, warning that they will be disappointed.

This isn’t necessarily a surprise, given the fact that Apple stated yesterday that iPhone Duo demand is “extraordinary,” and we’ve long known that there were production constraints that’d lead to limited iPhone Duo supply around launch.

However, this still serves as our first true sign that even if you line up at an Apple Store the night prior to the iPhone Duo launch, you might not actually end up getting a device. Some stores might receive no additional shipments beyond what was already pre-ordered.

	

As of now, iPhone Duo is sold out through January. If these supply constraints remain, it’ll probably be challenging to buy a device for the foreseeable future. Scalpers have also been charging absurd markups on iPhone Duo orders close to launch day.

If you truly want an iPhone Duo sooner than later, carriers and Best Buy seem to be a decent bet, at least in the US.

When you can’t decide between a “regular” watch and a smartwatch, a hybrid is the way to go. Just as it sounds, the Garmin Instinct Crossover successfully marries the physical, tactile feel of a standard sports watch with the usefulness and health-tracking wizardry of a smartwatch. title: tvOS 27.2 adds three new features to your Apple TV 4K
snippet: tvOS 27.2 is coming next week, bringing several new features to Apple TV 4K users—including some screen saver upgrades. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
tvOS 27.2 is coming next week, bringing several new features to Apple TV 4K users—including some screen saver upgrades. Here’s what’s new.

#1: Shuffle option for screen savers

tvOS offers a variety of great screen savers across multiple categories, including Aerials, Memories & Slideshows, Portraits, and Snoopy.

But historically, you’ve had to choose just one of these categories for your Apple TV screen savers, thus missing out on all the others.

In tvOS 27.2, Apple has a new ‘Shuffle’ option which will cycle through all available screen savers—regardless of category—throughout the day.

I’ve always favored Apple’s beautiful selection of Aerials. But I love that now I can continue enjoying Aerials while also benefiting from the other screen saver categories too.

#2: Apple TV app supports sign language

For select movies and shows that support it, the Apple TV app now lets viewers toggle sign language options inside the player controls. Per Sigmund Judge:

Update: tvOS 27.2 Beta 3 confirms upcoming Sign Language options for both American (ASL) and British (BSL) – allowing access to sign language options in player controls on selected movies and shows.

— Sigmund Judge (@sigjudge) October 5, 2026

ASL (American Sign Language) and BSL (British Sign Language) are available, expanding accessibility for content in the Apple TV app.

#3: Custom screen savers from Photos library

If you want to curate Photos screen savers, tvOS 27.2 lets you do that in a new and convenient way.

When setting up screen savers in the Memories & Slideshows or Portraits categories, you’re now able to manually select the content that’s included from your iPhone or iPad.

	

Thanks to this addition, you can enjoy Apple TV screen savers from Photos without being forced to let them access your full library.

title: Hands-on: UGREEN’s new 25W MagSafe battery for iPhone features liquid cooling
snippet: Last month, UGREEN introduced a new Qi2.2 25W 10000mAh MagSafe battery bank for iPhone. There have been plenty of these, but this one has an interesting new twist: liquid cooling. more…
fullText:
Last month, UGREEN introduced a new Qi2.2 25W 10000mAh MagSafe battery bank for iPhone. There have been plenty of these, but this one has an interesting new twist: liquid cooling.

On the back of the battery, there’s a window that showcases the liquid within the battery bank moving throughout it. This should help keep it a little bit cooler than most MagSafe battery banks.

UGREEN says that it’ll be around 18 degrees cooler than usual, and while that’s probably true – it’s worth nothing that it still isn’t a cold battery bank, it’s just cooler than usual. It’ll still feel warm in your hand.

On the bottom of the battery bank, UGREEN integrates a USB-C cable for charging your phone or any other USB-C device that can’t (or you prefer not to) charge wirelessly. I found it a bit handy at times, since of course wireless charging is never as energy efficient as wired charging.

I will admit, the battery bank is a little bit thick, and the lack of a kickstand is somewhat bothersome at this price point, especially when so many others offer one. That said, if heat is a concern of yours with MagSafe battery banks, this one will definitely solve that for you.

On the side, it offers a small display for showing battery percentage and charging speed.

One last thing of note: if you’re buying an iPhone Duo, this will stick out from the bottom of the phone, based on case dimensions I’ve tested it with. This is true for most MagSafe accessories on iPhone Duo, though.

The UGREEN MagFlow battery bank comes in at $149, which is quite pricey for a MagSafe battery of any kind. That said, UGREEN currently has it on sale for $95 on Amazon, making it much more palatable if you’re looking for a MagSafe battery bank that doesn’t get as hot as the competition.

title: Apple must open iPhone to alternative app stores in Australia after Epic Games ruling
snippet: An Australian federal judge has ordered Apple to make sweeping changes to its App Store rules following a years-long antitrust battle with Epic Games. Apple has confirmed that it plans to appeal. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
An Australian federal judge has ordered Apple to make sweeping changes to its App Store rules following a years-long antitrust battle with Epic Games. Apple has confirmed that it plans to appeal. Here are the details.

Epic scores major victory in Australia

Apple must allow iPhone users with Australian Apple Accounts to install apps from third-party app stores and websites starting March 1, 2027, a federal judge ordered today in a 235-page decision. Apple has until February 15 to request an extension until May 3, 2027, subject to court approval.

Today’s order follows a ruling last year that Apple violated Australian competition law by restricting alternative app distribution and payment methods, in a lawsuit brought by Epic Games similar to its long-running legal battle with Apple in the US.

In his decision, Justice Jonathan Beach said Apple held “a substantial degree of power in the iOS app distribution services market and the iOS in-app payment solutions market,” and used its developer agreements and App Store guidelines to restrict competition.

Among the practices singled out by the judge were:

Blocking app downloads and installations outside the App Store

Preventing developers from distributing apps through alternative channels

Requiring developers to use Apple’s in-app payment system

Prohibiting links to alternative payment methods

Requiring developers to offer content purchased elsewhere through Apple’s in-app purchase system as well.

Preventing developers from handling refunds directly

The ruling also cited Apple’s actions against Epic Games in 2020, including its refusal to allow Epic Direct Pay, Fortnite’s removal from the App Store, and the subsequent termination of Epic’s developer account.

Justice Beach described the latter two actions as “a paradigm example of Apple’s enforcement of its restrictive terms, in contravention of” section 46 of Australia’s Competition and Consumer Act 2010, which prohibits corporations with substantial market power from engaging in conduct that has “the purpose, or has or is likely to have the effect, of substantially lessening competition” in that market.

As a result, Justice Beach issued a wide-ranging series of orders requiring Apple to, among other things:

Allow alternative app stores and sideloading: Let Australian iPhone users download and install apps directly from websites and third-party marketplaces.

Allow alternative payment methods: Let developers use payment systems other than Apple’s, including within apps distributed through the App Store.

Permit external payment links: Allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods from within their apps.

Provide access to developer tools: Make the APIs and tools necessary for alternative app distribution available on substantially the same terms as those offered to App Store developers.

Restrict fees and other barriers: Prohibit fees for accessing alternative distribution channels, limit certain fees on external payments, and allow developers to offer lower prices outside Apple’s payment system.

Readmit Epic Games’ apps: Allow Fortnite and other eligible Epic Games apps back onto the Australian App Store, subject to compliance with applicable developer rules. (Importantly, this specific order is not subject to the March 2027 deadline, but rather takes effect immediately, with Apple required to act upon receiving a written application from Epic.)

The decision also addresses several other aspects of Apple’s App Store policies, including restrictions on its ability to turn off apps installed outside the App Store and requirements related to notarization.

The court also prohibited Apple from requiring developers to report transactions processed through alternative payment providers or offer Apple’s payment system alongside their preferred alternatives, both of which are requirements the company imposes in other regions, including Brazil and Japan.

When it comes to Apple’s wins in the decision, the list is much slimmer. Judge Beach rejected Epic’s request to extend the court’s injunctions worldwide and allowed Apple to maintain security scanning and notarization requirements for apps distributed outside the App Store. And while Apple must permit competing app marketplaces on iOS, it is not required to distribute them through its own App Store. This is a distinction he had already established in last year’s ruling.

Finally, the court ordered Apple to pay 85% of Epic’s legal costs incurred through the original trial, while reserving a decision on costs associated with the subsequent hearings over remedies.

Commenting on the decision, Epic confirmed “Fortnite is coming back to the App Store in Australia tomorrow,” and celebrated it as “great news for developers worldwide and iOS users in Australia who will benefit from an open mobile app ecosystem.”

In a statement to Reuters, Apple said:

“We will request a stay and appeal the outcome to seek a resolution ​that ​respects our ⁠intellectual property and protects the safe, ​secure experience that consumers ​and ⁠developers expect from the App Store.”

title: Apple’s iPhone Duo Should Get Reachability Accessibility in an Upcoming Update
snippet: The $1,999 foldable phone is harder to use for left-handed people and those with smaller hands.
fullText:
The iPhone Duo is reportedly getting a Reachability feature later this year.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Apple’s new iPhone Duo, which officially goes on sale on Friday, should be getting the Reachability accessibility feature later this year, according to reporting by Wired. Reachability is a setting that lets you move the top half of your phone display down, making apps and buttons easier to reach with one hand. 

If the $1,999 iPhone gets the feature for its wider screens, particularly its 7.6-inch inner display (which is only slightly smaller than the 8.3-inch iPad Mini), it should make it easier for folks to reach elements on the left or right edges of the screen. 

		

			

Reachability has been part of iOS since 2014, with the iPhone 6 and 6 Plus, which had 4.7-inch and 5.5-inch screens, respectively. The iPhone Duo’s outer display is 5.4 inches, and it would make sense for Apple to continue updating it to be easier to use.

While Apple hasn’t said how Reachability might work on the iPhone Duo, there is speculation that it will help left-handed users, or those with shorter fingers or smaller hands, navigate the screen both horizontally and vertically. Apple representatives didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Duo has already been a preorder smash, with estimated ship dates stretching into January.

Several controls, such as the App Dock, are located only on the right side of the iPhone Duo.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

While early reviews on Apple’s first foldable iPhone are largely positive, some apps and services haven’t yet been optimized to fill the displays. 

In her iPhone Duo review, CNET’s Abrar Al-Heeti noted that controls like the App Dock and Dynamic Island sit on the right side of the Duo’s cover and inner displays, which makes the phone geared for right-handed, not left-handed, use. “My condolences to all the lefties, as you can’t shift controls to the other side of the screen,” she said in her review. 

Al-Heeti told me that the Duo’s 5.4-inch cover screen is relatively compact, and that it would be great to have the Reachability feature on the larger 7.6-inch display. “In my experience, tapping through apps is easy enough with two hands, but Reachability could make it feel less unwieldy and therefore even more versatile by enabling one-handed gestures,” she said.

title: Someone made a Walkman music player for the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and it works with YouTube Music
snippet: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 app turns it into a Sony Walkman using your music, YouTube Music, and even Spotify very soon. more…
fullText:
The Galaxy Z Fold 8 app turns it into a Sony Walkman using your music, YouTube Music, and even Spotify very soon.

Foldables sort of walk that dichotomic line between nostalgic and futuristic. They remind us of flip phones from the 2000s, while running on an entirely different decade of tech.

Naturally, a Walkman-style app is a welcome addition to something like the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

One user developed an app called “Foldman” that uses your music from local storage or other apps and plays them in a virtual tape deck. On the Galaxy Z Fold 8, the app’s facade looks just like a cassette player. The app expands to show a wider stereo visual when the phone is opened up.

	

There’s a ton of cool little touches, like a volume slider and running tape counter on the virtual player. And the tape actually transfers from one tape reel to the other instead of a looping animation with no progressive movement! That’s such a nice little detail.

A Walkman-esque app fits so well on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 because of how wide and short the front display is, just like Sony’s original cassette player. That form factor is becoming increasingly popular, and it’s creating opportunities for some cool apps like this.

The app’s developer plans to integrate Spotify within the next couple of days and cautions that this early version has some rough edges. For now, it works with YouTube Music and Apple Music, as well as with files stored locally. The app is free and open source, stripped of ads or tracking.

We never recommend users download APKs outside of verified app stores, so do so at your own risk.

Beyond Spotify, they note that they’re looking into adding support for self-hosted streaming services, so users can use it with their existing library of digital files on their network. For now, it’s a simple little Walkman-style player, and that’s cool enough.

title: HomeKit Weekly: Get your Halloween and Christmas automations set up now
snippet: It’s time to get your Halloween decorations out and automate them because the gear you buy for October is the same gear you’ll use in December. Set it up once now, and all you’ll do in November is swap what’s plugged into your gear. My first real Apple Home project years ago was automating Christmas lights, and it’s still the easiest win in your entire smart home, and it’s really one of the most useful things you can do. more…
fullText:
It’s time to get your Halloween decorations out and automate them because the gear you buy for October is the same gear you’ll use in December. Set it up once now, and all you’ll do in November is swap what’s plugged into your gear. My first real Apple Home project years ago was automating Christmas lights, and it’s still the easiest win in your entire smart home, and it’s really one of the most useful things you can do.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

Start with a home hub

Before buying anything else, make sure you have a device that can serve as a home hub. That means having an Apple TV, a HomePod, or a HomePod mini signed into your iCloud. Without one, you can’t run automations or control anything while you’re away from your local, which defeats most of the purpose here. It isn’t technically required for Apple Home, but for holiday automations, it may as well be.

Outdoor plugs are the real purchase

This is the part that lets you use your system both holidays. In October, Halloween inflatables, projectors, and pathway lights make the perfect Apple Home setup for Christmas lights and yard decorations in December, all running off the same outlet you set up once. Buy outdoor-rated plugs, not indoor ones, and run an extension cord out a window. Indoor plugs aren’t built for cold, moisture, or rain, and you’ll be dealing with both by the time December arrives.

Onvis Outdoor Smart Plug

Meross Outdoor HomeKit Plug

Kasa Apple HomeKit Outdoor Smart Plug

Lutron Caseta Weatherproof+ Outdoor Smart Plug

Minoston Outdoor Smart Plug Outlet

Most of these plugs have two independently controlled outlets, which matters more than you’d think if you don’t set them up. One side runs your inflatable, the other can run a light, and you can put them on different schedules. I have one out year-round on my back porch for lamps

Indoors, a single smart plug turns your Christmas tree into an Apple Home automation, and the same plug handles a Halloween window display or a fog machine in October.

Eve Energy with Thread

TP-Link Tapo

Minoston Matter Smart Plug Outlet

Shelly Smart Plug

Eve Energy costs more than some others, but it supports Thread.

Halloween setup

Halloween is when Apple Home motion sensors are especially useful. If you put a sensor near the walkway, you can trigger a light when someone approaches the door. It’s the one holiday where having a reactive automation beats a scheduled one.

Bulbs that can change color on the porch are the other easy win. If you swap your normal porch bulb for a color-capable one, set it to orange or deep purple for October, then back to warm white in November. The Linkind Smart Light Stick would be an interesting option to have as well.

Christmas setup

Your Christmas tree is the obvious one to automate. Plug it into an Apple Home/Matter smart plug, name it something Siri will easily understand, and you’re set: “Hey Siri, turn on the Christmas tree.” That single automation is the one my family uses most, and it costs about $20 to set up. You can also simply automate using the tips below.

Building the automations

Once your devices are in the Home app, go to the Automations tab, tap the + button, choose Add Automation, and pick A Time of Day Occurs. Sunset is the setting you want for almost everything holiday-related, since it shifts automatically as the days get shorter. The step a lot of people can forget about: create a second automation to turn everything off. Sunrise works, but a fixed time like 11 PM is usually better in my experience.

Here’s a tip that I’ve learned from years of smart home use: name your devices very simple. Call the outdoor plug “Front Yard Lights” instead of “Christmas Lights,” and you won’t have to touch anything or rename devices when the season changes. The automation you built for Halloween keeps working in December. In fact, I’ve gotten to the point where I leave mine plugged in all year just so I don’t have to remove, reset, and re-add.

Wrap up

The best thing about Apple Home is that you can start with a single outdoor plug and an inflatable ghost, or with a Christmas tree, and build it out from there over time. The hardware is really inexpensive, the automations take about five minutes each, and doing it in early October means you’re not standing outside in the cold in December trying to pair a plug to your network. Set it up once in the fall, then run it for both Halloween and Christmas.

title: iOS Decoded: iOS 27.2 RC – hands-on w/ HomePod Sound Glow, TV profiles, Apple TV Home Theater assets, more [Video]
snippet: In this episode of iOS Decoded, we take the HomePod’s new Sound Glow feature for a test drive and try out the new Lock Controls feature to prevent accidental activation of its top cap. We also go hands-on with other changes, like the handy new profiles option for the TV app and Suggested Actions for Messages. Further, we take a look at and listen to some of the assets and sounds from Apple TV’s new surround-sound Home Theater functionality. Watch our full hands-on video as we dive into these changes and many more, and be sure to subscribe to our YouTube channel for more. more…
fullText:
In this episode of iOS Decoded, we take the HomePod’s new Sound Glow feature for a test drive and try out the new Lock Controls feature to prevent accidental activation of its top cap.

We also go hands-on with other changes, like the handy new profiles option for the TV app and Suggested Actions for Messages. Further, we take a look at and listen to some of the assets and sounds from Apple TV’s new surround-sound Home Theater functionality.

Watch our full hands-on video as we dive into these changes and many more, and be sure to subscribe to our YouTube channel for more.

Sound Glow

Starting with iOS 27.2, the HomePod mini and 2nd-generation HomePod will see their LED Matrix displays, which feature 19 and 37 RGB LEDs, respectively, used in a way they haven’t before, thanks to Sound Glow.

Sound Glow transforms the top cap into a color-matched animated visual canvas that matches the album artwork. The canvas glows and pulses in concert with the currently playing song or podcast, responding to changes in bass and treble. For Soundscape ambient sounds like rain, forest, fireplace, etc., bespoke RGB animations are used instead of the Sound Glow audio processing pipeline, since Soundscapes are very different from music.

Video: iOS 27.2 Top Features

Subscribe to 9to5Mac on YouTube for more videos

Users who have updated their iOS devices and HomePods to 27.2 will find a new Sound Glow toggle in the Home app under the HomePod settings.

I’ve tested Sound Glow fairly extensively, and I’ve been impressed by the feature. It gives music playback a slightly unique experience with each song. I’ve also been impressed by the sheer vibrancy of the display, as Apple is clearly making full use of all of the LEDs embedded under the top cap to generate unique colors based on the currently playing song.

Sound Glow is vibrant, but it’s not extremely bright, and won’t light up your room or anything. But if you place your HomePod in an area where the top cap is easily visible, it’s a really nice addition.

What’s more noteworthy is that Sound Glow isn’t just limited to new hardware like Apple’s recently announced HomePod mini 2. The feature also works with the first-generation HomePod mini and the second-generation full-sized HomePod. 

We’ve long known about the LED Matrix display that sits under the touch sensor, but it makes you wonder how long Apple has been sitting on such a feature internally, before deciding to announce it during the HomePod mini section of Apple’s recent HomeView hardware unveiling. My takeaway: Sound Glow may look simple on the surface, but there’s a lot of impressive engineering under the hood that generates these animations!

Lock Controls

Another new HomePod-focused feature found in iOS 27.2 is the ability to lock the touch surface to prevent both accidental and intentional interactions. Users will find a new Lock Controls toggle when opening the HomePod settings inside the Home app. Enabling this feature will disable touch interactions for touch, touch and hold, and volume controls.

When touching the top cap with Lock Controls enabled, you’ll see a red animation that shakes back and forth, as if it’s saying “no”. 

The red “no” indicator when using the touch panel with Lock Controls enabled

As I mentioned in the video walkthrough above, my cat sometimes paws at the top cap, causing the HomePod to play music. Enabling Lock Controls would eliminate that issue while still allowing human household members to control Siri by voice or via another iOS device.

In addition, Apple notes that Lock Controls will not interfere with the ability to interact with features such as timers, intercom alarms, check-in, or FaceTime calls via touch. All of those items will remain responsive to a touch of the top cap.

Apple TV Profiles

The TV app on iOS 27.2 now supports creating new profiles and switching between them, something we’ve already been using on tvOS. This feature is especially useful if you have small children who enjoy using your phone to watch content via the TV app. Now you can simply switch to your child’s profile, and they can enjoy their content without affecting your profile. In other words, no more episodes of Duck & Goose or Frog and Toad littering your Up Next queue.

TV app profiles come in handy when sharing your device with kids

Suggested Actions

The Suggested Actions feature for the Messages app first appeared in the initial iOS 27 betas but was eventually removed before iOS 27 shipped. Now, in iOS 27.2, Apple is ready to ship the feature that will automatically suggest actions based on what’s in your Messages thread. For example, if you paste an address, you might receive an Open in Maps suggestion, or if you type in a date, an Add to Calendar suggestion may appear.

Messages suggestions return for the first time since the iOS 27 beta

Users can fine-tune the types of suggestions presented in Settings → Messages → Suggested Actions. There, you can toggle on or off add to Calendar, Reminders, Notes, Show in Maps, and Flight and Packages suggestions. Apple also notes that suggestions that you don’t use will stop appearing after a month.

Apple TV Home Theater setup

We’ve discovered lots of interesting new assets that give us a behind-the-scenes look at the setup process for the fourth-generation Apple TV’s Home Theater capability, made possible by adding four HomePods in two separate stereo pairs.

A look at the different HomePod Home Theater configs with Apple TV 4th-generation

We also get a look at some of the animations used during that process, along with an impressive-sounding Celebration animation upon successfully calibrating your Home Theater. You can listen to the corresponding sound just below:

9to5Mac’s Take

These features are just the tip of the iceberg in terms of all that we uncovered in the iOS 27.2 beta. In our hands-on video, we discuss details about unreleased iPhone and iPad hardware we found. I let you hear and see lots of new sounds and assets from the HomeView setup process, and more. Stay tuned for future episodes of iOS Decoded, where we go deeper than the surface level in terms of new iOS releases!

title: Galaxy S27 reportedly skips Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 due to overheating
snippet: According to a new report, Samsung’s Galaxy S27 series might not use the latest Snapdragon chipset due to overheating problems. more…
fullText:
According to a new report, Samsung’s Galaxy S27 series might not use the latest Snapdragon chipset due to overheating problems. 

The Snapdragon vs Exynos debate has been around for years, with Samsung often mixing its two flagship chipset choices, but also occasionally going all in on one or the other. Snapdragon is almost exclusively used in the US, with the last time Samsung used Exynos entirely in the States being the Galaxy S6 over a decade ago. That was due to overheating problems with Qualcomm’s flagship chip at the time, and it seems we’re in for a case of deja vu.

Seoul Economic Daily reports that Samsung has “informed Qualcomm of the overheating issue” with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and is looking at Exynos 2700 as an alternative. The report claims:

Samsung is in talks with Qualcomm to resolve the heat issue within this month, according to sources. If Qualcomm meets the required performance, Samsung will adopt Snapdragon as originally planned; if not, it will have little choice but to consider the Exynos 2700 as an alternative, weighing performance stability and mass-production timelines.

Qualcomm announced its latest flagship chips in September and the top-tier Elite Extreme Gen 6 features a 2nm process and two 5GHz cores. Qualcomm claims a 13% boost in CPU performance over the Gen 5 chip, 44% improvement in GPU performance, and boosts to AI processing and power efficiency.

	

There have already been a few phones announced with the chip, including the US-bound Motorola Signature 27, but it’s too early to tell if overheating issues are going to be widespread.

Update: Qualcomm, in a statement sent to 9to5Google, says that the report is “inaccurate.”

Recent reporting about thermal issues related to Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 is inaccurate. We are proud of the innovation and strong momentum behind our next-generation flagship platform and continue to work closely with global OEMs to deliver premium user experiences.

title: iPhone Duo review roundup: The same problems Android foldables face, but with Apple’s polish
snippet: Apple’s first foldable has arrived, the better part of a decade after Android laid the groundwork for the form factor. iPhone Duo reviews are here and, while it sounds like a lot of the same problems that plague Android foldables still exist on Apple’s first-gen release, there’s certainly a level of polish there – and I’m not talking about the $9 cloth. more…
fullText:
Apple’s first foldable has arrived, the better part of a decade after Android laid the groundwork for the form factor. iPhone Duo reviews are here and, while it sounds like a lot of the same problems that plague Android foldables still exist on Apple’s first-gen release, there’s certainly a level of polish there – and I’m not talking about the $9 cloth.

Ahead of the first shipments arriving for customers later this week, the avalanche of iPhone Duo reviews has arrived today and, with it, the first look at what it’s like to live with Apple’s first foldable. 

Starting with our sister site 9to5Mac, of course, Chance used the iPhone Duo for a week and walked away “convinced that this form factor represents the future of the iPhone.” His in-depth review hits on every key aspect of this device, but his ultimate conclusion boils down to this being the future of Apple’s smartphones because the form fact “just makes sense” and that there’s “something special about a compact, notebook-like iPhone that unfolds into a tablet-like experience.”

9to5Mac: iPhone Duo review: The future is foldable

Looking at iPhone Duo reviews from the perspective of someone who’s been using Android foldables as their daily driver for over half a decade at this point, I can’t help but look at Apple’s first attempt and see the foundation it’s building on, but also the places where Apple’s inherent polish comes into play.

	

One big part of that seems to be the inner display. The nanotexture matte finish sounds like a big deal, with it making the crease visually not a problem. It’s still there, Chance stresses in his 9to5Mac review, but you “almost never” notice it visually unless you’re looking for it – just like most Android foldables. He adds that you’re more likely to feel it than see it. 

The app situation clearly seems to be running into the same early problems as Android foldables hit. Apps simply aren’t optimized for a radically new form factor yet. That’s what pushed Android foldables into the “phone that turns into a square tablet” trend they were stuck in for years, despite brands like Oppo and Google coming up with this iPhone Duo form factor way before Apple was a part of the conversation. Apple has the same problem, and it’s not going to be fixed overnight.

That said, it’s clear that it’s going to get cleaned up much quicker. WIRED‘s review opens up mentioning how “in the past day” key apps including “Instagram, Threads, Slack, and even the Google app now have navigational icons on the right rail instead of the bottom center, and the app content is better laid out to make use of the larger screen.”

“Mr Foldable” himself, Michael Fisher, explains in his review how apps that are not optimized are rough, comparing it to the early days of iPad, but that some key players are already stepping up. On top of that, smaller devs are building apps clearly inspired of this new form factor. “Tiny Computers” looks absolutely delightful.

David Imel mentions that “you can scale things up and they work, but they do look silly” in regards to unoptimized apps, and also makes a good point – not everything is going to get updated. iOS apps that aren’t actively maintained anymore are always going to be a mess on this device and, frankly, the scaling features Apple gives you make everything look way worse than an unoptimized app on an Android foldable has ever looked.

Look at the options you get for the yet-to-be-optimized Google Maps. Michael Fisher points out how it still doesn’t take up the whole display and that, if you rotate the phone, it just sends you back to square one. Sounds bad!

Apple’s new sidebar UI, which I still think looks funky, is personally my biggest fear as these wide foldable form factors take over, not because it’s a bad idea – Fisher points out that he actually loves it – but because Android apps will probably take a whole lot longer to adopt it. Seeing where things are starting out on the iPhone Duo, yeah, I’m sticking with that take.

That outer display, too, seems to be a hang up. The Verge says that “most Duo owners will find that the cover display is simply too small to use all the time.” That’s a problem I ran into a bit with Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 and its similar shout and stout form factor, but Apple’s device is even smaller, so I’m not shocked to hear this. 

That same review makes a case for Apple’s app split, saying that “the problem with the Duo is that the outer screen isn’t useful enough, so you want to open it all the time,” while saying that “the problem for most Android foldables is that the inner screens aren’t that useful so there’s no super compelling reason to open them.” I’m not sure I agree there – larger canvases and multitasking alone have sold me on a foldable for years – but seeing so many iOS apps going all-in on the new screen size certainly has me feeling a bit envious. 

Another review that caught my eye was from Joanna Stern, where she puts the iPhone Duo “through hell.” There are two things of note here. First, Joanna puts the Duo through over 32,000 folds on top of normal daily use, and the hinge unsurprisingly holds up well. Android brands have laid an incredible foundation here, so even if Apple took its own route, the technology is clearly up to par here for a strong foldable hinge. 

But also pointed out here is a problem that’s been on every single Android foldable I’ve ever used – the iPhone Duo gets warm. Joanna calls the device a “hand warmer” and, apparently, Apple said this was business as usual for the device’s heat management. I was curious if the thicker design of Duo would help alleviate this one, but it seems Apple is dealing with the same issue. It’s a lot harder to cool two halves of a device, and you feel that heat more when there’s more usable space on the device.

Virtually every review mentions how hefty the iPhone Duo’s hardware is, too. This is a problem that Android foldables have been chipping away at generation-by-generation, and that the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the poster child for. Smartphone weight continues to be something you don’t notice until it pushes over the edge and, while we’re not at Pixel Fold levels, iPhone Duo is very much at that edge.

Based on these early reviews, Apple didn’t reinvent the foldable, but it’s clear there’s a level of polish on the iPhone Duo that was lacking on Android foldables. Apple has a vision for its foldable and, while it’s tripped up on a few things on attempt #1, it’s undeniably a good start. 

What’s next for Android foldables? I look forward to seeing exactly that…

title: iOS 27.2 adds new setting to fix common HomePod annoyance
snippet: HomePod owners, have you ever wished you could disable touch controls on the top of your device? With iOS 27.2, Apple is finally adding that option. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
HomePod owners, have you ever wished you could disable touch controls on the top of your device? With iOS 27.2, Apple is finally adding that option. Here are the details.

HomePod touch controls can be disabled with ‘Lock Controls’ setting in iOS 27.2

If you have ever had an issue with your HomePod and phantom touches, or perhaps like me you have a young child, you may have wished for a way to disable touch controls.

According to leaker pdfu, that option is officially coming with iOS 27.2 and HomePod 27.2 next week.

All HomePod models will support the Lock Controls setting, according to HomePod software 27.2 RC.

You should see the setting in the Home app after updating both HomePod and iPhone. https://t.co/lAPVuRg3av

— pdfu (@itspdfu) October 19, 2026

As seen in the screenshot above, iOS 27.2 adds a new setting for ‘Lock Controls’ inside the Home app’s HomePod accessory settings. When enabled, here’s what it does per Apple:

Prevent HomePod from playing audio or taking action when the top cap is touched. Intercom, timers, alarms, Check In and FaceTime calls will still respond to touch.

If you control your HomePod primarily through your iPhone or another device, Lock Controls is a great option to have. Particularly if you have toddlers or cats at home, or if your HomePod experiences phantom taps, you might want to disable touch interactions.

As pdfu’s post today says, this new setting is coming to all HomePod models, even the first-gen HomePod from 2018.

Do you plan to use this new HomePod setting in iOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

title: HP Googlebook 14 Review: Great laptop, shame about the OS
snippet: HP’s first crack at a Googlebook laptop is a winner, or at least as much of one as the platform allows. While Googlebook as an operating system leaves a lot to be desired, the HP Googlebook 14 checks every single box for a fantastic laptop. more…
fullText:
HP’s first crack at a Googlebook laptop is a winner, or at least as much of one as the platform allows. While Googlebook as an operating system leaves a lot to be desired, the HP Googlebook 14 checks every single box for a fantastic laptop.

Kicking things off with the hardware, HP really has built a very good laptop here.

The design is subtle at a glance, but I appreciate the sharp corners of the underside where the feet hold the laptop up for air circulation. There’s a decent-sized gap in the back for airflow as well which almost feels like a handle when you’re carrying the closed laptop. It’s a far cry from something as flat and edgeless as a MacBook Air, but I’ve really come to like it while using the HP Googlebook 14. 

The machine is just 10.9mm thick, and weighs in at 2.74lbs (despite an error that doubles the weight on HP’s website). The aluminum build is sturdy with minimal flex in the deck, and it mostly passes the one-handed opening test. 

	

					

The HP Googlebook 14 is a well-built, speedy laptop sold at a good price for its specs, but it’s let down by a young and incapable operating system and launching at a time where your money is best spent elsewhere.

					

				

Pros

				

											

Excellent keyboard + trackpad

											

Vivid display

											

Thin and well-built hardware

									

			

					

				

Cons

				

											

Googlebook OS is not as capable as Windows or macOS

											

The Snapdragon X Elite runs well, but is also over 2 years old

									

			

			

The keyboard has been a tremendous highlight. Despite the thin design, there’s a ton of travel in this keyboard and it’s wildly comfortable to type on. The keys have a satisfying clack without being too loud to be used in public spaces, and the spacing is great, while the backlight is also perfectly pleasant. It took just a few minutes to feel completely at home typing, though Googlebook’s keyboard shortcuts do take a moment to settle into. The top row of function keys are simple and straightforward for the most part, but the window fullscreen toggle (F4) and screenshot tool (F5) both need better iconography — the screenshot key is incredibly vague.  

The trackpad is also quite good. While I still struggle with Google’s premium push on Googlebook’s first wave, I’m glad that haptic trackpads were mandated, though HP’s implementation feels just a tiny bit hollow. The placement of the trackpad going right up to the spacebar might prove troublesome for some users, but I never ran into any issues in my testing period.

As for the display, the 14-inch OLED panel is gorgeous. It’s crisp and colorful, and just bright enough. I’d love if it were a bit brighter for outdoor usage, but it’s perfectly acceptable as long as you’re not in direct sunlight.

Battery life is good enough, though not quite at the level of something like a MacBook Air. That’s a bit of a tough pill to swallow given Googlebook OS’ inherent limitations, but this is a far cry from the dark days of laptop battery life and easily on par with a Snapdragon-powered Windows machine. Standby time is good, and it’s actually quite nice having Android’s typical battery usage stats at the ready. Windows is far behind in this regard. Charging has been very quick and I commend HP for including a charger that feels like it belongs in this decade, though I typically stuck with whatever USB-C chargers I had at the ready both in at-home use and on a recent trip.

Performance on the Snapdragon X Elite with 16GB of RAM is unsurprisingly excellent. Seeing as Googlebook is built on Android, it’s a clear formula for a speedy machine. While I’ve absolutely run into my fair share of hiccups here or there, boot times are near-instant, and the overall performance is impossible to complain about.

HP Googlebook 14 has every piece of a great laptop, but sadly it all comes down to the software, and Googlebook is a drag on this machine.

Our Abner Li has already delivered a pretty in-depth review of Googlebook OS as a whole, so this is basically my own personal addendum on that.

Googlebook OS review: A post-smartphone PC, if Google can keep it

My view of Googlebook is that, frankly, it seems a bit pointless in this day and age. Google has rebuilt ChromeOS on top of a new foundation that, yes, presents more possibility for the future, but also fixes virtually none of the existing problems. Like ChromeOS, Googlebook has an incredibly limited library of desktop-class software, even more so given that Linux support has regressed tremendously. One could point at obvious examples like the Adobe suite here, but it really comes down to the niche apps and tools that have been built out for Windows, macOS, and Linux for decades now. That’s an impossible task for any new platform to deal with, but Googlebook feels as though it is actively ignoring that clear gap in functionality. As mentioned, Linux app support has been largely decimated, which was a major boon to the app situation on ChromeOS. There’s also no way to emulate apps for other platforms here, which would be another good way to meet the needs of users not satisfied by what can be found on the Play Store or the web. Google literally has the tools to do this and, yet, none of them can be found here.

	

In launching this platform, Google’s repeated line about who this is for is “it’s a laptop for Android users.” I’m absolutely sick of hearing that. It’s utterly meaningless.

In a smartphone-dominated society, smartphones are the tentpole. Yes, you want integration between devices, but you’re not buying a laptop for smartphone integration. You buy a laptop to do the things that your phone can’t, and Googlebook can’t really do much more than your phone, at least not yet. 

HP did a great job building out a very good laptop for Googlebook. The hardware is just let down by the software. You’d have a much better time using this laptop with Windows or even Linux compared to Googlebook right now. Especially at a time when the cost of laptops continues to skyrocket, I cannot recommend that anyone invests $1,200 into a Googlebook when you can get a Windows laptop, or even a MacBook, for the same price, if not less. There’s simply no reason to get less functionality for the same price. Fast-forward to when Googlebook is available on less expensive hardware and it might be a different story, but right now, eh.

title: You should pick up this $850 Pixel 10 Pro XL over its $1,300 sequel
snippet: Whether you’re in need of a new phone or you’re trying to get some early Christmas shopping out of the way, Amazon has a killer deal on a Pixel 10 Pro XL that might make you forget all about RAMageddon. more…
fullText:
Whether you’re in need of a new phone or you’re trying to get some early Christmas shopping out of the way, Amazon has a killer deal on a Pixel 10 Pro XL that might make you forget all about RAMageddon.

It’s no secret that consumer tech prices are continuing to balloon in the face of AI-driven RAM shortages, which makes any deal on last-gen tech always worth considering. It says a lot that, even removed from that context, this $850 Pixel 10 Pro XL in Moonstone remains an all-around great deal, saving you a whopping $450 over its successor without much in the way of meaningful sacrifices. In fact, considering the 256GB variant actually has more RAM than this year’s base Pro XL model, you might come out ahead in the long run.

Buy Pixel 10 Pro XL for $850 at Amazon

Still, it’s worth breaking some of those sacrifices down. In addition to the obvious downside of losing a year’s worth of software upgrades — since we’re a full 12 months further along the Pixel 10’s seven-year lifecycle — you’ll have to be willing to lose a handful of changes on both the hardware and software fronts. Other hardware changes include a Tensor G5 over the G6, a slightly dimmer display, a smaller telephoto sensor, and, of course, the lack of everybody’s favorite underbaked Google feature, HiLight.

But hey, at least you get a temperature sensor and a brighter flash.

On the software side, Camera Looks is the big missing tool, with no plans to bring my favorite Pixel camera feature to previous generations on the horizon. However, I wouldn’t say Camera Looks is worth the extra $450, especially when Camera Looks being backported certainly remains a possibility in play. The same goes for Google’s typical slate of AI features; tools like Rambler remain Pixel 11-exclusive for now, but considering third-party developers have already made their own moves in this regard, I would expect to see an improved take on the company’s latest voice-to-text model show up sooner rather than later.

	

Don’t sleep on this deal; we’ve already seen a $700 sale price for the smaller Pixel 10 Pro in 256GB sell out (though the 128GB model is still available for $750). If you’re looking for a new phone to help you weather RAMageddon — and you don’t want to break the bank to buy it — this Pixel 10 Pro XL might be your best hope.

title: Google TV shows off its ‘new’ features in fullscreen roundup when you turn on your TV [Gallery]
snippet: Google TV is rolling out its latest feature roundup, showcasing new features and additions that have rolled out in recent months. more…
fullText:
Google TV is rolling out its latest feature roundup, showcasing new features and additions that have rolled out in recent months.

Next time you turn on your Google TV, you might be greeted with the October 2026 roundup of new feature additions. Google has been sending out these occasional fullscreen summaries for a while, with the latest showing up this week on Google TV Streamer and other devices.

The new features Google is highlighting this month include:

New Freeplay channels & on-demand content

Watchlist relocation & tweaks

Google Photos search

Gemini-aided “Remix your photos”

Dynamic slideshows

These have mostly rolled out over the past few months. 

	
	

We clocked the new Freeplay channels last month, with Google TV now offering over 300 built-in channels. The expansion of free on-demand movies and shows was announced in August and rolled out shortly after. Dynamic slideshows launched back in April, and Photo search even further back in January.

The new Watchlist location change arrived in a homescreen redesign back in November of last year.

All is to say, your guess is as good as ours as to why Google chose to showcase these features as “new” right now, when realistically there’s only one new addition in tow. It’s not the first time this has happened, with these roundups showing up a couple of times a year on Google TV Streamer and other devices, but it’s certainly something to see such a broad window of what’s considered “new.”

title: iPhone Duo has a bigger battery than Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold
snippet: Apple’s iPhone Duo may be thicker and heavier than most Android foldables, but it makes use of that space with a bigger battery compared to its main competitors, with a bigger battery than both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and PIxel 11 Pro Fold. more…
fullText:
Apple’s iPhone Duo may be thicker and heavier than most Android foldables, but it makes use of that space with a bigger battery compared to its main competitors, with a bigger battery than both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and PIxel 11 Pro Fold.

The iPhone Duo measures in at 254g and is 11.3mm thick when closed. That’s considerably heavier and a fair bit thicker than virtually every other Android foldable on the market today, as we previously discussed.

iPhone Duo is thicker and heavier than basically every Android foldable

But Apple isn’t wasting that space.

Despite the short and stout footprint of the iPhone Duo, the device is packing a 4,883 mAh battery. That’s the rated capacity as confirmed on an EU energy label, that is, as Apple almost never publicly confirms the battery capacity of iPhones. MacRumors did find the same info on Apple’s own documentation of the same EU energy label.

	

That’s not exactly a huge number in the foldable space, but it’s bigger than the iPhone Duo’s main competitor offers. Citing the same EU data, here’s how Samsung and Google compared:

iPhone Duo: 4,883 mAh

Neither the Fold 8 nor the Pixel 11 Pro Fold have particularly bad battery life, but Apple having a bigger battery along with the host of other reasons that iPhone users are in Apple’s ecosystem makes it harder to convince anyone to look at Samsung or Google’s devices – the main competitors in the US – as a complete alternative to the Duo.

title: YouTube reportedly ‘looking’ into adding audiobooks to Premium
snippet: Based on a recent report, YouTube is apparently considering adding audiobooks as a new medium alongside music and video. more…
fullText:
Based on a recent report, YouTube is apparently considering adding audiobooks as a new medium alongside music and video.

According to a report by The Wall Street Journal, YouTube is “looking” into audiobooks for a future addition to the app. There’s little detail as to when it could become a concrete feature, or whether it would be offered as a standalone benefit.

The report does mention that Google is considering offering it with YouTube Premium, which costs $16/month. It would join ad-free music playback with YouTube music, in addition to the main selling point – ad-free videos.

	

YouTube has seemingly not confirmed the possibility. It wouldn’t be unheard of, considering Spotify and other major platforms have partnered with audiobook services to offer users a little more than just music.

	

While it isn’t entirely the same thing, Google Play Books’ YouTube channel has been a dedicated spot for audiobook previews, and this integration would just make it easier to connect the two products.

It also wouldn’t be the first time YouTube has donned another hat. Shorts was seen as a direct way to compete with TikTok, and it’s become a major part of the app for the company. But the YouTube Music app might be a better fit for audiobooks, rather than the main video hub.
