title: Here’s the difference the variable aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro makes at night
snippet: I previously tested the difference the wider aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro makes when it comes to depth of field. The executive summary is that the difference is small, but definitely present. I said at the time that I’d intended to test the difference it made to Night mode shots when an unmissable night video opportunity had me write about that instead. So belatedly, let me turn my attention to Night mode photos … more…
fullText:
I previously tested the difference the wider aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro makes when it comes to depth of field. The executive summary is that the difference is small, but definitely present.

I said at the time that I’d intended to test the difference it made to Night mode shots when an unmissable night video opportunity had me write about that instead. So belatedly, let me turn my attention to Night mode photos …

Once the ship had passed through the bridge, I stuck around to return to plan A: testing Night mode still photos. The new variable aperture lens offers two complementary advantages for night photography: allowing us to either increase or reduce the shutter speed depending on the effect we’re looking for.

Faster shutter speed

The widest aperture is boosted from f/1.8 to f/1.48. The wider the aperture, the more light captured for any given period of time. That should mean that Night mode shots have a shorter duration, meaning we don’t have to hold the phone still for quite so long. The shorter the duration, the lower the chances that inadvertent movement will spoil the shot.

I tested this with a number of shots and found that while the difference in duration was indeed rather small, as we’d expect from less than one stop of extra light, it may be enough to help in some circumstances.

For example, for this shot, switching from f/1.8 to f/1.48 reduced the duration from 2.1 seconds to 1.7 seconds.

Other test shots showed similar results. The biggest differences are likely to be in the darkest of environments, like astrophotography. However, living in London, this is about as dark as it ever gets, and we never get to see stars, so that wasn’t something I could test.

Slower shutter speed

Conversely, there may be times when we actually want a slower shutter speed. For example, having the shutter open for a longer period helps to smooth out choppy water, which can give a more pleasing appearance.

By manually reducing the aperture to the maximum of f/4 (a larger number is a smaller aperture), I was able to increase the exposure time to 4 seconds. This did indeed help give the water a smoother appearance.

This helps significantly with reflections on the water. For example, check out the reflections of the four spotlights on the floating pontoon under the Discover London from the Water sign. Drag the slider left and right to compare:

The other benefit of the smaller aperture is the starburst effect you get from lights. Again, compare those pontoon spotlights as well as the street lamp on the left.

However, if you want the ultimate glassy water effect, then you need a significantly longer exposure. On a standalone camera, the usual exposure we choose for this type of shot is 30 seconds, typically at f/16 or f/22, and on an iPhone that requires a third-party app to combine multiple shots into one. The shot below was taken from the same place using the Spectre app I reviewed back in 2024. This was a 30-second exposure taken on my iPhone 16 Pro Max, and you can see that it gives the water an ice-like glassy-smooth appearance:

Conclusions

Is the variable aperture lens enough reason to upgrade from the iPhone 17 Pro to the iPhone 18 Pro? Probably not. But if you’ve been considering an upgrade from an older iPhone, then these benefits might be enough to tip the balance.

title: This MagSafe battery pack is designed perfectly for iPhone Duo
snippet: Ahead of iPhone Duo’s launch on Friday, accessory maker BMX is releasing what appears to be one of the first MagSafe batteries designed specifically for Apple’s foldable. The BMX Duo is available to order now and can wirelessly charge your iPhone Duo (or any other iPhone) at up to 15W. You can pick it up on Amazon for $79.99. more…
fullText:
Ahead of iPhone Duo’s launch on Friday, accessory maker BMX is releasing what appears to be one of the first MagSafe batteries designed specifically for Apple’s foldable. 

The BMX Duo is available to order now and can wirelessly charge your iPhone Duo (or any other iPhone) at up to 15W. You can pick it up on Amazon for $79.99.

The iPhone Duo supports MagSafe, but because it’s shorter than a standard iPhone, many existing MagSafe accessories likely won’t fit—or will hang awkwardly off the bottom. The BMX Duo 5000mAh Power Bank is designed to fit exactly on the iPhone Duo: 

A custom-size 5,000mAh cell is shaped to the iPhone Duo’s folded footprint, so it sits flush on the cover panel instead of hanging past the edges. It was built around the Duo, and it snaps onto the iPhone 12 through 18 series just as securely. 

In addition to attaching via MagSafe for 15W wireless charging, it also has a built-in USB-C cable that can charge at up to 20W speeds. 

The BMX Duo also features a built-in ring that rotates a full 360 degrees. The full-color display on the back shows the exact battery percentage and live charging wattage. It uses semi-solid-state cells, which BMX says “use significantly less liquid electrolyte than conventional lithium-ion cells, which helps reduce the risk of battery fires.” 

The BMX Duo 5000mAh Power Bank is available to order today for $79.99. We expect to see a bunch of iPhone Duo accessories roll out to the market soon.

title: YouTube starts hiding the dislike button on normal videos
snippet: After removing dislike counts years ago, new UI tests at YouTube are making it harder to even using the dislike button at all. more…
fullText:
After removing dislike counts years ago, new UI tests at YouTube are making it harder to even using the dislike button at all.

Update 10/22: YouTube has confirmed this is not a public-facing test.

YouTube says it’s not hiding the dislike button – this is what’s actually happening

In 2021, YouTube removed the dislike count as a way to “de-weaponize” the button – effort that had been ongoing for years – with YouTube even acknowledging that it was a decision that users might disagree with. Now, following similar changes to Shorts, YouTube appears to be testing further hiding the dislike button.

A report on Twitter/X highlighted by Neowin showcases YouTube hiding the dislike button under an overflow menu, hiding it from view despite the like button remaining front and center. This appears to be on the desktop website, though we couldn’t replicate the same behavior on our end.

	

It’s not the only case of this happening, though.

	

Over the past couple of weeks, reports on Reddit have seen the dislike button vanish, with another web user seeing a slightly different UI to the one above, but with the same result of offloading the button to an overflow menu alongside the “Report” button. 

YouTube runs tests like this frequently, but given the same change was made to the dislike button on Shorts several months ago, it’s all but certain that the same will happen to standard videos.

What do you think of the change?

title: iOS 27.2 adds new features in six iPhone apps, here’s what’s coming
snippet: iOS 27.2 launches next week with new features for iPhone users, including improvements across six Apple apps. Here’s what’s coming. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 launches next week with new features for iPhone users, including improvements across six Apple apps. Here’s what’s coming.

Messages

One of my favorite additions to Messages this year, Suggested Actions, debuts in iOS 27.2.

Suggested Actions appear underneath messages in a conversation when relevant. They can suggest creating a calendar event or reminder, adding to a note, and more based on the context of the message.

The feature was originally part of the iOS 27 beta this summer, but didn’t make the public build. Now it’s back in iOS 27.2, new and improved. There’s also an option to fine-tune which types of suggestions you’ll see.

Read more: iOS 27.2 adds new Messages feature that’s already a favorite

Apple TV

Every major streaming service has its own profiles feature, letting users on the same account keep their viewing history and recommendations separate. Apple TV has long offered such a feature in tvOS, but now with iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 it’s coming to iPhone and iPad too.

When you launch the TV app in iOS 27.2, you’ll be greeted by a new profile selection screen. You can easily disable it if you don’t want to see if again. But if you ever share your iPhone with kids, the new profiles feature should come in handy.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone

FaceTime

Dual Capture is one of FaceTime’s best new features in years. Added in iOS 27, on compatible iPhones it lets you keep your front and rear cameras both active at the same time while on a FaceTime call.

iOS 27.2 brings a key upgrade to Dual Capture: it’s now available for Group FaceTime calls.

To use the feature, just hit the flip camera button like usual, and by default on iPhone 17 and newer you’ll stream both camera feeds simultaneously.

Read more: iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime’s best new feature even better

Home

Timed with its new Home products push, Apple adds a pair of new Home app features in iOS 27.2 for compatible smart locks.

‘Lock After Closing’ is a new automation setting that lets you choose how long after a door is closed that it should lock automatically. Previously you could only set a duration based on the time since a door was unlocked, not closed.

‘Door Left Open’ tackles a related, but distinct problem: a door being left open too long. With compatible locks, you can configure the Home app to automatically notify you if a door has been left open for a certain period of time.

Read more: iOS 27.2 has three new changes just added this week

Apple Podcasts

Apple Podcasts keeps getting better, with AI-powered automatic chapters and transcripts some of my favorite features. And in iOS 27.2, Apple has a welcome change to the Up Next queue on the Home tab.

Up Next is now being split into two separate queues: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

	

New Episodes contains only the latest episodes from shows you follow, while Continue Playing is a hub for all the episodes you’ve previously started but haven’t yet finished.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple Podcasts the big fix I’ve wanted for years

Games

Apple’s Games app has a couple smaller upgrades for its Home tab in iOS 27.2 as well.

The Home tab now shows you recently downloaded games that you haven’t yet played. Previously, you would only see games with some play activity. And Apple says achievement progress and leaderboard scores have been updated in the Home tab to be easier to track.

snippet: iOS 27.2 is launching soon for all users, but Apple keeps introducing new updates with each beta release. Here are three changes added to iOS 27.2 this week. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 is launching soon for all users, but Apple keeps introducing new updates with each beta release. Here are three changes added to iOS 27.2 this week.

#1: Messages settings for new ‘Suggestions’ feature

The Messages app adds a ‘Suggestions’ feature in iOS 27.2 that was originally meant for iOS 27.0, but was ultimately pulled from the summer beta.

Suggestions let you quickly, conveniently take action on a message you received. For example, by creating a new calendar event or reminder based on the message’s content.

In iOS 27.2 beta 4, Apple added a new option to enable or disable different types of suggestions. Inside Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Messages ⇾ Suggested Actions, you’ll now find toggles for five suggestion types:

Add to Calendar

Add to Reminders

Add to Notes

Show in Maps

Flights and Packages

#2: New Home app features for smart locks

It was a big week for Apple Home announcements. Joining the HomeView, new Apple TV 4K, HomePod mini 2, and Apple Home collection, the iOS 27.2 beta added a pair of Home app features for smart locks.

As discovered by leaker pdfu, ‘Lock After Closing’ is a new setting in the Home app when you have a compatible smart lock. It lets you choose how quickly your door should automatically lock itself after it’s been closed.

Similarly, pdfu found a new ‘Door Left Open’ notification option. It lets you program automatic alerts to notify you if a door was left open. You can choose from ‘Off’ or after 5, 10, 15, or 30 minutes.

#3: Apple Music’s new icon and design updates

Apple Music introduced some unexpected design changes in iOS 27.2 beta 4, including a new app icon, changed accent color, and refreshed widgets.

Essentially, Apple has stripped the iconic red accent color from the Music app’s branding. Now, app icons are a simple black and white, and widgets lose red backgrounds too in favor of black.

Additionally, the Music app’s tab bar now uses a blue accent color for the currently active tab—it was previously red.

So far reception online to these changes seems overwhelmingly negative. It will be interesting to see if Apple reverts any of these design updates moving forward. Though they clearly appear part of a broader rebranding effort for Apple Music.

title: New App Store chief discusses Apple’s gaming strategy, future of Apple Arcade, more
snippet: In an interview with Polygon, Apple’s new head of App Store Worldwide, Carson Oliver, discussed the company’s broader gaming ambitions, the growing number of premium iPhone games, and where Apple Arcade fits into its strategy. Here’s what he said. more…
fullText:
In an interview with Polygon, Apple’s new head of App Store Worldwide, Carson Oliver, discussed the company’s broader gaming ambitions, the growing number of premium iPhone games, and where Apple Arcade fits into its strategy. Here’s what he said.

New App Store chief talks App Store gaming

Apple’s ambitions to be seen as a proper gaming platform owner aren’t exactly new. Over the years, the company has repeatedly attempted to attract major game developers and convince players to take gaming on its devices more seriously, with varying degrees of success.

And those efforts show. As Apple has repeatedly highlighted during WWDC keynotes and product announcements, the company has introduced hardware-accelerated ray tracing, made significant improvements to its Metal graphics framework, and developed tools that make it easier to port PC and console games to its platforms.

Early last week, shortly after Carson Oliver’s promotion to vice president of the App Store was reported, Apple announced Indie Games Week, highlighting seven new and upcoming games for iPhone and iPad, including:

Sifu

Vampire Crawlers

No Man’s Sky

Little Kitty, Big City

9 Kings

Dome Keeper

Yes, Your Grace 2: Snowfall

In light of that, Polygon conducted an email interview with Oliver, who shared some interesting details about the state of gaming on the App Store and Apple’s plans for the future.

Oliver told Polygon:

“We’ve seen incredible growth of games coming to the App Store, in general, with more premium games releasing on the App Store this year than last. […] While many of those are indies, we’re also seeing more console and PC franchises coming to mobile, as it is a burgeoning audience for those games. These seven games featured in Indie Games Week capture where gaming on iPhone and iPad is heading: incredible diversity and creativity with no compromises on quality.”

Oliver also touched on the technical improvements Apple has made over the years, some of which we mentioned above, as well as the role that younger generations of players have had in shaping the mobile gaming market.

According to Oliver, “an entire generation of players” grew up with an iPhone as their first gaming device, rather than a traditional console or PC.

He added:

“These users embrace direct touch as their primary controller, making iPhone and iPad the ultimate canvas for indie innovation.”

As for Apple Arcade, and how it fits into Apple’s broader gaming strategy alongside the growing number of premium games launching directly on the App Store, Oliver told Polygon it comes down to giving game developers more flexibility:

“We want to give developers a trusted place to reach users around the world, support them at each stage, and help them build successful businesses. […] To achieve that goal, we provide developers with flexible business model options. That means a breakthrough phenomenon like Balatro can thrive as a premium download, and it can also find a home as part of the Apple Arcade service. The important thing is that we give developers the flexibility to make the best choice for every game and players the freedom to play how they want.”

title: I’ve struggled to use Samsung displays for years, but the Galaxy S27 may finally fix that; here’s why
snippet: The Samsung Galaxy S27 display may be getting a DC-dimming upgrade, and that will be a huge boon for people sensitive to PWM dimming. more…
fullText:
The Samsung Galaxy S27 display may be getting a DC-dimming upgrade, and that will be a huge boon for people sensitive to PWM dimming.

Ever since the Galaxy Z Fold 4, I’ve had difficulty using Samsung phones for long periods of time. The problem, for me, is the company’s use of low-frequency PWM dimming, which causes me horrid headaches, followed by eye pain, and eventually nausea. It’s not fun, and I’ve learned through resources like r/PWM_Sensitive and LEDStrain.org that I’m not alone.

Thankfully, Samsung’s Galaxy S27‘s display may give users the option to use DC dimming, according to one rumor (via GSMArena). Motorola has offered DC dimming as an option on all its OLED-equipped phones for years, and it’ll be great to see Samsung do the same. DC dimming is a more traditional dimming method used by lightbulbs and displays since the dawn of each technology, and is often considered more comfortable than PWM dimming by advocacy groups.

Sure enough, as I learned more about PWM dimming in my personal struggle over the years, phones that use DC dimming are often the most comfortable for me. The only other alternative is to use much higher frequency PWM dimming; 2,000Hz or higher, while the $1,300 Galaxy S26 Ultra only uses 480Hz.

	

Samsung has long prioritized PWM dimming on its displays for several reasons. First, PWM dimming offers better display quality in low-light situations, as DC-dimmed OLEDs can sometimes exhibit “mura” at low brightness levels, which means individual pixels don’t dim at the same rate. This creates what’s referred to as a “noisy” display, and often looks a bit like old film cameras (see the image below for an example).

Second, is efficiency. While it hasn’t been proven to have a drastic effect, PWM dimming can be loosely linked to better battery life. This has become a bigger deal in recent years as Samsung has lagged behind other companies in battery technology, but will be less of a sticking point as the company finally adopts silicon-carbon batteries more widely.

Third, is cost. DC dimming traditionally requires extra hardware to regulate voltage, while PWM dimming is (typically) done entirely via software. Extra hardware means a phone costs more to manufacture, even if it’s just a small amount per unit.

But people who are sensitive to PWM dimming typically cannot use Samsung phones at all, so none of these “positive” points matter to them. Companies like Apple and Google have begun making changes to cater toward PWM-sensitive individuals, but neither have adopted full DC dimming as this Galaxy S27 display rumor suggests Samsung might do.

If the Galaxy S27 display doesn’t adopt DC dimming next year, that will make the Motorola Signature 27 the only flagship in the US to support the technology. OnePlus used to offer DC dimming on its flagship phones in the US, but the company no longer sells its phones outside of China.

title: Airbnb limits chores for guests, sparking backlash from hosts
snippet: Hosts are threatening to leave the platform after Airbnb says that they can no longer require guests to strip beds or do other time-consuming cleaning chores.
fullText:
Airbnb is taking steps to limit the chores that hosts can require of guests prior to checkout, addressing a long-standing grievance among customers who often pay cleaning fees and are told they must do a list of tasks themselves.

In a new policy update, Airbnb prohibits hosts from mandating that guests strip beds, wash and put away dishes, start laundry, or remove trash from the property. This new guideline will apply to reservations made on or after November 20.

This change comes in response to years of backlash regarding overly burdensome checkout instructions and hefty fines for not disposing of trash. Many guests have voiced their frustrations on social media, questioning why they should be responsible for cleaning tasks after already paying a cleaning fee.

However, some hosts aren’t pleased with the update. Within Airbnb’s community forums, some argue that basic cleaning responsibilities are essential for maintaining sanitary conditions and protecting their properties. They point out that hosts must manage the costs and practical demands of preparing their properties for the next guests.

One host expressed concern that the new policy leans toward a hotel-like model, which detracts from the unique appeal of Airbnb.

“Guests are given complete freedom to be lazy while the hosts bear the risk,” the host wrote. “The major distinction between commercial hotels and my private home is the personal touch. Guests can certainly be expected to wash their dishes or put them in the dishwasher and remove their dirty linens. In exchange, they enjoy a personal connection and a unique environment that a hotel simply can’t provide. Plus, every potential guest has the opportunity to read the listing beforehand and decide what they prefer. If these restrictions are removed, it could lead me to withdraw my listing and bid farewell to Airbnb after twelve years.”

Airbnb has outlined some exceptions to the new policy, though. Hosts may still ask guests to conserve water during droughts or use bear-proof trash containers in areas where wildlife poses a risk.

The policy change highlights the challenge Airbnb faces in balancing the expectations of guests versus hosts and is another step taken in addressing guests’ concerns. The company faced scrutiny in 2024 over price transparency from hosts tacking on cleaning fees after guests booked their listings. In 2023, the company said more than 260,000 hosts had reduced or eliminated their cleaning fees. In May 2025, Airbnb began displaying total prices — including fees but excluding taxes — by default in search results worldwide.

It will be interesting to see how many hosts decide the new restrictions make Airbnb less attractive as a platform. But the move could also draw in more travelers who want the convenience of a rental without feeling as though they are both paying for housecleaning while still expected to clean the home themselves.

title: PSA: Apple’s official silicone iPhone Duo case will require adhesive to stick
snippet: iPhone Duo is just about a week away from launching, and now that preorders have opened, Apple’s official iPhone Duo accessories have started to hit stores for early purchases. After purchasing, some users have noticed that the silicone case has a little bit of a caveat. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo is just about a week away from launching, and now that preorders have opened, Apple’s official iPhone Duo accessories have started to hit stores for early purchases. After purchasing, some users have noticed that the silicone case has a little bit of a caveat.

Apple designed two cases for iPhone Duo: a $79 silicone case, and a $129 folio case. This concern is about the former.

With the silicone case for iPhone Duo, you’ll actually need to expose adhesive on the case for it to stick to your iPhone. Apple decided to opt for adhesives rather than using magnets. Presumably, the case would fall off if you don’t use the adhesive. This isn’t a new concept for foldable cases.

The unfortunate thing about this is that you likely can’t swap cases or go caseless as easily, and even if you do, the adhesive wouldn’t be as effective after you take it off.

	

This isn’t a super major deal, but something to keep in mind if you’re going to purchase Apple’s official silicone case for iPhone Duo. On the other hand, Apple’s folio with kickstand does seem to be rather nice, though it does carry a premium price tag.

If you aren’t interested in Apple’s official cases, some good options include Spigen’s Ultra Hybrid Pro and ESR’s Classic Hybrid with kickstand.

fullText:
Emma Roth

 

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Apple is rolling out a new badge in the App Store to indicate whether an app is optimized for its new foldable. The new “Made for iPhone Duo” badge will appear across apps and games that work with the device’s extra screen real estate.

Though Apple doesn’t include an image of what this badge might look like, it highlighted some of the ways apps are taking advantage of the Duo’s inner and outer screens. Netflix, for example, will display shows and movies that take up the whole inner display, while allowing you to watch its feed of short-form clips on the outside. Amazon’s Prime Video will let you watch shows and movies with the Duo partially folded, with the content on top and details about the cast on the bottom.

Meanwhile, Apple says Microsoft Word and Outlook will offer a “desktop-class” experience on the Duo, with Word placing its formatting tools alongside a document, and Outlook displaying your inbox next to a full email. Zoom can also display a video conference alongside shared content across the iPhone Duo’s inner screen. Other apps optimized for the Duo include Paramount Plus, NYT Cooking, Yelp, Lyft, and United Airlines. But, as The Verge’s Nilay Patel found during his Duo testing, some apps “optimized” for the device, like Instagram, still have some bugs.

Apple says it’s going to launch editorial collections for the iPhone Duo on Friday, “with additional app updates rolling out throughout the year.” The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 and launches on Friday, with “limited” quantities available on a walk-in basis.

title: Test Driving an iPhone Duo? 6 Things to Try at the Apple Store
snippet: Apple’s first foldable has a lot going for it, but there may be some compromises you aren’t expecting. See for yourself if the Duo is for you.
fullText:
If you weren’t able to preorder an iPhone Duo last week, you’re out of luck until January — but come Friday, you’ll finally be able to walk into an Apple Store and try out the new foldable phone. It’s possibly the most exciting product the company has released in a long time. Whether you want to try it before you buy or are just curious about how it works and feels in your hands, the wait is almost over.

But what should you be looking to do when you actually pick up the iPhone Duo? While the foldable phone might have a fun, unique design, you may run into things you’re unfamiliar with — or even dislike — when using it day to day. You’ll want to be confident that the device is a good fit for your needs before plunking down $2,000 or more for the folding phone.

We’re going to break down a series of things you should check out when you finally get to play with it at the Apple Store.

			

More from CNET

The opening animation

The iPhone Duo’s unfolding animation is neat.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

When the Duo was first revealed, Apple showed off a very intriguing animation when you unfold the it. Leave it to Apple to make a function so simple look so aesthetically pleasing. 

It’ll likely be the first thing you notice when you first open the Duo up to see its inner display, and there’s a good chance you’ll continue to open and close the device to see the effect. At the end of the day, it’s a parlor trick — but a very good one, adding delight to ordinary use. 

Admire the matte screen and minimal crease

Foldables, well, fold, and they typically come with creases. The Duo has a minimal crease and a matte display, both of which are wins. That said, even the most noticeable creases tend to “disappear” when you’re viewing content — you just get used to them while watching TV shows or YouTube videos. The Duo’s minimal crease should be even easier to ignore.

And let’s not forget about the matte screen. Several foldables ship with glossy displays, but the iPhone Duo will have a less shiny screen, making it easier to view in bright environments without annoying reflections.

Apple demonstrated how Netflix will be optimized for the Duo’s displays — from the cover screen to the main display to this half-open configuration with controls on the bottom half. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Watch videos

The outer passport-size display on the iPhone Duo may be a little awkward for watching videos because of how it crops content to fit the new aspect ratio. Still, it’s handy to prop the phone up in tent mode and watch shows that way. You also have a large inner display to work with, but because of its passport-style design, even that screen has a different aspect ratio than the widescreen format people are used to on regular phones, so there will likely be some letterboxing in videos.

Try watching something with the phone set up in both ways to see if it bothers you enough to dissuade you from buying the phone.

Again, it’s not an iPhone Duo issue but a foldable phone issue — the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the same size and format. The aspect ratio of the display might crop the top or sides of videos, so it’s worth trying out if you expect to watch a lot of full-screen videos. 

The Duo supports drag-and-drop functionality when multitasking.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

See how apps act in different orientations

Like videos, apps on foldables can sometimes appear a little weird, and that could be the case with the iPhone Duo‘s aspect ratio. When you’re at the Apple Store, check out how your most-used apps look and feel on both the inner and outer displays, and make sure you rotate the inner screen to see how apps behave in this orientation, too — that wide screen could be great for watching vertical videos or scrolling through social media. 

If some apps, such as Instagram, look a little different or are wonky, it’ll hopefully be just a matter of time until the developers make an update that optimizes the experience for this new design. Keep in mind that you can also have two apps open onscreen at once, making it easier to multitask.

Explore the cameras

The iPhone Duo has two 48-megapixel rear cameras.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

If you want the best camera experience on an iPhone right now, you should be looking at the iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max, but that doesn’t make the Duo a slouch for shooting photos, either. 

Yes, the Duo is missing a third camera (telephoto), and if that’s important to you, then you probably shouldn’t even be considering Apple’s foldable. But still, if you’re going to shell out this much money for a new phone, test out those cameras — even if it’s in a controlled environment like an Apple Store.

Another thing to check out before you pull the trigger is your selfie shots with this new phone. There are two main ways to do this: with the phone closed, holding it up in the regular way you’d take a selfie using the outer screen’s 12-megapixel front-facing camera, or with the inner display open and shooting with the twin 48-megapixel rear cameras (the outer screen will show a preview of the shot).

There’s also a front-facing camera underneath the inner display, which is mostly for video calls — and which we suspect would produce the least-impressive shots from the device. Try them all and see what you think of the pics. And since you’re at an Apple Store, make sure you delete them afterward.

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Try typing on both displays

The odd but interesting aspect ratio of the front display on the iPhone Duo may be a little awkward for typing, so it’s best to do a typing test when you have one in front of you. While the inner display will provide a roomier and more comfortable typing experience, you probably won’t want to have to open up the Duo every time you want to shoot off a quick text to someone. If you have bigger hands, typing on the front screen could be a bit of a nightmare. 

Typing one-handed on the small cover screen should be manageable, but try it out to see if it works for you. Some may find it convenient; others may find it cumbersome.

And when you’re typing on the inner display, try the Duo in both portrait and landscape orientations to see which feels better. You can also choose between a split keyboard and larger keys. It’s thoughtful of Apple to offer options that let you tailor the typing experience to your preferences, but you may find that none of them suit your style.

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

When installing macOS 27 (Golden Gate), Rosetta is automatically removed. If you manage a fleet with any legacy Intel-only software still in use, you need a plan in place before your users start experiencing issues. Here is what I’m doing, and I have some thoughts on vendors who are waiting until the last minute to deploy Apple Silicon-native tools.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

The silent failure problem

One thing I need to clarify is that macOS 27 removes it, but macOS 28 will no longer support it. For traditional apps, macOS 27 will prompt the user to reinstall it with an easy-to-follow GUI prompt. That’s actually the workable scenario, because at least the user knows something is wrong, and macOS reinstalls it. The tools I’m worried about are the ones that won’t do that. I have a handful of menu bar utilities from vendors who haven’t shipped a native Apple Silicon build yet, and in my testing this summer, they are just silently failing. There’s no error prompt. It just fails to work. That makes auditing your fleet before macOS 27 rolls out more important than it might seem at first glance.

What I’m doing in my device management system

My short-term fix is to automatically push a Rosetta reinstallation script to every Mac that joins my macOS 27 Dynamic Device Group. In Mosyle, the setup is really straightforward. You create a new script profile, name it something obvious like “Rosetta Install macOS 27,” and enter the following command in the script tab:

softwareupdate --install-rosetta --agree-to-license

Under Execution Settings, pick your preferred trigger, then assign the profile to your macOS 27 Dynamic Device Group and save. When a device appears in that group, Mosyle automatically pushes the script, and Rosetta (hopefully) gets installed before the user ever runs into a problem. It’s not a permanent fix, but it buys time while I work on the real solution: getting vendors to ship native builds.

On the vendors

I want to be direct about this. Apple Silicon shipped in late 2020. We are now in late 2026. Any vendor still telling customers that a native Apple Silicon build is “on the roadmap” before Rosetta stops working in macOS 28 has had five-plus years to solve this problem and has chosen not to. That is not a resource issue or a technical challenge at this point. It is a prioritization choice, and one that falls squarely on the IT teams managing their software. Even if these vendors ship Apple Silicon-native versions before macOS 28, the shipping delay makes me question their commitment to macOS.

Wrap up

If you haven’t audited your fleet for Rosetta-dependent software yet, do it now while there’s still time to either push a script workaround or have the harder vendor conversations before users start running into problems. Most enterprise fleets are likely doing a 90 day block on Golden Gate for final testing/QA, so now is the time to work on your final plan. The script fix in Mosyle takes about five minutes to set up. Vendor conversations will take longer, and migrating to new solutions will take a bit longer.

title: iPhone Duo reviews: The absolute best foldable phone, but not without compromise
snippet: We posted our own review of the iPhone Duo yesterday, and Chance Miller was left convinced that “this form factor represents the future of the iPhone,” while acknowledging that the first-gen iPhone Duo comes with trade-offs. I think what surprised me most is the degree of consensus found across the reviews, given the generally polarized appeal of foldable phones. That’s not to say reviewers think everyone should buy one, but there is widespread agreement on the pros and cons – starting with five key takeouts … more…
fullText:
We posted our own review of the iPhone Duo yesterday, and Chance Miller was left convinced that “this form factor represents the future of the iPhone,” while acknowledging that the first-gen iPhone Duo comes with trade-offs.

I think what surprised me most is the degree of consensus found across the reviews, given the generally polarized appeal of foldable phones. That’s not to say reviewers think everyone should buy one, but there is widespread agreement on the pros and cons – starting with five key takeouts …

Five key takeouts

First, all the reviews I’ve read and watched say that the iPhone Duo is hands-down the best foldable phone on the market. Apple waited a very long time before joining the foldable party, and it seems clear that it was absolutely right to do so.

Second, this phone is absolutely not for everyone. Even leaving aside the high purchase cost, the form factor currently involves compromises that would rule it out for some.  If you expect to use the outer screen most of the time and only unfold it a few times a day, then the trade-offs of the heavy weight when held in one hand and the unusual display shape are just too big a drawback. This phone really only makes sense if you expect to make frequent use of the larger unfolded screen in your day-to-day use.

Third, Apple hasn’t made the crease invisible, and indeed has made no claims to do so. You can see it in certain lights at certain angles, and you can feel it when running your finger across the screen. But everyone agrees that this is the least intrusive crease ever seen on a foldable, and that it’s simply not an issue in real life use. More on this in a moment.

Fourth, a great many apps haven’t yet been updated, and in the worst case that means seeing an iPhone screen layout stranded in the middle of a mostly black inner display. The optimistic view is that this will rapidly change, but be prepared for some disappointments with third-party apps in early usage.

Finally, going back to Touch ID is a significant compromise after being used to Face ID. We do have to bear in mind that reviewers have only had a chance to use the device for a week, but certainly in that time most say they didn’t really get used to it and would absolutely prefer Face ID.

Fold testing

A couple of reviewers used machines to subject the iPhone Duo to thousands of folds and unfolds to test two things. Does the crease become significantly more visible over time, and how does the hinge hold up? 

In both cases, there is a measurable impact. Joanna Stern’s tests found that the hinge is affected across tens of thousands of folds, but interestingly becomes stiffer rather than looser – the opposite of what we would expect. However, while this change was measurable using a strain gauge after 32,000 folds, she said she couldn’t feel it in normal use.

HTX Studio did the most scientific testing of the impact of thousands of folds on the crease. The depth of the crease when new was measured at just 48 microns, about half the thickness of a sheet of paper, while the slope of the crease measured at less than 0.1 degrees – both markedly better than competing foldables. After 3,000 folds, the depth of the crease increased to 167 microns and the slope increased to 1.24 degrees. That brings it more in line with the measurements of other foldables after the same number of tests.

The bottom line

There are links to the full reviews, but here is the bottom line from each …

Joanna Stern:

After 20 years of iPhones that look mostly the same, it’s exciting to see Apple chart a new course. But the Duo is still one of the most early adopter Apple products I’ve tested in a long time. It’s easy to imagine what Gen 2 will look like. It’s lighter, there’s Face ID, a better camera inside, and hopefully a lower price. Also, it’s got a telephoto camera, and it’s no longer a hand warmer. 

The good news is most of my other frustrations can be fixed with software updates and developers figuring out how to make great apps for two very different screen sizes. Sure, early adopters have to navigate some choppy waters, but as Apple developers catch up, I can see smoother sailing ahead.

HTX Studio:

Apple’s first attempt [at a foldable] brings plenty of fresh ideas with real purpose behind them that deserves credit. But think about it: these ideas mostly fix flaws built into the folding design rather than pushing the phone experience forward. 

[Will this make foldables mainstream?] I still doubt it because this design has two fundamental conflicts at its core. First, the [aspect ratios] of two screens work against each other. Improve the outer screen and the inner screen becomes a big empty square. Favor the inner screen [as Apple has done] and the outer screen becomes a passport that’s hard to grip. It’s a zero-sum game. More importantly, whatever the balance, you get a makeshift phone outside and a cut down tablet inside. Neither delivers the best

experience.

Second, the benefits are occasional, but the cost are constant. To fit a hinge and the big screen, it sacrifices weight, battery life, cooling, performance, cameras, and most importantly, price. But use one or watch other people do and you’ll see they mostly use the outer screen […] You enjoy the benefits some of the time but pay the price all the time.

Daring Fireball:

If you really want to do something, or sit back and read or watch something, the big display is fantastic. But that Duo-as-tablet experience is so cumbersome compared to the “just look at it” experience of using a regular iPhone uno that you simply cannot do it every time you use the Duo. You will use the outer display quite a bit. And using the outer display delivers the worst iPhone experience ever. I mean, some iPhone has to be the one that offered the worst iPhone experience ever. That iPhone is the outer half of the iPhone Duo […]

If you’d rather trade your iPhone for an iPad Mini that you can fold in half to carry around, the iPhone Duo might be the form factor for you. Even if that’s the case, though, this first iPhone Duo might not suit you, for all the various irritations and shortcomings I’ve documented […] It’s been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I’ve gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype — not a finished product that I’d want to buy and carry.

CNET:

Aside from some minor shortcomings, Apple appears to have stuck the landing with its long-awaited foldable. Hopefully, future iterations will add elements such as Face ID while improving the camera capabilities, either by adding a telephoto lens or bolstering the inner screen’s FaceTime camera. It would be nice to see multitasking become more dynamic in the future, too.

[But] most people just don’t need a phone that doubles as a tablet. [While the Duo] is a foldable experience that feels cohesive, intuitive and genuinely useful, which could help win over more people to foldables in general, I think that broader appeal is still a ways off.

Gizmodo:

Whether you’re an iPhone fan, foldable evangelist, or Android user who’s just been waiting to see what Apple offers, I think we can all agree that the iPhone Duo has already achieved what competing foldables have not been able to in seven years: generate considerable buzz for foldable phones […] This is what we’ve been waiting for after more than a decade of matured bar-style phones. Finally, phone hardware and software are genuinely exciting again, which is something to celebrate […]

As for whether you should get the iPhone Duo—that depends on if you can afford it, either buying it outright, paying in installments, or leasing it through the Apple Upgrade program. Do you want a foldable phone, and why? Will you use the larger screen often, and how much value will you get from it? Will the weight bother you? Do you need better cameras? There are so many personal factors to consider before you decide. The iPhone Duo isn’t the “definitive” iPhone to own. Apple’s iPhone lineup now caters to every budget and every type of user. Only you can be honest with yourself about your needs.

Tom’s Guide:

The iPhone Duo is the best designed foldable phone I’ve ever tested, with a sturdy and premium build and a nano-texture display that hides the crease. I also like the multiple usage modes and split-screen multitasking. However, while fully updated apps for the Duo look great, non-optimized apps do not. And the lack of a telephoto zoom is a bummer for a $2,000 phone […]

I like the iPhone Duo’s nano texture display in that it greatly reduces glare outdoors and minimizes the crease better than any foldable I’ve tested. But you give up perfect blacks with this matte panel and more saturated colors versus the iPhone 18 Pro Max. You also sacrifice a telephoto lens and Face ID. I can live with those trade-offs, but that doesn’t mean I like them.

In a way it’s a good thing that the iPhone Duo is backordered for many until December or January. That will give developers plenty of time to update their offerings for this foldable. I don’t think it will take that long, though, based on the high demand.

Overall, though, I think the iPhone Duo is the best designed foldable yet with the most polished, intuitive and fun software experience.

Wired:

This is often the case with first-generation products, but it may be prudent to wait for the Duo 2—not because there are glaring issues but because I suspect Apple may tackle the weight problem with the next version, just as Samsung did on its latest iteration.

Folding phones will never be for everyone. Some people do not care for the bigger screen. Others have durability concerns, and a device with more moving parts will never be as repairable or robust as its single-slab counterpart. Price is a barrier for others—but, on that note, the Duo is surprisingly on par with its competitors (though still expensive).

But the folding category is here to stay. I know people who swear by the fold and won’t buy anything else. I’m starting to convert, especially with the newer passport-style shape. Now if only someone could figure out how to put a real zoom camera on there.

The Verge:

There’s a lot of potential in the Duo, but right now it is a first-gen device in every possible way. It is expensive, it’s full of compromises, and it can be incredibly frustrating to use. Switching from the Duo back to one of our standard slab phones to get something done often felt like a relief […] But all of the risk and weirdness of the Duo is also fun, in the way the best early adopter devices are fun. It’s incomplete as a product, but complete enough as an idea that you can see where things are going […]

We’ll see what happens with the Duo, but as it stands, it is very much an open question whether Apple made the right choices about the Duo’s screen sizes and aspect ratios. Most Duo owners will find that the cover display is simply too small to use all the time […] Apple also made some very real compromises around the camera […]

But the Duo is a more cohesive idea about foldables than most of its Android competition, precisely because Apple has a better app and developer story to lean on. Right now the problem for most Android foldables is that the inner screens aren’t that useful so there’s no super compelling reason to open them. The problem with the Duo is that the outer screen isn’t useful enough, so you want to open it all the time […] The real answer is somewhere in the middle — for both screens to be interesting and useful. Someone’s going to get there, and we’ll see if Apple can be the first.

title: Apple Limits iPhone Duo Purchases to 2 Foldable Phones Per Person
snippet: For the first time in many years, Apple is limiting how many phones you can buy.
fullText:
If you were hoping to score multiple iPhone Duo devices from Apple when the new foldable becomes available on Friday, we have some bad news for you: The tech giant is limiting sales of the phone to two per person.

In keeping with the limitation reported earlier this week by MacRumors, when we attempted to add more than two to our bag on the Apple Store, we got the following message: “A maximum of 2 iPhone Duo can be purchased per customer. Please adjust the total quantity of iPhone Duo in your order before checking out.”

Screenshot by Corinne Reichert/CNET

The limit of two foldables per purchase will presumably also apply to those shopping in-store when the phone finally launches on Friday. 

			

More from CNET

While preorders are backed up until the end of January — our estimated delivery when adding two to our bag is Jan. 25, as of the time of publication — Apple will have limited stock of the iPhone Duo in stores, though you may have to wait in line overnight to be one of the few people able to get their hands on one (or two).

While companies may limit the number of devices in each order, especially for stock-scarce products like game consoles, it’s been a while since Apple has restricted how many phones people can buy at once. Nearly two decades ago, the company launched the original iPhone to great fanfare in June 2007, but limited buyers to two per order (later easing it to five by the holidays). The restriction returned in 2012, when Apple limited orders to two iPhone 5 preorders per customer.

If you do want to buy more than one iPhone Duo, we found that we could add multiple to our carts while shopping at Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile and Best Buy, though all of those purchases require you to sign up for a line of service with a carrier. Preorders are likewise back-ordered until the end of January, however.

The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first foldable phone, entering the mobile niche that Samsung and Motorola have been fighting over since 2020, with Google entering the fray with the first Pixel Fold in 2023. Chinese phonemakers like Huawei and Xiaomi have also released their own foldables, though none have been sold widely in the US.

Despite refined devices like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Motorola Razr Ultra 2026 and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold releasing earlier this year, analysts predict that Apple’s new device will carve out a significant chunk of the market: The International Data Corporation expects the Duo to amount to 31% of the foldable phones market by the end of the year, growing to 40% in 2027. 

Customer preorders seem to have followed those predictions, though we’ll have to wait and see whether that appetite continues throughout the holidays and into the new year. Early reviews have been positive, with CNET Senior Reporter Abrar Al-Heeti noting that despite some downsides attributable to a first-generation device, the Apple foldable’s finer details make the experience feel fluid and cohesive. 

“Personally, I have no plans of switching back to a slab phone anytime soon,” Al-Heeti said in her review. 

Correction, Oct. 22 at 8:24 a.m. ET: This story initially gave an incorrect month for the original iPhone’s launch. That iPhone first went on sale in June 2007.

title: EA Shutters BioWare, Creator of Mass Effect, Dragon Age, KOTOR and More
snippet: The legendary studio has been shut down just months after EA was acquired by a private equity consortium.
fullText:
Video game publisher Electronic Arts is closing the venerable studio BioWare, maker of legendary series like Mass Effect and Dragon Age, it announced on Wednesday. 

Recent years have seen record layoffs across the gaming industry as companies scaled back expansion during the COVID-19 pandemic, disrupting tens of thousands of careers and closing many studios. The shuttering of BioWare is a symbolic and substantial blow, presumably ending multiple fervently adored game series and carrying implications for the industry at large. The closure reportedly involves around 400 layoffs, about 50 of which were at BioWare, according to Bloomberg. 

EA confirmed in a blog post Wednesday that the closure of BioWare accompanies the choice to stop development on the next game in the Mass Effect series, which BioWare first teased on Nov. 7, 2020 — otherwise known as N7 Day to fans, an in-universe reference that has become an annual day to share appreciation for the sci-fi roleplaying series. 

			

More from CNET

It hasn’t been lost on fans that the shuttering of the 31-year-old studio comes just weeks before N7 Day, and social media has been awash with mourning for the many franchises that came out of BioWare.

The studio made a name for itself with Baldur’s Gate in 1998, its sequel Baldur’s Gate 2 and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic before branching into original game series with Jade Empire in 2005, the first Mass Effect in 2007 and Dragon Age: Origins in 2009.

BioWare found its niche in roleplaying games with well-written narratives and deeply detailed characters. The studio was lauded for developing rich arcs for “companion” characters with varied sexualities, some of whom the player could romance. Its queer representation earned the studio a devoted fanbase.

It’s worth noting that BioWare was shuttered shortly after EA closed a deal in August to be acquired by a business consortium that includes Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund. Saudi Arabia has criminalized homosexuality and transgender expression, imprisoning people and reportedly sentencing them to punishments including fines, flogging and death. The oil-rich country has also invested heavily in real-world sports, including boxing, golf and soccer, and EA’s blog post mentions “deepening” its core of sports games, which include the annual EA Sports FC and Madden NFL games.

“We believe we can use our experience building interactive entertainment, together with our relationships in sports, to create entirely new ways for fans to engage with the teams, athletes and sports they love,” the company said. “These will be disciplined investments that only scale when they demonstrate real potential.”

The business consortium that acquired EA for $55 billion also included the equity company Silver Lake and investment firm Affinity Partners, which is headed by Jared Kushner, son-in-law of President Donald Trump.

BioWare’s rocky recent years amid a changing industry

After a lengthy development, Dragon Age: The Veilguard launched in 2024 to favorable reviews, but its sales were far below expectations.EA

As the news went out, BioWare fans took to social media to remember the studio’s formative games, but few of its recent ones. 

Backlash over the controversial ending of 2012’s Mass Effect 3 led the studio to develop a new trajectory for the series with Mass Effect: Andromeda in 2017, which got a lukewarm reception from fans. While Dragon Age: Inquisition was a hit in 2014, its sequel was reportedly mired in development difficulties and was reworked into the 2024 title Dragon Age: The Veilguard, which met with favorable reviews but a poor reception from fans, and fell short of EA’s sales expectations, IGN reported. Between those, the studio’s attempt at an action-adventure live-service game, 2019’s Anthem, launched in a flawed state, and its road to recovery of updates was cut short in 2021 when the studio stopped development. 

BioWare’s last decade saw departures of people who had headlined the games that fans grew up playing, and the more recent missteps led to a cooling of the studio’s beloved reputation. But plenty of things changed in the larger games industry over that span, too, with development time extending from a few years to five or even longer, increasing the costs of making every game. That puts more pressure on new games to be big hits, selling millions of copies to float ever-longer development cycles. When they don’t, it has increasingly led to studio closures.

EA’s blog post announcing the BioWare departure reflects this new era of gaming, and perhaps changing tastes. It’s no surprise to hear the publisher is refocusing on “core areas” and thinning out existing teams, as any business does during an industry contraction. These seem to be shooters like Battlefield 6, action-adventure games like the upcoming Marvel’s Iron Man and the next Star Wars Jedi game (presumably referring to Respawn’s sequel to Jedi Survivor), EA’s sports franchises, The Sims and its skateboarding series, Skate. BioWare’s closure is nestled between those updates, and notably absent is any mention of other RPGs.

But amid recent years of gaming layoffs and shuttered studios, it’s hard to see BioWare’s closure as anything but a swan song for an era of gaming long passed on a new road paved by more laid-off developers and headed toward uncertainty. It’s not as much of a surprise, as analysts confided their worries about the future of EA-owned franchises to Polygon when the business consortium first announced its intent to acquire in September 2025.

There’s a dim hope that private ownership will liberate EA from shareholder pressure to try new risky gaming ideas, but the loss of BioWare is deeply felt among gamers who grew up playing risks that paid off for a time — and ensconced stories and characters in their hearts.

title: Samsung says the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is more popular than ever thanks to iPhone Duo
snippet: Apple’s debut in the foldable market was always going to have an impact on Android foldables, with many brands having been optimistic that it would have a positive ripple effect. For Samsung, that appears to be true, as the company says that interest in its Galaxy Z Fold 8 remains significantly higher following the iPhone Duo’s announcement. more…
fullText:
Apple’s debut in the foldable market was always going to have an impact on Android foldables, with many brands having been optimistic that it would have a positive ripple effect. For Samsung, that appears to be true, as the company says that interest in its Galaxy Z Fold 8 remains significantly higher following the iPhone Duo’s announcement.

Speaking to Forbes, Samsung’s UK VP over mobile said that demand for Galaxy Z Fold 8 has risen following the debut of iPhone Duo, with search interest even higher — apparently up by 300%.

Samsung’s foldable momentum is undeniable… Customer demand for the Galaxy Z Fold8 family has increased 16% since launch, and with a 300% increase in active Google searches for Samsung foldables in the last month alone, our market leadership is stronger than ever.

It’s not hard to imagine why this might be the case.

Apple’s massive and loyal fanbase means that the launch of iPhone Duo put foldables under the spotlight for effectively the first time for a lot of potential buyers, so it only makes sense that at least a portion of those users are curious to see what else is out there. Samsung’s lower prices and more refined design might also have a few folks interested enough to give the alternative a shot.

	

Galaxy Z Fold 8 is currently available for $1,699 on Amazon, $300 less than iPhone Duo, while Samsung.com is offering the Fold 8 for even less than that, with a special discount on the 1TB trim that offers the device for just $50 more than Apple’s base 256GB model.

title: Apple’s ‘Designers of Tomorrow’ highlights creative projects from emerging designers
snippet: Apple, in collaboration with Design Miami, is highlighting four creative projects from emerging designers in this year’s ‘Designers of Tomorrow’ exhibition, which opens today at Hôtel de Maisons in Paris. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple, in collaboration with Design Miami, is highlighting four creative projects from emerging designers in this year’s ‘Designers of Tomorrow’ exhibition, which opens today at Hôtel de Maisons in Paris. Here are the details.

Apple showcases 2026 Designers of Tomorrow

Apple today published an interesting press release highlighting the work of five designers, who “integrated Apple products into their creative processes” to develop their projects.

Now in its second year, Apple’s “Designers of Tomorrow” initiative is organized in partnership with Design Miami. As Apple explains, this year’s participants were selected by a jury that included the company’s vice president of industrial design, Molly Anderson.

Here’s Apple on this year’s theme and the designers’ approach to it:

“Apple’s Designers of Tomorrow showcase, in collaboration with Design Miami, returns for a second year to spotlight the best in emerging talent, this time focusing on the theme of presence. Exploring what still holds the public’s attention amid the hurried pace of the modern world, designers Salem S. Charabi, Isabel Rower, Yoonjeong Lee, and Parafernalia (Genki Matsumura and Sebastián Zorrilla) crafted original works that invite reflection and aim to shift perspectives, engage the senses, and kindle curiosity.”

According to Rodman Primack, the program’s curator, the artists’ works “demonstrate the power of objects to shape our physical environments and transform the human experiences that are possible within them.”

Throughout the press release, Apple details how the selected designers used its products to develop their projects. Egyptian-Danish architect Charabi, for instance, relied on a MacBook Pro for sketching and 3D modeling, while Seoul-based designer Lee used an iPad Pro and Apple Pencil to sketch ideas and take notes.

Lee’s New Form sketches (left) and Parafernalia’s MonoAmbiente 1 sketch (right)

Brooklyn-based designer Rower says she used an iPhone to document her creative process and Keynote to experiment with images and text, while the duo behind Mexican design studio Parafernalia said they used the iPhone, iPad Pro, and Procreate to collaborate remotely between Monterrey and Mexico City via FaceTime.

As with Apple’s recent showcase of the “From Earth to Sky” fashion collection, it may be tempting to dismiss the exhibition as a marketing effort. But if you’re into design, it’s always interesting to see how professional designers use the same tools we’re familiar with to come up with such different kinds of creative work.

Update, 4:56 p.m. ET: Apple’s Greg Joswiak shared a post on X featuring a video highlighting the designers’ work:

Different paths. Different crafts. One shared spark.

Check out four emerging designers at Design Miami Paris, each bringing their vision to life with iPhone, iPad Pro, Apple Pencil Pro, and MacBook Pro. pic.twitter.com/pZfMV1Gsf8

title: John Ternus talks his involvement with design teams at Apple
snippet: Last week TIME shared select quotes from a new interview with Apple CEO John Ternus, but today the full video has been published, including a discussion on Ternus’s involvement with Apple’s design teams. more…
fullText:
Last week TIME shared select quotes from a new interview with Apple CEO John Ternus, but today the full video has been published, including a discussion on Ternus’s involvement with Apple’s design teams.

John Ternus says that at Apple ‘design means everything to us’

Ever since John Ternus officially became CEO last month, reporting has indicated that he’s spending lots of his time hands-on with Apple’s design teams.

In a recent interview with TIME, Ternus discusses his new role, the transition, and his current priorities. And design comes up in the conversation.

At one point he’s asked directly: “How involved with design are you still?”

Here’s what Ternus said:

It’s funny because as a product designer—I’m a mechanical engineer by background—the team that the product designers work most closely with are the industrial designers. So, I’ve been working hand in hand with industrial designers at Apple since I started. And it’s an amazing relationship. 

I think what’s so special about this place is design is at the center of it. Design means everything to us. And what’s incredible is our designers, both on the software side and the hardware side, they really understand the engineering. And the engineers have a very deep appreciation for design. And so it’s a really powerful collaboration. It’s not [like] a designer sketches something up and then throws it over the wall and says, “Go make that.” From the very beginning the teams are collaborating, and it’s just a wonderful thing to be a part of.

Without explicitly saying that he’s been especially hands-on with the design teams, Ternus emphasizes that he’s always worked closely with Apple designers, and reiterates how central design is to the company.

title: Older Pixel phones appear to be getting Google’s new 3D emoji
snippet: Google’s redesigned 3D emoji library debuted on the Pixel 11, but might now be slowly appearing on older Pixel devices. more…
fullText:
Google’s redesigned 3D emoji library debuted on the Pixel 11, but might now be slowly appearing on older Pixel devices.

One Pixel 6a user on Reddit shared his new 3D emoji library, noting that his choices switched over from the traditional designs. Given that this is on a Pixel 6a, it signals Google might be slowly switching devices over from 2D to 3D emojis. Only one other commenter shared the same experience, which means the rollout, if it’s actually going live, is very gradual.

Without many other reports, it’s hard to nail down Google’s intended device targets. We know the Pixel 11 is how Google wanted to release the new 3D emoji set, but what comes after has seemed slow. So far, it looks like a majority of devices represented in that thread haven’t received an update. The one user who said they got the new Noto 3D emoji set said they appeared after a Google Play Store update.

Like them or hate them, Google is replacing the standard cartoonish emoji library with 3D designs that closely emulate them on all Pixel devices going forward, starting with Android 17. There are subtle differences across Android’s emoji selection, and they’ll likely take some time getting used to if you’ve been using Android devices for some time.

title: Slow Horses showrunner explains finale shock ending, season 7 trailer debuts
snippet: The Slow Horses season 6 finale is available now, with a shocking ending that is explained by new showrunner Gaby Chiappe in an interview. Plus, Apple has debuted the first trailer for season 7. more…
fullText:
The Slow Horses season 6 finale is available now, with a shocking ending that is explained by new showrunner Gaby Chiappe in an interview. Plus, Apple has debuted the first trailer for season 7.

Here’s what happened in that surprise Slow Horses finale ending, plus the new trailer for season 7

If you haven’t yet watched the Slow Horses season 6 finale, stop reading here.

**major spoilers ahead**

Slow Horses was marked this season by a high number of character deaths.

That continued in the finale that just aired with the death of Emma Flyte at the hands of River’s father, Frank Harkness.

But in the final moments of the episode, there’s another character who seemingly dies too, and in far more shocking fashion: River Cartwright.

It’s not entirely clear what caused the death, though. Here’s the official explanation from head writer and season 6 showrunner Gaby Chiappe (via Gold Derby):

Actually, the groundwork is laid in Episode 2 when Jim and Jane [the assassins played by Kyle Soller and MyAnna Buring] come knocking on the door and River and Sid are hiding. You see Jim looking around and there’s a little bottle lying on the table. He looks around and sees the crowbar that River brought in with him, and we have to assume that he paints it with what’s in the bottle, which — given that there have been nerve agent attacks elsewhere — it’s a Novichok attack.

We had a lot of debate about that. Will people know what it is and what’s happening? It’s taken from the book, but in the book it’s left on a doorknob, which is slightly different. It’s still the idea that something happened in the corner of your eye, but you didn’t quite know what it was. And the assassin who laid it is long dead now.

Though Chiappe doesn’t technically confirm that River is dead, the season 7 trailer certainly suggests that’s what has happened.

fullText:
The iPhone Duo is the biggest change to the iPhone’s form factor in its nearly 20-year history. It combines a compact, notebook-style design with an iPad-like inner display. It might look a little awkward, but that’s for good reason. 

I’ve spent the last week using the iPhone Duo. Here’s everything you need to know about Apple’s first foldable iPhone.
