title: Review: The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is a gut punch in a post-OnePlus world
snippet: OnePlus is dead. The enthusiast-focused brand turned Oppo for the rest of the world was shuttered, ironically only for the rest of the world, earlier this year and its memory loomed large over my past few weeks using the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max. For as great is this phone is, it’s a sad reminder that phones like these are going to be lacking in some parts of the world going forward, and that’s a crying shame. more…
fullText:
OnePlus is dead. The enthusiast-focused brand turned Oppo for the rest of the world was shuttered, ironically only for the rest of the world, earlier this year and its memory loomed large over my past few weeks using the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max. For as great is this phone is, it’s a sad reminder that phones like these are going to be lacking in some parts of the world going forward, and that’s a crying shame.

The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is a beast on paper, though not quite the Find X9 Ultra I fell head over heels for earlier this year. To quickly summarize what you’re getting here (specifically for the EU variant):

6.78-inch AMOLED display (144Hz, LTPO, 3,600 nits peak brightness, 3,840Hz PWM)

MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro

12GB RAM

512GB UFS 4.1

7,150 mAh battery

80W wired/50W wireless charging (no Qi2 magnets)

Ultrasonic fingerprint sensor + camera-based face unlock

Cameras: 200MP main, 200MP 13mm ultrawide, 200MP 70mm (3x optical) telephoto, 50MP front-facing

By basically every measurement, a true flagship. The cameras, as mentioned, aren’t quite at the level of the Find X9 Ultra, but it’s still impressive to see three 200MP sensors on board here.

And those cameras perform very well.

	

Oppo touts killer video from this setup, including 4K/60fps, 4K/120fps, and 8K/30fps from every rear-facing lens, as well as improvements to HDR and stabilization. These can certainly go a long way in creator spaces, and I was impressed at the quality even in more casual use cases. Oppo worked with Instagram, for example, to improve uploads from the Find X10 series and the results speak for themselves.

As per usual, I found myself mostly using the camera here for stills, and I still find myself loving the experience of shooting on an Oppo flagship. Shots are generally crisp and clean, and the app is very easy to use despite all of the options it builds in. Compared to the Ultra I last used, I found myself wishing the telephoto lens had more range, as the 3x optical zoom quickly felt its limits kicking in. Oppo supports up to 120x hybrid zoom, but the quality falls off long before that, and the AI-powered enhancements really struggle to bridge the gap on anything beyond 10x. I wish the company had just used a 5x lens here rather than 3x. Still, most shots I took were excellent, and that 3x lens is the best shooter of the bunch, producing excellent natural bokeh in its shots. The 200MP sensor and Oppo’s software go a long way in ensuring that anything in the 3x-8x range, give or take, comes out at full quality. Not to mention the color processing – it nailed the colors of an absolutely gorgeous sunset I captured a couple of weeks ago. My Pixel would never. 

Adding on Oppo’s 10x teleconverter takes the whole thing up a notch, with levels of natural bokeh that just aren’t achievable on a smartphone otherwise. It’s not as crisp as a “real” camera with the same lens setup, but the results are often stunning.

View full-size samples on Google Photos.

But, outside of the camera, how does the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max hold up?

Frankly, very well. 

The hardware itself is fantastic. I reviewed the “Lumos White” trim which is a tiny bit lighter than others, but it’s still a fairly hefty phone regardless. I don’t mind the weight, though, when a phone is delivering powerful camera hardware. The same goes for the camera bump which pops out of the back quite a ways. I do loathe that Oppo opted for this dual-size camera bump where the main square off to the left is taller than the secondary bump used to house the flash and color-focused camera lens. It results in a phone that rocks back and forth on a table when not in a case, despite such an obvious solution sitting right there. It’s annoying, but I do appreciate other touches here such as the knurling around the camera lens and the splash of orange from the Hasselblad partnership (though the little ridge picks up dust like crazy).

This is where I’ll throw in the mention that I found myself using Oppo’s carbon fiber case throughout my entire review period, not because I felt the phone needed a case, but because this is yet another Android flagship forgoing built-in Qi2 magnets. The excuses are just lame at this point, especially with Oppo pretty heavily investing in magnetic accessories. It’s getting old saying this in every review, but I’m going to keep bringing it up until it becomes the standard it should be.

The frame has power and volume buttons off to the right side and they’re as tactile and satisfying as ever, while a “Snap Key” on the opposite side is a blatant clone of Apple’s Action Button, right down to the UI used to customize it. Still, I appreciate the shortcut and use it for the flashlight/torch, but I wish Oppo would take this up a notch with single-press and double-press actions, rather than limiting it solely to the long-press that Apple uses. While we’re on that topic, I wish Oppo would finally adopt the double-press power button gesture for activating the camera in global markets. This phone has a great camera, but lacking this shortcut is an absolute pain.

The display is gorgeous, as you’d expect from any modern flagship, and the built-in screen protector has held up remarkably well over roughly a month of use. 

As for the software, ColorOS 17 very much leans into the whole Liquid Glass clone trend, and I’m not a fan. But, to Oppo’s credit, you can easily tone down the transparency to get a much more visually pleasing design. That won’t change the Apple copycat looks found throughout system apps, but it makes it a much better experience on the whole.

I’ve always been more of a fan of Pixel UI and even One UI over most Chinese Android skins, but ColorOS has grown on me. Once you get over the initial learning curve, it’s a very user-friendly experience in so many ineffable ways. It’s truly hard to describe why it’s a pleasure to use, but I find myself with fewer complaints. They’re still there, of course – just a couple of quick hitters: Notification icons disappear inconsistently, the lockscreen shows notifications on top of the fingerprint icon which leads to a lot of misclicks, etc – but I find myself overall still feeling comfortable using ColorOS nowadays.

And it runs smooth just as promised. That’s probably in part thanks to Oppo’s continued optimizations, but also the MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro under the hood. The chip also stays cool. I threw everything from high-GPS use, 90°F days to video exports and more at this phone, and it never once warmed up even a little bit. Are we missing out without these MediaTek flagships in the States? Maybe!

Finally, let’s talk battery life.

The silicon-carbon battery here gives the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max a whopping 7,150 mAh battery in the EU, and the endurance rocks. This is not quite a 2-day phone in my testing thus far, but even heavy days won’t kill it. Whether I was running hotspots, editing videos, or playing games, Find X10 Pro Max never ended a day below 30%. I would imagine the 8,000 mAh version found in other regional variants pushes it over the edge of being a 2-day phone, but the point is you’ll be happy with this battery life. And, thanks to speedy SuperVOOC and USB-C PD charging on board, I never found myself needing to plug this phone in overnight. It almost acts like a smartwatch – a quick charge while I’m in the shower and getting ready for the day has been plenty to keep it topped off most of the time.

And after using all of that for a few weeks, I’m just about as sad about the situation surrounding this phone as I have been happy in using it.

The end of OnePlus means that Oppo phones like this one simply aren’t coming Stateside anymore. Of course, OnePlus’ versions were typically diluted compared to Oppo’s anyway (and that’s even true with the OnePlus 16), but it was better than nothing. It’s increasingly frustrating to be losing out on devices like these in the States, because Android brands like Oppo have been massively stepping up on quality in recent years.

Pricing, though, is against this one. In Europe, the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is €1,799. That’s a crazy amount of money for a smartphone that doesn’t fold.

If you live in a region where the Find X10 series is for sale, I think you’ll be thrilled by the Pro Max. The standard Find X10 Pro is not one to sleep on either. It’s a bit smaller despite having the same battery, and the cameras aren’t too far behind. 

					

The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is a complete package, with excellent cameras and battery life, and speedy software.

					

				

Pros

				

											

Triple 200MP cameras

											

Excellent battery life

											

ColorOS is quietly one of the best Android skins

									

			

					

				

Cons

				

											

Smaller battery on EU models

											

No Qi2 magnets

											

Very high pricing

title: Nest’s Halloween doorbell chimes are live now through November 1
snippet: With Halloween just a couple of weeks away, it’s the perfect time to make sure you’re ready for trick-or-treaters. It’s not enough just to buy candy in bulk, of course; you’ll also need to make sure your home feels appropriately spooky, and with Nest’s annual Halloween doorbell chimes now available, the hardest part is already done for you. more…
fullText:
With Halloween just a couple of weeks away, it’s the perfect time to make sure you’re ready for trick-or-treaters. It’s not enough just to buy candy in bulk, of course; you’ll also need to make sure your home feels appropriately spooky, and with Nest’s annual Halloween doorbell chimes now available, the hardest part is already done for you.

Google began rolling out its Halloween-themed doorbell chimes to users yesterday, as spotted by 9to5’s Ben Schoon. This year includes nine different tones to swap between at any time, and thanks to a recent app update from Google, you can preview them without having to ring your own doorbell. As with all of Nest’s seasonal chimes, you’ll find these settings available in the Home app under “Seasonal themes.” You should see a prompt right from the main page in the app.

If you’re looking to make the most of this year’s spooky chimes, though, make sure you set it up as soon as possible. title: Your HomePod has a colorful new party trick: how to enable Sound Glow
snippet: Apple is rolling out a new feature for HomePod mini and the second-gen big HomePod called Sound Glow. This lights up the touch surface of your speaker with colors that reference the album artwork of the currently playing song, perhaps adding some additional ambience to a party vibe. Here’s how to enable the new Sound Glow feature … more…
fullText:
Apple is rolling out a new feature for HomePod mini and the second-gen big HomePod called Sound Glow. This lights up the touch surface of your speaker with colors that reference the album artwork of the currently playing song, perhaps adding some additional ambience to a party vibe.

Here’s how to enable the new Sound Glow feature …

Sound Glow is supported by HomePod mini and HomePod mini 2, and the second-generation HomePod. The original 2018 HomePod is not supported.

	

Sound Glow shows animated ambient light effects based on what’s playing, so you have to be playing music or a podcast with album artwork for it to work. In practice, you see two or three dominant colors from the artwork appear on the illuminated surface. The balls of color bounce around to give a bit of motion.

The output brightness of a HomePod ‘screen’ is not that bright, but if you have the HomePod against a white wall, you can get some visible color cast in a dark room, even if you can’t see the top of the HomePod itself.

How to enable Sound Glow on HomePod

To enable Sound Glow, make sure to update to the latest software version 27.2 (currently in release candidate beta). Then, open the Home app, long-press on your HomePod and scroll down to the settings. There will be a new toggle for Sound Glow. Just enable it to activate and start playing music to see it in action.

You can also enable Sound Glow from the Control Center on an Apple TV, when paired to HomePods. Long-press on the Apple TV remote, scroll across to select the HomePod menu item, and then click to enable or disable Sound Glow. It’s quite handy that it is easily accessible here as that means you can quickly turn it on if you are hosting a party, and easily turn it off for the rest of the year when it might be too distracting.

title: Apple poaches longtime Meta executive to lead global litigation
snippet: Bloomberg reports that Apple has hired Scott Tucker, who spent nearly six years as Meta’s vice president and deputy general counsel for global litigation. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Bloomberg reports that Apple has hired Scott Tucker, who spent nearly six years as Meta’s vice president and deputy general counsel for global litigation. Here are the details.

Apple’s legal team overhaul continues

Earlier this year, Meta’s former chief legal officer Jennifer Newstead joined Apple as its new general counsel, replacing longtime executive Kate Adams.

Newstead’s responsibilities eventually expanded to include government affairs following the retirement of Lisa Jackson, who had previously overseen the division.

The changes brought Apple’s legal and government affairs teams under a single executive, with former CEO Tim Cook, now Apple’s executive chairman, also remaining directly involved in managing the company’s government relations.

As part of the reorganization, Apple also hired former American Airlines executive Nate Gatten as its new vice president of government affairs.

Now, Bloomberg reports that Newstead is bringing in a former colleague from Meta, Scott Tucker, who joined Mark Zuckerberg’s company in 2021 and previously held a senior legal position at Morgan Stanley.

The company has hired Scott Tucker, a longtime deputy general counsel and litigation chief at Meta, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

[…]

Tucker is becoming Apple’s vice president of global litigation and financial services, a newly created position overseeing commercial and patent litigation worldwide, said the people, who asked not to be named because the move isn’t public. He’ll also manage legal matters involving the company’s financial offerings.

The report adds that as a result of Tucker joining the company, Heather Grenier, Apple’s vice president of commercial and competition litigation, will now report to him rather than directly to Newstead. Bloomberg notes, however, that Grenier will retain her position on Newstead’s legal leadership team.

Finally, Bloomberg says Apple is also expanding the responsibilities of longtime legal executive Kyle Andeer, who will now oversee matters involving “international legal matters and functions involving online child safety, cybersecurity and law enforcement.”

title: The COROS Pace 4 is a smartwatch for running and clear reasons to buy over Wear OS
snippet: Acclaimed Japanese marathon champion Suguru Osako’s special edition COROS Pace 4 lasts a whopping 19 days on a single charge, including over 41 hours of real-time GPS tracking. more…
fullText:
Acclaimed Japanese marathon champion Suguru Osako’s special edition COROS Pace 4 lasts a whopping 19 days on a single charge, including over 41 hours of real-time GPS tracking.

If you’re a runner, chances are, you’re already using a COROS smartwatch. But if you’ve been using one for a while, you might want to consider the company’s latest watch, named after acclaimed marathon runner Suguru Osako, which brings a unique style along with the COROS Pace 4’s already top-notch specs.

For the basics, this one packs a 1.2-inch AMOLED display with completely flat glass up top and a 6000-series aluminum alloy casing to keep it protected.

A unique yellow action button adorns the left side, letting you quickly use your voice to start or control a workout, make voice notes, and set reminders. I’ve used the voice notes feature more than once during a run to remind myself of something that happened, usually during a trail run, in my case.

	

The whole package comes in a matte gray-green colorway with a unique, supple silicone band adorned with Osako’s motto, “now or never,” which may just give you the boost you need during a particularly strenuous run.

Like the regular Pace 4, the Suguru Osako edition comes with free workout and training plans, race predictor, virtual pacer, personalized marathon plans, and a lot more in the COROS app.

You can buy it right now at COROS for just $289, making this a surprisingly affordable way to track all the miles you’re about to run to keep warm this winter.

Why choose a COROS Pace 4 over Wear OS?

We certainly love our Wear OS watches for their extraordinary capability and deep integration into Android, but even after years of evolution and innovation, most of them suffer from the same big issue: battery life. Take the Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 on my wrist in the photo above, for example. I took it out for a hike on Saturday and didn’t wear it at all yesterday (Sunday), yet it’s at 7% battery already.

The COROS Pace 4 would still be in the 90-95% range after the same exact scenario, and it’s why I almost never wear Wear OS watches anymore. And I’m definitely not alone here. When I go to my weekly run club, at least half of the folks there use a COROS watch, with the remaining watches typically bearing Garmin or Amazfit branding. Rarely do I see people using Wear OS or Apple Watches there.

There’s also no subscription fee just to get access to your data (or a virtual training coach), as the COROS app has everything built in. So if you’re an athlete that’s sick of your watch being dead every time you want to use it, COROS is the right choice, and that’s just one of many reasons runners love the brand.

title: Jason Sudeikis gives update on Ted Lasso seasons 5 and 6
snippet: Ted Lasso season 4 wrapped up earlier this month, and there’s still no official word on the show’s future. But on a recent podcast appearance, Jason Sudeikis shared a new update on Ted Lasso season 5 and beyond. more…
fullText:
Ted Lasso season 4 wrapped up earlier this month, and there’s still no official word on the show’s future. But on a recent podcast appearance, Jason Sudeikis shared a new update on Ted Lasso season 5 and beyond.

Here’s the current status of Ted Lasso season 5 and beyond

On a new episode of the podcast Talk Easy with Sam Frogoso, Jason Sudeikis discusses his experience returning to Ted Lasso for season 4, and addresses the current status of season 5 and plan for more seasons.

After season 3 concluded, Apple and it seemed the entire cast wanted more Ted Lasso. But repeatedly in interviews, everyone involved deferred to Sudeikis when asked about a potential season 4. The creative leader behind Lasso wasn’t sure if he wanted the show to go on.

This time around, however, things sound different. 

Here’s what Sudeikis said during his podcast appearance about more Ted Lasso seasons:

Sam Frogoso: So what does this all mean for you moving forward? You want to keep going back to the well? Do you have season five and six mapped out? Is that the plan?

Jason Sudeikis: I mean, that was the endeavor of going back into it, just sort of like, oh, I think there’s more in there…We’ll see. It takes a village.

Frogoso: Do you want to do it?

Sudeikis: I would like to, yeah. I think it would be fun.

Frogoso: You’re being mighty coy about whether there’s going to be more seasons of the show.

Sudeikis: Oh, unintentionally.

Frogoso: Do you just not know?

Sudeikis: Yeah, I just don’t know. We haven’t started a writers room or anything like that.

Frogoso: But Apple would do it if, presumably, you want to keep going.

Sudeikis: I would assume so.

Reading between the lines, it sounds like there are some behind-the-scenes negotiations still ongoing regarding additional seasons.

Before season 4 began, reporting indicated Sudeikis had a new three-season arc in mind for the show. That’s what Frogoso refers to in his initial question. And while Sudeikis sounds fully onboard and ready to move forward with his plan for more seasons, clearly something is holding up the show.

	

During its season 4 run, Ted Lasso was consistently the top-viewed show on Apple TV. While it didn’t hit nearly the heights that season 3 enjoyed, it was still very much a hit for the streamer.

If you’re looking for another Apple TV comedy to watch, Small Prophets has been hailed as “the finest show to hit Apple this year.”

title: iPhone Duo orders are delayed into 2027; here are the Android foldables you should try instead
snippet: The iPhone Duo is already delayed for months just hours after pre-orders have opened, leaving those interested in foldables unable to get Apple’s take anytime soon. If you’re seriously interested in a foldable, though, may I interest you in some Android alternatives? more…
fullText:
The iPhone Duo is already delayed for months just hours after pre-orders have opened, leaving those interested in foldables unable to get Apple’s take anytime soon. If you’re seriously interested in a foldable, though, may I interest you in some Android alternatives?

Apple opened up pre-orders for the iPhone Duo earlier today and, as our sister site 9to5Mac points out, delivery dates slipped immediately. The first wave arrives later this month but, within less than an hour, every configuration had been delayed to January 2027 or later. 

Oof.

So, if you really want to try out a foldable, here are some Android alternatives to take a look at.

	

Galaxy Z Fold 8: Same difference

The obvious choice here is Galaxy Z Fold 8, the foldable that’s directly benefiting from the sheer existence of iPhone Duo. And that’s largely because the comparisons are obvious. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 shares nearly the same form factor as the iPhone Duo with its short and wide outer display, and its wide inner display. It also has virtually no display create, an anti-reflective display (admittedly much less aggressive than Apple’s), and the same basic camera setup.

Review: The Galaxy Z Fold 8’s new shape isn’t for you – it’s for everyone

It’s more or less the same phone, just not made by Apple. That does mean you’re losing out on some of Apple’s integrations, but the Galaxy Z Fold 8 does support iMessage-like texting over RCS, as well as AirDrop support with MacBooks, iPad, and other iPhones. 

And it’s cheaper, too.

Galaxy Z Fold 8 starts $100 less than the iPhone Duo at $1,899, but it’s frequently on sale and easier to find around $1,600-1,700 at any given time.

Samsung.com

Best Buy

Amazon

Motorola Razr Fold: For the stylus and battery

If you don’t want Apple’s exact form factor, the Motorola Razr Fold is an underrated option. Starting at $1,899, it has a typical smartphone display on the outside and a square-ish inner display. That bigger canvas is still useful for multitasking and media just like the Duo, just in a different shape.

Motorola Razr Fold Review: Shockingly great

The benefit of Razr Fold is that you get a way bigger battery than anything Samsung is offering, as well as stylus support on both displays. They’re both big reasons to go for Motorola’s foldable.

Motorola.com

Best Buy

Oppo Find N6: If you can get it

If you can get it, and that’s a big “if,” the Oppo Find N6 is absolutely worthy of consideration.

Like the Motorola Razr Fold, it has a huge battery and stylus support, but with stronger cameras and a thinner design, as well as one of the best display creases in the business. The software, especially following the latest ColorOS update, will also feel very iPhone-like.

But, in the US, it’s almost impossible to get it.

The Oppo Find N6 is the best foldable you can’t buy, again

Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra: The standard for a reason

Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra isn’t the “new” option, but it’s still a great one. A thin chassis, all of the camera lenses you’d want, and a bigger battery than past generations while checking every box in terms of hardware and software features.

Review: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra ticks every box, but it’s the boring option now

Not exciting, but excellent. And heavily discounted quite frequently. You can get a Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra for around $1,899 pretty easily, around $200 off its usual price, and it’s well worth your consideration.

Samsung.com

Best Buy

Amazon

Honorable mention: Pixel 11 Pro Fold

Google’s Pixel series is one of the standouts in the industry because it’s not just copying Apple’s playbook. And, if you’re going to switch away from iPhone, this might be the best place to go. Between clean and stable implementations of cross-platform features like RCS, AirDrop over Quick Share, and more, the Pixel is very much the best choice in terms of experience alone.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold, however, lags behind in the overall foldable space. It’s a perfectly fine foldable that’s still thinner than Apple’s, but it also lacks the polish of Samsung’s foldables. 

Review: Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold just barely keeps up

It’s fourth-best, but that’s still “last” for the time being. You’ll be happy with it, just don’t expect anything crazy.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 is excellent, but I find myself missing this one software feature
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 has been a marvel of an upgrade, at least for me. I’ve written about it WHOOP. That said, in my past month testing it, there’s one WHOOP feature I’ve found myself missing. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 has been a marvel of an upgrade, at least for me. I’ve written about it many times, and personally – I have found that the Apple Watch Series 12 is a competent replacement for the WHOOP. That said, in my past month testing it, there’s one WHOOP feature I’ve found myself missing.

Yes, I know – the Series 12 is old news, and there are much cooler things to think about, like iPhone Duo and HomeView. That said, the Apple Watch Series 12 was quite charming to me, primarily because it felt like a little bit of a surprise.

We knew we’d be getting an always-on heart rate monitor, and we knew Apple was working on a new Health app, though we didn’t know when it would ship. Seeing the two together actually felt like quite a novel launch. That’s besides the point, though. Let’s talk about the redesigned Health app and what I feel it’s missing.

New Health app

Frankly, Apple did a lot really well here. For one, there’s the fact that the interface actually feels easy to read and navigate. On top of that, the new features like Readiness and Health Age make it feel like a much more meaningful app. Plus, existing features like Vitals and Sleep being integrated means I’ll actually go look at it daily.

This Health app isn’t shipping yet. It was available in iOS 27.2 for a little while, but has since been removed. Apple says it’ll come back in a later iOS beta prior to releasing it later this year. In all likelihood, this means iOS 27.3, which should enter beta before the end of the month and ship before the end of December.

What I’d like to see

For me, and this is more of a small personal preference than a true flaw with the app or how it’s designed, I’d really like to see Apple copy WHOOP’s approach to measuring days: sleep.

With WHOOP, your days aren’t measured on a fixed 24 hour clock, they’re based on when you go to sleep. That means if you do a workout past midnight, it still counts for the existing day. Or, if you were out late at night, your walk home counts towards the day that you started on, rather than counting towards the next day. I personally prefer this concept of tracking fitness goals.

Of course, it could be an option, though I do think fixing peoples “days” to their sleep is a little more sensible than basing it on a normal clock, especially when it comes to tracking exercise.

title: iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: Here’s every key difference
snippet: Apple has strong pitches for all of its flagship iPhones this fall, but which model is right for you? Here’s an overview of the key differences between iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro. more…
fullText:
Apple has strong pitches for all of its flagship iPhones this fall, but which model is right for you? Here’s an overview of the key differences between iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro.

Form factor and dimensions: Foldable vs traditional

It’s the most obvious difference, but should be stated regardless. With iPhone Duo you get a very different form factor: it’s a foldable device. With iPhone 18 Pro, you get a traditional iPhone experience.

If you’ve never used a foldable, it’s hard to explain the difference in how each model might feel in practice. But generally speaking, with iPhone Duo you get essentially an iPhone and iPad in one device. The displays are unique shapes and sizes compared to a traditional iPhone though, which may take some adjustment.

Here is how each model’s dimensions compare:

iPhone Duo might seem more sleek than iPhone 18 Pro Max, but it ultimately weighs slightly more.

Displays: Dual vs single in varying sizes

iPhone Duo has two displays: a 5.4-inch outer display and a 7.6-inch folding display.

With iPhone 18 Pro, you can choose from the standard 6.3-inch size or 6.9-inch Pro Max model.

So with the Duo, you can enjoy a “small iPhone” experience while also having the option of a larger inner screen than what iPhone 18 Pro Max offers.

iPhone Duo’s folding display also comes with a nano-texture finish, a first in an iPhone.

Cameras: Clear advantage for iPhone 18 Pro

Cameras are one of the most important iPhone features. And in this department, iPhone 18 Pro is the clear winner.

iPhone 18 Pro has the new 48MP Main camera with variable aperture. iPhone Duo lacks the variable aperture feature, so its Main camera lags behind the Pro line.

With iPhone 18 Pro, you also get the Telephoto camera that’s missing from iPhone Duo.

In terms of software features, each model has its own unique exclusives:

iPhone Duo: Smart Take, Kid Cue, Duo Preview

iPhone 18 Pro: Smart focus tracking, Pro controls, Apple Reference Image

iPhone 18 Pro also exclusively supports ProRes video recording up to 4K at 60 fps with external recording, a “studio-quality four-mic array,” Spatial video recording at 1080p at 30 fps, Spatial photos, ProRes RAW, Genlock, and more.

Battery: Excellent battery life on all models

Because iPhone Duo has two displays, its quoted battery life varies depending on which display you’re using. But overall, Apple is promising strong battery life on both the Duo as well as iPhone 18 Pro.

Here are Apple’s quoted numbers:

iPhone Duo outer display: Up to 44 hours

iPhone Duo folding display: Up to 31 hours

iPhone 18 Pro: Up to 36 hours

iPhone 18 Pro Max: Up to 45 hours

Everyone’s use patterns will differ, but if you split the difference between the two iPhone Duo battery estimates, you’re looking at around 38 hours in average video playback.

All the other big and small differences: Face ID, buttons, software, Apple Pencil, more

Authentication differs between iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, with the former using Touch ID and the latter Face ID.

iPhone Duo does not have an Action button, but does offer Camera Control.

iPhone Duo comes with several multitasking advantages in iOS 27, like the ability to use apps in Split View and have unique landscape views. It also has other fun software additions like a partially-folded StandBy mode.

Apple Pencil (USB-C model) will be supported on iPhone Duo later this year, another advantage over iPhone 18 Pro.

A new C2 modem is included in both iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, but iPhone 18 Pro Max uses a Qualcomm modem.

Colors for iPhone 18 Pro are Burgundy, Glacier, Black, and Silver. iPhone Duo only offers two colors: Star White and Night Sky.

Finally, design materials differ: iPhone 18 Pro has an aluminum unibody design, while iPhone Duo uses titanium.

Pricing and availability: Big gaps in both

Pricing is another major difference between Apple’s new models. Here are starting prices for 256GB models:

iPhone Duo: $1,999

iPhone 18 Pro: $1,199

iPhone 18 Pro Max: $1,299

iPhone 18 Pro has been available for nearly a month, while iPhone Duo pre-orders just went live today. However, if you haven’t ordered one yet, shipping estimates are already delayed into 2027. So if you need a new iPhone sooner, iPhone 18 Pro is the way to go.

title: Spotify podcast memberships let you support your favorite shows and get added perks
snippet: Spotify may not be a dedicated podcast platform, but it is launching a big new feature in podcast memberships that let you support your favorite shows in exchange for added perks. more…
fullText:
Spotify may not be a dedicated podcast platform, but it is launching a big new feature in podcast memberships that let you support your favorite shows in exchange for added perks.

Available starting today, Spotify podcast memberships work similarly to Patreon and other membership programs. Hosts can create support tiers with a monthly fee that deliver perks to their audience and, in turn, support the show. 

Spotify says examples of what creators can provide in these memberships include “exclusive audio or video, bonus episodes, fewer ads, early access, access to a show’s archive” and more. Multiple tiers can be created and pricing is customizable. 

Shows launching membership programs today include The Adam Friedland Show, Making Sense with Sam Harris, The Shawn Ryan Show, The Sculpt Society, Two Hot Takes, and 12 shows across the YMH Studios network.

	

Creators keep 90% of the revenue generated by memberships.

Spotify podcast memberships are available in Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hong Kong, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Singapore, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the UK, and the US to start.

title: Apple announces special event for October 28: ‘Pro and tell’
snippet: Apple today announced its second experience of the month, taking place next Wednesday, October 28 at 10 a.m. PT. The tagline for this event is: “Pro and tell.” Here’s what to expect. more…
fullText:
Apple today announced its second experience of the month, taking place next Wednesday, October 28 at 10 a.m. PT. The tagline for this event is: “Pro and tell.” Here’s what to expect.

This marks Apple’s second event of the month, following the “Welcome home” product launch on October 13 in New York City. That event included the debut of the new HomeView smart display, the HomePod mini 2, and a new Apple TV 4K.

Apple’s October 28 event will take place in Los Angeles. You can see the invite artwork above, which was sent to members of the press and posted on social media by Greg Joswiak.

Rumors say Apple has a slew of new products to announce at its next event, headlined by its first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen and OLED. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, here’s what’s on the docket:

New 14-inch and 16-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro models with OLED displays. They will also have a Dynamic Island for the first time and will be “significantly lighter” than the current models. The new MacBook Pro models are expected to be powered by the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

A revamped iPad mini with an OLED screen, a “revamped speaker system,” and a relocated FaceTime camera

New iMac and entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro models powered by the M6 chip, which will “look like their current versions.”

What are you most excited to see at Apple’s October 28 event? Are you planning to buy anything? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Moto Tag 2 is no longer $19.99 as the UWB tracker gears up for Pixel Tag competition
snippet: The Moto Tag 2 was always supposed to be $30, but a long-running introductory discount left the Find Hub tracker cheaper. Now, that deal has ended. more…
fullText:
The Moto Tag 2 was always supposed to be $30, but a long-running introductory discount left the Find Hub tracker cheaper. Now, that deal has ended.

Moto Tag 2 is inarguably the most capable tracker for Android’s Find Hub network thanks in no small part to its inclusion of UWB. On top of Bluetooth pings for general location, the tracker also lets you pinpoint its exact location when you get up close.

That’s why its $20 introductory price was so attractive.

The discount brought its price below virtually every other Android Find Hub tracker on the market despite the added hardware. But that price has now vanished from both Motorola’s website and from Amazon, where Moto Tag 2 is now sold for $29.99. A 4-pack costs $100, but Amazon is still selling it for less.

	

Moto Tag 2 at Motorola.com

Moto Tag 2 at Amazon

Moto Tag 2 (4-pack) at Amazon

It’s still a good value at that price – especially the 4-pack deal at Amazon – but the $10 hike certainly stings for anyone who waiting too long to score the initial price point. Even at $30, though, Moto Tag 2 remains a great value. Comparable trackers from Pebblebee and Chipolo are sold for $35 or even $40, and those don’t even have UWB. You will still need some sort of add-on if you want to mount the Moto Tag 2 to a keychain or backpack, though, as the AirTag-like form factor lacks any built-in mounting points.

Meanwhile, there’s finally another UWB tracker on the horizon in Google’s Pixel Tag. The oblong tracker was announced back in August and is set to go on sale for the same $29.99 as the Moto Tag 2 was always supposed to sell for. It’s entirely possible that Motorola will drop that price again by the time Google launches its option, but these two are currently set to battle at the same price point.
